The trees, stripped bare, stood like specters against the gray sky.  Strange forms, vaguely human, lay half-buried in the mire, their faces obscured by the mud.  He prodded the soggy ground with his boot, and it shuddered beneath his weight, a living thing, a beast of the earth.  The wind whispered through the reeds, a mournful sound, and the trees swayed and creaked, their branches clashing like bones.He turned back, the path ahead too treacherous, too unreal.  And there, on the road, he saw a blind man, tapping his way along with a cane, a strange serenity on his face.  The man smiled, a smile that held no malice, no despair, just a quiet acceptance of his fate.  Did he know where he was going? Had anyone told him that the road led nowhere, that the world had ended?He watched the blind man disappear into the distance, a figure of futility in a futile world.  The road stretched on, a path to oblivion, and the wind howled, a lament for the living and the dead.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: He walked down the empty road. There was nothing there but charred remnants of trees now quivering in a sullen breeze. The land, like Holme, was ash-strewn and barren. It was all black and gray and there was nothing else. Further along he passed into a swamp made up of naked trees and other dimly hominoid forms that moved too slowly and caught their breath at each others' fingerlike edges. Holme tested the swampy mire. It spat at him then sucked his foot deeper as the wind picked up through the clashing trees, through their cavernous notchhole mouths. He took a step back. Retracing his steps Holme came across a blind man on the once-empty road, tapping his way along with a surprising calm. His step was sure. The blind man acknowledged him with a smile, though Holme was standing still and had offered no greeting. The man’s shirt was stained rust red. Has anyone told him? The irony was dark and clean. Empty too as was everything else. He was tapping his cane on to nowhere. Holme let pass this sign of life on a futile journey. Was it better to know? No, a gift to be unseeing. There is nothing to see. I have been ruined by all the nothing. Holme turned away from the blind man and pulled his jacket close to him. Behind, where Holme was heading, the sky had already blackened.

written_by_MFA018.Excerpt1: Wendy gasped as she stumbled up the stairs, holding onto the railing with one hand. Each step sent a sharp pain through her side. She would’ve liked nothing better than to take a short rest but Jack’s voice behind her kept her going. “Wendy,” he slurred, grinning through bloody teeth, “come back here, sweetheart, so I can crush your bones like garlic cloves, what do you say?” She imagined feeling a gust of wind from the swing of Jack’s mallet behind her. At least the thundering of her pulse dulled the pain in her side. She turned corner after corner. Her feet barely touched the steps. The stairs seemed to stretch on endlessly. Finally, she reached the landing. She thought she had a second to breathe, when suddenly, a man—or something similar to a man— burst from a door. He wore a green ghoul mask and his suit reeked of mildew. Blowing a party favor that flapped in the air like a severed tongue, he shrieked, “Party time!” Wendy screamed and not knowing where else to go, stumbled backwards. The man vanished as abruptly as he’d appeared, slamming the door behind him. Wendy’s chest heaved. She collapsed to the floor. Her eyes felt heavy, but she told herself to stay awake, to just stay awake. Beneath her trembling fingers, the carpet seemed to writhe, its pattern shifting back and forth. She heard a ‘ding’ from the elevator. Jack’s footsteps followed. The mallet whistled past her shoulder, but Jack’s momentum betrayed him as he crashed to the floor. Blood splattered in jagged streaks across the still shifting carpet. This was her moment. If not now, then when? Wendy got up, staggered, pain exploding in her side, and started running. Every step felt slow and heavy, as though she moved through quicksand. She imagined Jack rising behind her, unstoppable, coming closer by the second. She glanced back once, only once, before running headlong into the dark corridor.
written_by_MFA018.Excerpt2: Wendy’s breath hitched in her throat, a sob trapped in the cage of her ribs. Pain splintered through her side, a white-hot fire that threatened to consume her. But Jack was coming. She could hear his ragged breathing, the scrape of his workboots on the stairs, each footfall a hammer blow against her terror.He was grinning, she knew, a rictus of madness splitting his face, blood trickling from the corner of his mouth like a macabre smear of lipstick. The roque mallet, clutched in his fist, was an obscene promise of violence. “Wendy, my dear,” he’d croaked, the words thick with menace, “time for your medicine.”She scrambled to her feet, the pain a living thing in her side, a clawing beast that wanted to drag her down. But she couldn’t stop, not now. The corridor stretched before her, an endless tunnel of shadows and dread. A door flew open, and a man in a green ghoul mask lurched out, bellowing, “Party time!” He thrust a plastic horn at her, confetti raining down like grotesque snowflakes. Then he was gone, the door slamming shut behind him, leaving her in the echoing silence.The elevator whirred, the cables groaning like a tortured beast. Jack was still coming. She stumbled, her legs leaden, the carpet a treacherous bog beneath her feet. He was close now, she could feel the heat of his rage, smell the stale beer on his breath. The mallet whistled through the air, a whisper of death that grazed her shoulder. He lurched forward, off balance, and crashed to the floor with a sickening thud. Blood bloomed on the carpet, a crimson flower against the sickly green.He lay there, a broken doll, the mallet clattering away like a discarded toy. A moment of respite, a stolen breath in the suffocating darkness. But the elevator was moving again, its gears grinding like the teeth of a hungry monster. He would be back. He would always be back.
written_by_MFA018.Reason: Excerpt one feels like it has the same voice and style of the original excerpt because of the more active voice. Excerpt one has more sentences that follow the structure and flow of the original excerpt and has more of the 'she did this' type of structure compared to excerpt two.
written_by_MFA018.Original: Wendy risked another glance over her shoulder. Jack was on the sixth riser, clinging to the banister much as she was doing herself. He was still grinning, and dark blood oozed slowly through the grin and slipped down the line of his jaw. He bared his teeth at her.“I’m going to bash your brains in. Bash them right the fuck in.” He struggled up another riser.Panic spurred her, and the ache in her side diminished a little. She pulled herself up as fast as she could regardless of the pain, yanking convulsively at the banister. She reached the top and threw a glance behind her.He seemed to be gaining strength rather than losing it. He was only four risers from the top, measuring the distance with the roque mallet in his left hand as he pulled himself up with his right.“Right behind you,” he panted through his bloody grin, as if reading her mind. “Right behind you now, bitch. With your medicine.” She fled stumblingly down the main corridor, hands pressed to her side.The door to one of the rooms jerked open and a man with a green ghoulmask on popped out. “Great party, isn’t it?” he screamed into her face, and pulled the waxed string of a party favor. There was an echoing bang and suddenly crepe streamers were drifting all around her. The man in the ghoulmask cackled and slammed back into his room. She fell forward onto the carpet, full-length. Her right side seemed to explode with pain, and she fought off the blackness of unconsciousness desperately. Dimly she could hear the elevator running again, and beneath her splayed fingers she could see that the carpet pattern appeared to move, swaying and twining sinuously.The mallet slammed down behind her and she threw herself forward, sobbing. Over her shoulder she saw Jack stumble forward, overbalance, and bring the mallet down just before he crashed to the carpet, expelling a bright splash of blood onto the nap.

written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: Wendy’s breath came in ragged gasps, the sharp pain in her side like a splintered knife twisting deeper with each step. Behind her—too close, Christ, too close—came the whisper-thump of Jack's feet, a sound she'd once found comforting during their late-night kitchen raids but now sent ice-water terror coursing through her veins. His laughter floated up, thick and wet with blood, a madman's carousel music. "Honey, come back! I just want to bash your brains in!" The roque mallet whooshed through the air, stirring her hair like a lover's caress. written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: There came a point in my life when I seemed to have to "prove" my Blackness, despite my inherent identity as a Black man. As a result, I joined the Black Panther Party in college. I needed some validation that I was, indeed, who I appeared to be, not only on the outside but on the inside as well. Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). This applied not only to my physical appearance and manner of speech but also extended to my intellect and my books.My most recent manuscript was denied by every major publisher. From a reviewer: "While somewhat compelling and an interesting take on the retelling of Aeschylus, we just don't see how it relates to the Black experience." Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. What we're seeking are the true, gritty stories of Black life—write that, then give me a call."I told him, "My stories are Black stories." And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer? The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. I saw its real-world consequences: police brutality, discrimination, violence. I didn't know if that meant I was supposed to take part in any of it.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: The Black Panther Party, a whirlwind of raised fists and righteous fury, had been my crucible. I'd joined partly to prove a point, to silence the whispers that trailed me like a shadow. "Not Black enough," they hissed, both Black and white voices mingling in a chorus of disapproval. My crime? Muttering "Egads" during a heated basketball game, perhaps. Or maybe it was my novels, those unruly beasts that dared to explore the retelling of Aeschylus, drawing accusations of elitism and worse, cultural betrayal. One particularly scathing review declared, "His Aeschylus is a betrayal of his Black heritage, a misguided attempt to elevate himself above his roots." The New York literary party, a swirling vortex of ambition and pretense, was no different. A literary agent, her eyes scanning the room for the next big thing, dismissed my work with a wave of her hand. "Forget Aeschylus," she scoffed, "write true, gritty real stories of Black life. That's what sells." I wanted to retort, "My life, my experience, isn't that Black enough for you?" But the words caught in my throat, choked by the weight of expectation. The agent, sensing my hesitation, moved on, her attention snagged by a performance artist reciting a monologue about the Black experience. The irony was thick enough to cut with a knife.  Later, nursing a drink and a bruised ego, I found myself staring out at the city lights, their glittering expanse a stark contrast to the darkness within. Race, that insidious construct, was a ghost I couldn't shake. I didn't believe in it, rarely dwelled on it, except when guilt gnawed at my conscience. Yet, I couldn't deny its power, its ability to shape lives, to inflict violence, to perpetuate discrimination. The world saw me as Black, and that perception carried a weight I couldn't ignore. As the night wore on, the party's revelry faded into a distant hum. I was left with my thoughts, my identity a tangled knot of contradictions. Was I Black enough? Was my experience valid? The questions swirled, unanswered, unresolved. But in the quiet solitude of that late hour, I found a strange solace. My journey, my struggle, was uniquely my own. And that, I realized, was enough.

The writer uses a combination of literary references ('Aeschylus') to impress upon the reader his educational credentials, combined with somewhat visceral imagery ('thick enough to cut with a knife,' ' Guilt gnawed at my conscience') to suggest and 'prove' his 'blackness' and commitment to anti-intellectual expression.
written_by_MFA015.Original: While in college I was a member of the Black Panther Party, defunct as it was, mainly because I felt I had to prove I was black enough. Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing. I have heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused and, on a couple of occasions, on a basketball court when upon missing a shot I muttered Egads. From a reviewer: "The novel is finely crafted, with fully developed characters, rich language and subtle play with the plot, but one is lost to understand what this reworking of Aeschylus’ The Persians has to do with the African American experience.".One night at a party in New York, one of the tedious affairs where people who write mingle with people who want to write and with people who can help either group begin or continue to write, a tall, thin, rather ugly book agent told me that I could sell many books if I’d forget about writing retellings of Euripides and parodies of French poststructuralists and settle down to write the true, gritty real stories of black life. I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one. He left me to chat with an on-the-rise performance artist/novelist who had recently posed for seventeen straight hours in front of the governor’s mansion as a lawn jockey. He familiarly flipped one of her braided extensions and tossed a thumb back in my direction.The hard, gritty truth of the matter is that I hardly ever think about race. Those times when I did think about it a lot I did so because of my guilt for not thinking about it. I don’t believe in race. I believe there are people who will shoot me or hang me or cheat me and try to stop me because they do believe in race, because of my brown skin, curly hair, wide nose and slave ancestors. But that’s just the way it is.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: As a college freshman, I joined the Black Panther Party. I didn't quite fit in; I didn't wear my beret tilted just right, didn't raise my fist with enough fury, didn't speak with the necessary cadence that marked the truly radical. I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. White classmates with their predictable condescension said I was "articulate," while Black peers muttered under their breaths, "Not Black enough." A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. My first novel was a retelling of Aeschylus—a reviewer described it as “a charming but ill-advised venture into the Greeks, woefully devoid of authentic Black experience.” I reread the critique three times, marveling at how one could misinterpret authenticity as a monolith.Years later, I stood in a dim Manhattan loft at a literary party where the wine was as dry as the wit was acidic. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Write something real. Something gritty, raw, Black life in the streets. That’s what sells.” He patted my shoulder, as though certifying my potential to commodify my identity, then floated off to fawn over a performance artist wearing a gown made of egg cartons.I sipped my wine, the bitterness cutting through my amusement. The transactional nature of the room was suffocating, the smiles wide but hollow, the handshakes quick but calculating. Authenticity, here, was a currency as fleeting as the trends that shaped it. I thought of race—the way it sat heavy on me when others decided it should, the way I refused to believe in it except when guilt or societal violence forced it into my consciousness. Guilt for what? For not being Black enough? For being too Black? It was endless. I walked to the window, feeling the cold glass against my palm, and let the city’s hum drown out the noise of the room. “Authenticity,” I whispered, watching my breath fog the glass, “is just another mask they want me to wear.”

I muttered "Egads" during basketball games, to the collective horror of my teammates, who were often split between exasperation and bemusement. A professor once called me “fascinatingly displaced,” as though I were a museum artifact. This dislocation seeped into my writing. A literary agent in a glinting blazer cornered me by the hors d’oeuvres, leaned in conspiratorially, and said, “Listen, you’ve got talent, but all this Greek tragedy nonsense—leave it behind. Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing. I have heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused and, on a couple of occasions, on a basketball court when upon missing a shot I muttered Egads. From a reviewer: "The novel is finely crafted, with fully developed characters, rich language and subtle play with the plot, but one is lost to understand what this reworking of Aeschylus’ The Persians has to do with the African American experience.".One night at a party in New York, one of the tedious affairs where people who write mingle with people who want to write and with people who can help either group begin or continue to write, a tall, thin, rather ugly book agent told me that I could sell many books if I’d forget about writing retellings of Euripides and parodies of French poststructuralists and settle down to write the true, gritty real stories of black life. I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one. He left me to chat with an on-the-rise performance artist/novelist who had recently posed for seventeen straight hours in front of the governor’s mansion as a lawn jockey. He familiarly flipped one of her braided extensions and tossed a thumb back in my direction.The hard, gritty truth of the matter is that I hardly ever think about race. Those times when I did think about it a lot I did so because of my guilt for not thinking about it. I don’t believe in race. I believe there are people who will shoot me or hang me or cheat me and try to stop me because they do believe in race, because of my brown skin, curly hair, wide nose and slave ancestors. But that’s just the way it is.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. The Panthers, to their credit, were more amused than offended by my professorial affectations, though one member did suggest I try saying "damn" instead. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. Yet its consequences were undeniably real, manifesting in broken bodies and broken dreams, in rejection letters suggesting my characters weren't "relatable enough" to my own people. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: I joined the Black Panthers in college, not out of revolutionary fervor but from a peculiar need to authenticate my Blackness, as if membership cards and raised fists could offset my tendency to mutter "Egads" during pickup basketball games. The Panthers, to their credit, were more amused than offended by my professorial affectations, though one member did suggest I try saying "damn" instead. My novels drew similar bewilderment – a reviewer once wrote, "While technically accomplished, his adaptation of Aeschylus' Oresteia to a housing project seems more interested in postmodern discourse than authentic Black experience." As if authenticity came with a manual, complete with approved vocabularies and prescribed narratives. At a Manhattan literary soirée, between sips of overpriced wine and precisely cubed cheese, a literary agent cornered me with the air of someone about to dispense life-changing wisdom. "Look," she said, adjusting her horn-rimmed glasses with manicured precision, "nobody wants to read about Black people discussing Aristotelian ethics. Write something real, something gritty. Give me projects and pimps, give me struggle." She might as well have asked me to perform a soft-shoe routine. The irony of being told my Black experience wasn't Black enough by someone whose closest connection to the culture was probably watching "The Wire" wasn't lost on me. I watched her glide away to fawn over a performance artist who'd painted himself in crude oil to protest environmental racism – now there was some authentic Blackness she could sell. Standing alone by the cheese plate, I contemplated how race was like quantum mechanics: a construct I didn't believe in but couldn't ignore, something that only seemed to materialize when observed or when guilt compelled me to notice it. The violence of these expectations was subtle but persistent, like water wearing away stone, and I found myself wondering if authenticity was just another mask we wore to please the observers of our particles, another performance in the endless theater of racial identity where even our silences were scripted and our rebellions came with stage directions. I smiled at my reflection in the wine glass, watching it distort and fragment like truth itself.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Marianne sits on the worn leather couch, her fingers absently tracing the cracked armrest while Connell stands by the window, his reflection fragmenting in the rain-spotted glass. The conversation hangs between them like something delicate and inevitable, the kind of moment that will later be dissected in therapy sessions or late-night emails. "I wouldn't have any of this without you," he says, and Marianne notices how he gestures vaguely at nothing in particular, at everything, at the literary magazines on the coffee table, at his MacBook with half-finished submissions to publishing houses. She thinks about how they've grown together, feeding off each other's neuroses and ambitions like some sort of symbiotic organism, each taking what they needed and giving what they could. The irony doesn't escape her - that their relationship, which started in whispered conversations in empty school corridors, had somehow shaped them into people who could write about love and loss in ways that made strangers feel seen. A notification lights up her phone: an email from her agent, or maybe just Deliveroo. She doesn't check. Instead, she watches Connell's hands, remembering how they used to nervously adjust his collar during their first readings together at literary festivals. Now they're steady as he explains why he has to leave, using words like 'growth' and 'space' that sound like they've been borrowed from a self-help podcast. The truth is, she's not the same person who needed his validation to feel real anymore. That girl, who used to check his online status compulsively and craft clever responses to his texts, seems like a character in someone else's story now. People change each other, she thinks, that's just what they do, like weather systems colliding and creating something new. She doesn't say this out loud. Instead, she says, "Okay," and watches his reflection blur further in the glass.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.
written_by_MFA008.Reason: I feel excerpt B is more similar to the original text. I think this is because of the short sentence structure in both pieces. The short and direct thoughts convey the introspection and intimacy of the scene described. written_by_MFA008.Original: That's ridiculous, he says. I'm not going to New York without you. I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for you.It's true, she thinks, he wouldn’t be. He would be somewhere else entirely, living a different kind of life. He would be different with women even, and his aspirations for love would be different. And Marianne herself, she would be another person completely. Would she ever have been happy? And what kind of happiness might it have been? All these years they've been like two little plants sharing the same plot of soil, growing around one another, contorting to make room, taking certain unlikely positions. But in the end she has done something for him, she’s made a new life possible, and she can always feel good about that. I'd miss you too much, he says. I’d be sick, honestly. At first. But it would get better. They sit in silence now, Marianne moving the brush methodically through her hair, feeling for knots and slowly, patiently untangling them. There's no point in being impatient anymore. You know I love you, says Connell. I'm never going to feel the same way for someone else. She nods, okay. He's telling the truth. To be honest, I don’t know what to do, he says. Say you want me to stay and I will. She closes her eyes. He probably won’t come back, she thinks. Or he will, differently. What they have now they can never have back again. But for her the pain of loneliness will be nothing to the pain that she used to feel, of being unworthy. He brought her goodness like a gift and now it belongs to her. Meanwhile his life opens out before him in all directions at once. They’ve done a lot of good for each other. Really, she thinks, really. People can really change one another.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: The Manhattan skyline at night is, for me, an argument against the concept of singularity, not merely because it’s the result of innumerable hands and minds, bundled debts, and traces of antidepressants in the water but because the multiplicity of its forms evokes a sublimity alien to natural landscapes. Standing there, breathing in air tinged with blossoms or exhaust fumes, my gaze skips between the architectural vastness and the tiny illuminated windows, each a human-scale element folded into a collective fabric that feels, somehow, alive. The skyline is not a skyline; it is a second person plural, an as-yet-unrealized "we" that all art addresses, even the most intimate. This thought emerges less like revelation than residue, clinging stubbornly to my attempts to organize experience into some semblance of narrative. The more I reflect on the idea of this "we," the more it unravels into the sublime traffic of urban life—the shifting weather patterns mirrored in high-rise glass, the ebb and flow of bundled debts that keep the city afloat, and the anonymous networks of pipes, trains, and storm drains humming just below the surface.It is in this interwoven complexity that I find my vocation as an artist, not to produce artifacts but to transform what I’ve termed “bad forms of collectivity” into fleeting glimpses of unity—never full, never final, but enough to sustain a flicker of hope for a communal body. In this endeavor, Noor—or, perhaps, the fiction of Noor—becomes a locus, a gravitational pull around which my fragmented thoughts and projects reorganize themselves. Noor is not Noor; they are the shorthand for an idea, an abstraction that reminds me how little of myself is mine, how often I am alien to my own being. And yet, in that discomfort, that acknowledgment of not being fully identical with oneself, there lies the faint shimmer of possibility—a utopian flicker in which past and present collapse into a unified whole, not resolved but reinterpreted.I am, however, just a body on a bench at midnight, my bandanna flattening my hair, my hands sticky with the juice of unsulfured mango as I project myself into futures too many to count. A mild lacrimal event—a phrase borrowed, revised—wets my cheek. written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Standing before Manhattan's impossible geometry at midnight, I felt arrested not by anything in the natural world—I had long since ceased to find redemption in sunsets or mountain ranges—but by the peculiar dialogue between scales, how the tiny illuminated windows punctuated the massive edifices, creating a syntax of light I could almost read. The skyline manifested what I'd come to think of as the second person plural, the collective "you" to which all art, even the most intimate, must ultimately be addressed. I thought about the bundled debt floating above us, the antidepressants cycling through the water system, the neural network of traffic patterns, all these bad forms of collectivity that somehow contained within them the kernel of their transformation. When Noor appeared in my mind, as she inevitably did, the fiction of the world reorganized itself around her presence—not Noor as an individual exactly, but Noor as a figure for my own dissolving sense of self, my growing awareness that I wasn't identical with myself, which was both terrifying and, paradoxically, hopeful. The city seemed to pulse with the possibility of a communal body yet to emerge, one that would transform these alienated moments into components of a shared experience, a new kind of "we" that would retroactively justify my conviction that art could still matter, could still gesture toward utopia. The warm spring air carried traces of cherry blossoms from somewhere distant, maybe Brooklyn, and I found myself contemplating how each illuminated window represented a story, a fragment of the collective consciousness I was simultaneously part of and alienated from. I sat there on the bench, my hair flattened against my skull by a bandanna, working through an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, its sweetness almost medicinal on my tongue, as a mild lacrimal event began. I watched the clouds pass between me and the fluorescent towers, feeling time curl around the edges of the evening, imagining a future moment in which this present would be reinterpreted, in which my tears would signify something other than what they did now, although I couldn't specify what. The city's vastness seemed to collapse and expand simultaneously, each moment pregnant with the possibility of transformation, each solitary figure on each bench somehow connected through the invisible threads of urban consciousness that bound us all together in our collective solitude.

written_by_MFA012.Original: I breathed in the night air that was or was not laced with anachronistic blossoms and felt the small thrill I always felt to a lesser or greater degree when I looked at Manhattan’s skyline and the innumerable illuminated windows and the liquid sapphire and ruby of trafﬁc on the FDR Drive and the present absence of the towers. It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_MFA027.Excerpt1: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: The night air, maybe tinged with the scent of some flowering tree I can’t identify, swirls through the gaps in the fencing. I’m high up enough to see the bridges spanning into Brooklyn and Queens.  I imagine the collective exhalation of eight million people, the collective inhalation, the movement of hands over innumerable screens, the scrolling, the tapping, the repetitive stress injuries.  I picture the vast network of pipes, mains, and cables extending below the streets, the nighttime deliveries to bodegas, the movement of trains underground.I see the skyline as the material manifestation of a second person plural, a collective to which all art, even the most intimate, is addressed.  A yet-to-exist “we” glimpsed in the bundled debt, the traces of antidepressants in the water supply, the elaborate traffic system, the weather patterns.  I resolve to become the kind of artist who can transform bad forms of collectivity—bedbugs, or the crowds now surging toward Times Square—into glimpses of their potential for a kind of unity, a communal body. I’m having a mild lacrimal event, quietly tearing up.I’m never fully identical with myself.  There’s always a part of me that’s alien to me. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I thought Valentine Farm was a delusion, a dream-land. There was a real question in my mind as to whether a place like it ought to even exist for Black people. Too much blood was on American ground and in it for such a place to exist. The only thing more fake was America - I thought America was the grandest delusion of all. White men had slaughtered Native Americans and taken the land for themselves, enslaving Black folks to work on it. They warred with each other, forcing us to fight in their battles. There was something fundamentally wrongheaded about the idea that there could be a place of safety and refuge amidst all of that violence and suffering, past and present. And I wondered if there was any point in hoping that things would get better. I wasn't sure of it, and I thought that maybe it would be best to just close Valentine Farm's doors altogether. Or - head West, try to escape the past by moving into the future. Forget all that suffering, all that blood. We needed to do something, but I didn't know what. I didn't even know who "we" was, really. They liked to tell us we were all the same, but I knew better. Back in Africa, we were thousands of different tribes, each with our own language, our own dances, our own gods. We could tell each other apart, and then we crossed an ocean and suddenly we were all Black. We were all Black, and we were told to work, and we waded through the blood fresh on the earth to build this whole country. The roads, the cities. The White House. All of us with our hands, each one calloused and worn in its own unique way, each one different. All of us Black, and all of us our own people, with our own wants and desires, impossible to condense into just one solitary thing.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm, a delusion. Could a race of people so wronged ever truly find a place of respite, a sanctuary where wouldn't follow? History, that blood-soaked chronicle, argues not. And America, the grandest delusion of all, built on murder, theft, and the cruel arithmetic of slavery, is no exception. The white race, with its unyielding belief in its right to take, to conquer, to enslave—a nation built on such a foundation defies justice. Gradual progress, they call it, a slow crawl towards equality while our people still suffer under oppression. Should we close our doors to those still in need, those fleeing the very horrors we seek to escape, in a bid for our own fragile peace? Or should we move ever westward, seeking a horizon where the long shadow of slavery wouldn't reach? I have no answers, only a heart heavy with our collective sorrow. And who are "we" anyway? From the shores of a continent as vast and varied as Africa, we come, speaking different tongues, holding different customs, our histories as unique as the patterns woven into our kente cloth. Slavery, that great homogenizer, has forged us into a single, undifferentiated mass, that never truly was. Yet, it is our hands that build this nation. The skilled hands of craftsmen, the nurturing hands of midwives, the calloused hands of laborers—all have a part in raising the very structures that symbolize America's power, that gleaming white beacon of democracy, the White House. We build this nation, yet it refuses to recognize us as its own, as citizens deserving of the same rights, the same dignity, freedom it so readily bestows upon others. But we are not a monolith, not a single voice, a single story. We are a symphony of hopes, dreams, and experiences, as diverse as the land from which we were stolen. No one voice can speak for us all, no single path can lead us all to liberation.

written_by_MFA001.Original: Valentine farm is a delusion. Who told you the negro deserved a place of refuge? Who told you that you had that right? Every minute of your life’s suffering has argued otherwise. By every fact of history, it can’t exist. This place must be a delusion, too. Yet here we are.And America, too, is a delusion, the grandest one of all. The white race believes—believes with all its heart—that it is their right to take the land. To kill Indians. Make war. Enslave their brothers. This nation shouldn’t exist, if there is any justice in the world, for its foundations are murder, theft, and cruelty. Yet here we are.“I’m supposed to answer Mingo’s call for gradual progress, for closing our doors to those in need. I’m supposed to answer those who think this place is too close to the grievous influence of slavery, and that we should move west. I don’t have an answer for you. I don’t know what we should do. The word we. In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. It’s quite large. Brother Valentine has the maps of the world in his splendid library, you can look for yourself. They had different ways of subsistence, different customs, spoke a hundred different languages. And that great mixture was brought to America in the holds of slave ships. To the north, the south. Their sons and daughters picked tobacco, cultivated cotton, worked on the largest estates and smallest farms. We are craftsmen and midwives and preachers and peddlers. Black hands built the White House, the seat of our nation’s government. The word we. We are not one people but many different people. How can one person speak for this great, beautiful race—which is not one race but many, with a million desires and hopes and wishes for ourselves and our children?

written_by_MFA001.Original: Valentine farm is a delusion. Who told you the negro deserved a place of refuge? Who told you that you had that right? Every minute of your life’s suffering has argued otherwise. By every fact of history, it can’t exist. This place must be a delusion, too. Yet here we are.And America, too, is a delusion, the grandest one of all. The white race believes—believes with all its heart—that it is their right to take the land. To kill Indians. Make war. Enslave their brothers. This nation shouldn’t exist, if there is any justice in the world, for its foundations are murder, theft, and cruelty. Yet here we are.“I’m supposed to answer Mingo’s call for gradual progress, for closing our doors to those in need. I’m supposed to answer those who think this place is too close to the grievous influence of slavery, and that we should move west. I don’t have an answer for you. I don’t know what we should do. The word we. In some ways, the only thing we have in common is the color of our skin. Our ancestors came from all over the African continent. It’s quite large. Brother Valentine has the maps of the world in his splendid library, you can look for yourself. They had different ways of subsistence, different customs, spoke a hundred different languages. And that great mixture was brought to America in the holds of slave ships. To the north, the south. Their sons and daughters picked tobacco, cultivated cotton, worked on the largest estates and smallest farms. We are craftsmen and midwives and preachers and peddlers. Black hands built the White House, the seat of our nation’s government. The word we. We are not one people but many different people. How can one person speak for this great, beautiful race—which is not one race but many, with a million desires and hopes and wishes for ourselves and our children?

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm was a delusion, a sweet lie whispered against the gales of history. We made the beds, turned the soil, raised walls and roofs that might as well have been twigs against the wind. Some believed it, some needed to. That we could carve out a sanctuary and let the world forget us, or let us forget the world, as if blood didn’t mark the path here, as if blood wouldn’t soak the ground when they came to burn it down. Maybe they were right to dream. But history doesn’t honor dreams; it devours them. America itself was the grandest delusion, a conjuring trick where theft turned to deed, murder to progress. The white man built his monuments atop stolen land, wrote his laws with stolen hands, waged war and called it destiny. Justice was a rumor.But what choice did we have? Close the doors, shut out those still running, pretend we could hoard freedom like it wasn’t leaking through the cracks? Move west, find a new dream? And who was this “we” anyway? We were taken from different shores, speaking different tongues, cleaved from our histories, thrown into a common suffering and told to make a nation from the scraps. But we were never one thing. No more than they were. There were the ones who bent and the ones who broke, the ones who learned the master’s tongue and the ones who spit it back in his face.Yet still, we built. The houses and halls of power, the roads that carried their armies and their commerce, the fields that fed them, the White House itself, its name an irony lost on no one. This country was ours as much as theirs, though they would never admit it. And so, we waited to see if history would bury us or if we would carve our names in its stone.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is a delusion. It's no more real than one of those heat shimmers that disappear as you step closer. How could Black people even have a haven like that? The transatlantic ships, the endless days of toiling, the many nights of dying—they already preclude the possibility of a sanctuary. It's too late. It's impossible. The scars can't heal—they're white, carved on our cheeks. And America itself is the grandest delusion, a series of territories thrown together on the basis of mass murder, theft, and cruelty. The white race believes it has the right to do all this—the right to take land, start wars, enslave us. The very existence of America defies the notion of justice. Now, I suppose there are two possibilities left. We can pursue gradual progress: reform, speech-making—and close our doors to those in need. Or we can move west, to someplace far from the violent grasp of slavery, to somewhere fresher and less polluted. I don't have an answer. I can't even say who "we" are. Aren't "we" many peoples, descended from all over the vast continent of Africa? It may not be the case anymore, but generations ago, "we" spoke different languages. "We" worshiped different gods. "We" had different kings, farmed different vegetables, sang different songs with different instruments. There is only one thing that unites us: slavery. Here, now, in this foreign land, we are craftsmen, midwives, laborers. We are everything to this violent country. It was Black people who quarried the stone of the White House, who assembled its roof and walls. And we are not a monolith. Each of us holds a singular amount of courage, of ambition, of love. Each of us has suffered in unique ways. Each of us sees something different when we look into the eyes of our children. There is no single voice that can speak for us. Not even mine.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Valentine Farm stood there like America itself—a delusion wrapped in prettier lies, each one more fantastic than the last. The white race had crafted their own mythology: manifest destiny was just another word for theft, democracy a mask for murder. They built their temples on stolen land with stolen hands, then acted surprised when the walls started bleeding. Every brick in the White House had black fingerprints, every railroad tie was soaked in black sweat, but they wrote their histories in white ink on white paper and called it truth. The question of "we" haunted the halls of Valentine Farm like a restless spirit. "We" were not one people but many, a thousand different tongues silenced into one murmur, a hundred nations chained into one forced march across the Atlantic. Some said close the doors, keep safe what we've built. Others looked west, as if distance from slavery's reach could heal its scars. But the poison was already in the soil, in every field from Georgia to California. The craftsmen's hands still built, the midwives' fingers still caught babies, the laborers' backs still bent—but now their labor wrote a different story, each callus and scar a letter in a language that spoke of both survival and subjugation. In the end, all their stories bled together like rain on a window pane, impossible to separate one drop from another. The farm sat there in the wilderness like a challenge to history itself, each morning's sunrise asking the same impossible question: Could a sanctuary built by the hunted ever truly offer shelter, or was hope itself the grandest delusion of all? There were no answers in the dirt or the sky, only the endless work of hands trying to build something true out of America's lies. Their sweat fell on the same earth that had soaked up their ancestors' blood, and still they built, because what else was there to do but keep building?
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Valentine Farm is what you get when a bunch of world-weary people dream of sanctuary. Like a dream, this collective delusion is gone by morning light. It’s fake, a lie. written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: The winter light was dimming, Saint Patrick’s Day fading into a muted gray.  I sat beside her bed, the green Jell-O untouched on the bedside table, a festive offering she couldn’t partake in.  Outside, the snow was falling, the last of winter’s icy grip, the sunlight reflecting off the white expanse in a dazzling display.  But in this room, there was a different kind of dimming, a slow, inevitable burning down to smoke.She wasn’t asleep, not quite, but somewhere between here and there, her breath shallow, her body still.  Yet, her eyes, those strikingly blue eyes, remained open, vivid against the pale skin, the stark white sheets.  It was in those eyes that I saw it all unfold – the bitterness that had clung to her like a shroud, the bewilderment at the body’s betrayal, and then, finally, a quiet heroism.  The blue, so vibrant, so alive, was a defiance, a refusal to let go, even as the current pulled her away.I watched her, my mother, her spirit flickering like a candle flame in the gathering darkness.  And in those blue depths, I saw the echo of the life she had lived, the love she had given, the strength she had shown.  It was a story written in the language of the heart, a story that would live on, even as the last embers of her life faded away.

written_by_MFA012.Original: I watched my mother. It was March, and outside, the sun glinted off the sidewalks and the icy edges of the snow. It was Saint Patrick’s Day and the nurses brought my mother a square block of green Jell-O that sat quivering on the table beside her. It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open. They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake. They were the color of the sky on the best day of your life.My mother died fast but not all of a sudden. A slow-burning fire when flames disappear to smoke and then smoke to air. She never once closed her eyes. First they were bitter and then they were bewildered and then they changed again to something else, to a state that I have had, finally, to see as heroic. Blue, blue eyes. Daggers of blue wanting and wanting. To stay, to stay.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick’s Day, though there was no room for festivity in the hospital room where my mother lay suspended between this life and the next. Outside, the sunlight refracted sharply off the icy snow, casting a dazzling brilliance that mocked the stillness inside. Beside her, a bowl of green Jell-O sat untouched, its lurid color out of place in the solemnity of the moment. My mother’s eyes, blue and unyielding, remained open, vivid against the pallor of her skin and the muted sterility of the room. She was there but not there—unresponsive, yet undeniably present. I watched her, saw her dying like a fire slowly extinguishing into smoke, the embers of her vitality winking out one by one. Her eyes, once fierce with bitterness, shifted to bewilderment, and finally, to a quiet, unspoken heroism. They were the eyes of someone who clung to life even as it slipped from her grasp, a desperate yearning embedded in that piercing blue. The blue of her eyes became my lodestar, a symbol of her fight, her grace, her inevitability. And as I held her hand, I knew that when she closed those eyes for the last time, they would remain etched in me forever, as luminous as the snow outside.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: The moment I saw her, I was convinced that time had halted to let her pass—a striking woman who seemed neither of this world nor any other. Her skin was the sun-dappled bronze of desert sands at twilight, her eyes the unfathomable green of jade worn smooth by centuries of whispers. She moved with the languid elegance of a lioness in repose, her steps unhurried yet commanding, as if she carried an invisible crown. Her long scarf of woven gold and crimson thread draped over her shoulder like a relic stolen from Byzantium, glimmering faintly under the harsh fluorescent lights of Charles de Gaulle. The terminal swirled with the metallic clink of luggage carts, the nasal calls of final boarding, and the mingling scents of espresso and frost melting off winter coats. Outside, snow veiled Paris, but inside, the air buzzed with the restless vitality of spring—a contradiction that matched her presence. Behind an elderly Dutch woman stubbornly arguing with the ticket clerk over the weight of eleven battered suitcases, I stood transfixed, calculating how the infinite could fit into the brief arc of her passing. When my turn came, I mumbled a question to the clerk about love at first sight. She glanced up, her eyes carrying the faint smirk of someone long weary of life's questions. "Impossible, monsieur," she replied with practiced precision. "Only everything else is." I laughed, but it was hollow, for the woman who had remade time itself was already gone.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Walking into Charles de Gaulle Airport, I saw a woman, exotic and striking in her beauty. Astonished, I stood frozen in the terminal as I gazed at her timeless features. Her skin was dark and glowed with youth, her eyes were clear as a glacial lake. She wore a garment of gold and red fabric that looked as though it came from a culture that was entirely unfamiliar to me, and I stood for a long time admiring it, as though in a trance. Her look suggested an aura of antiquity, and she moved in grace like a lioness, striding confidently across the bright, balmy terminal that contrasted with the snowy world beyond its walls. In a moment, she was gone, her presence as fleeting as it was alluring. I took my place in line, and for a moment I found myself distracted by an elderly Dutch woman who took it upon herself to argue with the ticket clerk about the weight of eleven suitcases, “I’ve weighed them at home,” she said, “they can’t possibly be more than 10 kilograms—” and by the time I reached the front of the line I found myself in a pensive and dreamy mood. Who was that woman of such incredible mystery and poise, whose eyes shone so brightly? Smiling, I asked the ticket clerk if he believed in love at first sight. He laughed and replied that of course he did, how could he not. "Anything short of this , would be impossible", the clerk said.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: Excerpt one keeps the dreamy, romantic mood of the original. The descriptions are rich and poetic, and it stays close to the original structure and feeling. It mirrors the elegance, setting, and pacing better than excerpt two, which feels more modern and plain. Excerpt one sounds exactly like the original.
written_by_MFA011.Original: She was beautiful and lithe, with soft skin the color of bread and eyes like green almonds, and she had straight black hair that reached to her shoulders, and an aura of antiquity that could just as well have been Indonesian as Andean. She was dressed with subtle taste: a lynx jacket, a raw silk blouse with very delicate flowers, natural linen trousers, and shoes with a narrow stripe the color of bougainvillea. ‘This is the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen,’ I thought, when I saw her pass by with the stealthy stride of a lioness, while I waited in the check-in line at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris for the plane to New York.She was a supernatural apparition who existed only for a moment and disappeared into the crowd in the terminal.It was nine in the morning. It had been snowing all night, and traffic was heavier than usual in the city streets, and even slower on the highway, where trailer trucks were lined up on the shoulder and automobiles steamed in the snow. Inside the airport terminal, however, it was still spring.I stood behind an old Dutch woman who spent almost an hour arguing about the weight of her eleven suitcases. I was beginning to feel bored when I saw the momentary apparition who left me breathless, and so I never knew how the dispute ended. Then the ticket clerk brought me down from the clouds with a reproach for my distraction. By way of an excuse, I asked her if she believed in love at first sight. "Of course," she said. "The other kinds are impossible."
