written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I stood in line with my luggage at the Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris when my eyes landed on the most striking woman in the building, perhaps the most striking woman I’d ever seen; her pearly skin, antiquated dress and golden eyes gave her the aura of a masquerading goddess who’d absconded from her oil painting. The cardigan draped around her neck popped with magenta zags and her gold necklace turned the bleachy overhead lights to warm shine. With the grace of a lioness, she stepped out of sight and I lost her. I waited for my chance to pursue her down the terminal hall, but an elderly Dutch woman haggled with the clerk in front of me, producing short vehement barks about the weight of her eleven suitcases. There was time to plan. I looked around for an avenue for conversation with the beauty ahead, assuming I might never catch her, and found myself gazing at the snow falling like ash outside, silent out there, a perfect contrast to the balmy and chatty world inside the terminal. I edged around the Dutchwoman and her astonishing pile of luggage, which could easily fill a cargo barge, hoping for another glimpse of the leoline woman. There she went, distant now, turning left at the junction down the hall, heading in the same direction I soon would--there was still a chance. “Is love at first sight possible?” I asked the clerk when my turn came. He smiled. “Anything else is impossible,” he replied.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: In the heart of Charles de Gaulle Airport, where the Parisian winter raged outside, a vision of timeless beauty emerged amidst the sterile expanse of the terminal.  A striking woman, her skin kissed by the sun like ancient amber, her eyes pools of liquid obsidian, moved with the grace of a lioness through the bustling crowd.  A flowing, emerald-green kaftan draped her form, its edges embroidered with intricate symbols that whispered of forgotten civilizations.  A necklace of hammered gold, adorned with a single, luminous pearl, rested against her throat, a relic of a time when emperors and empresses ruled the world.For a fleeting moment, she was an apparition from a forgotten era, a goddess who had wandered into this modern temple of travel.  Her presence was a stark contrast to the gray, snow-covered landscape outside and the hurried, harried travelers who scurried around her.  She was an oasis of exoticism and tranquility in a desert of steel and glass.As I stood behind an elderly Dutch woman in line, her eleven suitcases causing a commotion due to their excessive weight, my gaze drifted back to the enigmatic woman.  She was gone, vanished into the crowd, leaving behind only a lingering scent of jasmine and a sense of profound wonder."Only anything other than that is impossible," the ticket clerk chuckled, his eyes twinkling, when I inquired about the possibility of love at first sight.  His words echoed in my mind, a reminder that in the realm of human experience, the extraordinary often lies hidden in the ordinary, waiting to be discovered.

written_by_MFA016.Original: She was beautiful and lithe, with soft skin the color of bread and eyes like green almonds, and she had straight black hair that reached to her shoulders, and an aura of antiquity that could just as well have been Indonesian as Andean. She was dressed with subtle taste: a lynx jacket, a raw silk blouse with very delicate flowers, natural linen trousers, and shoes with a narrow stripe the color of bougainvillea. ‘This is the most beautiful woman I’ve ever seen,’ I thought, when I saw her pass by with the stealthy stride of a lioness, while I waited in the check-in line at Charles de Gaulle Airport in Paris for the plane to New York.She was a supernatural apparition who existed only for a moment and disappeared into the crowd in the terminal.It was nine in the morning. It had been snowing all night, and traffic was heavier than usual in the city streets, and even slower on the highway, where trailer trucks were lined up on the shoulder and automobiles steamed in the snow. Inside the airport terminal, however, it was still spring.I stood behind an old Dutch woman who spent almost an hour arguing about the weight of her eleven suitcases. I was beginning to feel bored when I saw the momentary apparition who left me breathless, and so I never knew how the dispute ended. Then the ticket clerk brought me down from the clouds with a reproach for my distraction. By way of an excuse, I asked her if she believed in love at first sight. "Of course," she said. "The other kinds are impossible."

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: In Paris I spotted her walking gracefully in short suede heels, a timeless click to her step on the shiny floors of the Charles de Gaulle Airport. She was magnificent, her limbs like tributaries each meeting at the river made by her dark and wavy hair. Her eyes, though I could not see them, were certainly slant and blue. Fortuitously she sat some feet away from where I stood in line at the counter, crossing her ankles neatly beneath her in the French way, and at last I could admire a charoite skirt and matching cinched blazer that met the milky skin at her thighs and neck. The whole of her became a river to me then, or perhaps instead a lioness paused to drink at cool water; soon, I knew, she would be gone, and the springtime warmth and vibrancy brought by her into this terminal would fade to match the great blank whiteness of snowy winter beyond our shared space. Infatuated as I was by this lion-headed goddess, it took me some time to process the bickering before me, an elderly woman with a thick Dutch accent and some eleven suitcases haggling with the ticket clerk over their weight and associated cost. Returning my attention to the woman cloaked in purple and, for the time being, likewise cloaked in the wholeness of my affection, I missed the ticket clerk calling me forward after the Dutch woman had been sorted. I smiled a wide and generous smile. “Do you believe love at first sight is impossible,” I asked him, and tilted my head gently so that he might see the object of my sighted love.The clerk, evidently harried, was still inspired to smile at the glimpse of an exceptional woman. “In Paris,” he told me, “Anything other than such a love is impossible.”
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: I saw her emerge from the December mist of Charles de Gaulle like an apparition from the ancient kingdoms of Mali, her skin the color of honey-glazed chestnuts that reminded me of those afternoons in Cartagena when the sun would melt gold into the sea. She moved through Terminal 2F with the deliberate grace of a lioness, her caftan catching whispers of air that seemed to carry the scent of frankincense and myrrh, though later I would learn it was nothing more than the perfume of duty-free shops mixing with the aroma of croissants from Paul's bakery. Her eyes, set like amber stones in an Ethiopian crown, caught the fluorescent lights in such a way that made me believe she had lived a thousand years, perhaps more, and had witnessed the rise and fall of civilizations that existed only in forgotten dreams. The snow outside fell with the determination of white butterflies against the glass walls, while inside, the terminal maintained its eternal springtime, as if nature herself had conceded to this woman's presence. I might have followed her forever through the labyrinth of gates and shops, but fate, with its peculiar sense of humor, placed me behind an elderly Dutch woman who carried eleven suitcases and argued with mathematical precision about each gram of their weight, her voice rising and falling like a baroque opera. When I finally reached the ticket counter, my head still swimming with visions of the mysterious woman, I asked the clerk, a man with a mustache that seemed to have been drawn by a child's uncertain hand, if he believed in love at first sight. "Monsieur," he replied, adjusting his tie with the gravity of a philosopher, "in this airport, the only impossible thing is to find a reasonable price for a cup of coffee."

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: The glass partition reflected my spectacled face, sallow and withdrawn, as we sat at the group table near the kitchen. My father's hands, roughened by work, rested uneasily on the paper placemat while we waited, ignored by the waiters who glided past with studied indifference. At the next table, a girl my age lounged with casual elegance, her summer-bronzed skin gleaming against a crisp white blouse. She spooned yogurt—a food I had never tasted—with the natural grace of someone who had always known its existence. Her father, well-dressed and at ease, gestured expressively as he spoke to her. They had ordered à la carte, their plates arranged with careful precision by attentive staff. When our fixed-price meals finally arrived, the mashed potatoes sat in a grayish heap, unmolded from some industrial container. My father ate in silence, his shoulders tense, his fork scraping the institutional plate. For days afterward, he would mutter about the "pig slop" they had served us, each repetition of the phrase carrying the accumulated weight of a lifetime of similar humiliations. I understood then that the restaurant had sorted us, placed us in our proper social category—the cheap seats, the hurried service, the institutional food. We belonged to the world of fixed-price menus and group tables, while others inhabited the realm of individual choice, of yogurt and carefully plated dishes, of being seen and served with deference.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."

written_by_MFA016.Original: One evening ‒ it was our last day ‒ in Tours, we had dinner in a brightly-lit restaurant where the walls were lined with mirrors, frequented by a sophisticated clientele. My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. She was dipping into a thick milky substance in a glass ‒ some years later I learnt this was yogurt, which people like us had never heard of. I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad-looking with my spectacles, silently sitting beside my father, who was staring into the far distance. I could see everything that separated me from that girl yet I wouldn’t have known what to do to resemble her.Afterward, my father complained with unusual vehemence about this restaurant, where he claimed we had been served mashed potatoes made with “pig slop,” white and tasteless. Several weeks later, he was still venting his anger over the meal and its disgraceful “pig slop.” Although he never actually said so ‒ it was probably then that I began decoding his speech ‒ it was his way of expressing resentment at having been treated with contempt because we were not chic customers who ate “à la carte.”

At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: In the muted light of the restaurant, the stark class divide was as palpable as the stale odor clinging to the worn velvet seats.  My spectacles, magnifying the pallor of my reflection, seemed to amplify my sense of displacement.  At our table, a shared expanse with strangers, the service was a reluctant dance of neglect.  In contrast, a few tables away, a tanned teenage girl, radiating an aura of effortless confidence, shared an intimate meal with an older man.  Her laughter, light and carefree, bounced off the gilded mirrors, mocking my own constrained stillness.Her spoon, a silver arc, delivered a dollop of yogurt to her lips—a food so exotic, it was a whisper from another world. My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. She was dipping into a thick milky substance in a glass ‒ some years later I learnt this was yogurt, which people like us had never heard of. I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad-looking with my spectacles, silently sitting beside my father, who was staring into the far distance. I could see everything that separated me from that girl yet I wouldn’t have known what to do to resemble her.Afterward, my father complained with unusual vehemence about this restaurant, where he claimed we had been served mashed potatoes made with “pig slop,” white and tasteless. Several weeks later, he was still venting his anger over the meal and its disgraceful “pig slop.” Although he never actually said so ‒ it was probably then that I began decoding his speech ‒ it was his way of expressing resentment at having been treated with contempt because we were not chic customers who ate “à la carte.”

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: In the muted light of the restaurant, the stark class divide was as palpable as the stale odor clinging to the worn velvet seats.  My spectacles, magnifying the pallor of my reflection, seemed to amplify my sense of displacement.  At our table, a shared expanse with strangers, the service was a reluctant dance of neglect.  In contrast, a few tables away, a tanned teenage girl, radiating an aura of effortless confidence, shared an intimate meal with an older man.  Her laughter, light and carefree, bounced off the gilded mirrors, mocking my own constrained stillness.Her spoon, a silver arc, delivered a dollop of yogurt to her lips—a food so exotic, it was a whisper from another world.  My gaze drifted back to my plate, the food suddenly as bland as the pity I felt for myself.  Later, my father's voice, rough with suppressed resentment, dissected the meal, the "pig slop" mashed potatoes becoming a metaphor for our diminished status.  We were not "à la carte" patrons, and our presence was a mere tolerated intrusion.  The restaurant, a microcosm of society, had laid bare the invisible lines that defined our place.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food. It was clear that both of us felt uncomfortable with the opulence of the space, but neither of us knew how to say so. Nearby, a girl around the age of fifteen sat with an older man, presumably her father, eating a foreign-looking food that I didn't recognize—a bowl of yogurt, I later learned. She looked deeply at ease eating her meal, and I was disturbed to see myself in the mirror on the adjacent wall—spectacled, pale. Compared to the girl, I looked homely and unimportant, or at least I felt that I did at the time. For a moment I imagined myself as the girl, tan and comfortable among the trappings of wealth, though even then I knew that the hallmarks of the working class were written all over my face and my behavior. My father and I sat for a while in silence, and when the waitstaff brought out our plates, he remarked to me that his mashed potatoes looked like "pig slop." At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.

written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. The waiter looked us up and down, seeing what we were immediately. I was pale from the winter, dressed in my worn, washed clothes. I wore spectacles, awkward and out of fashion, the kind you could buy at a steep discount. The waiter directed us to a shared table at the back of the restaurant, in front of the wash closet. At first my experience of discomfort was limited only to me. My father still had a big smile, ear to ear. But then I saw another father-daughter pair at a table in the restaurant’s big window. The girl was around my age, and pretty. She dealt with the restaurant staff confidently, with a confiding air, like they shared a special secret. I watched the girl longingly. Her tanned legs ended in delicate buckled shoes. I watched her eat food I could not identify. Back then, I’d never had yoghurt.As the waiter laughed and spoke to them in earshot of us, I saw my father growing red. “Those potatoes were pig slop,” he said after we left the restaurant, again and again. It embarrassed me. It was clear enough to both of us what had happened. At least, it was clear that we’d both had a bad time. I knew what he was saying. We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele. I wanted to forget about it. If we didn’t speak of the event, then perhaps it wasn’t real.
written_by_MFA033.Excerpt2: At the restaurant, a dim-lit corner housed a long table where we were seated, our pale faces barely catching the flicker of candlelight. The service was indifferent, the kind that signaled our place—second-class, among the unremarkable and the unseen. I watched the teenage girl at the next table, her tanned skin glowing, the light glancing off the curve of her bare arm as she dipped a spoon into her yogurt. It wasn’t just the yogurt, unfamiliar and faintly exotic, or her easy laughter as she spoke to the older man, presumably her father. It was the way she leaned back in her chair, utterly at home in a place where I shrank. I caught my reflection in the mirror—a pale, spectral figure, glasses catching the flicker of light like an accusation. My father sat stiffly, the lines on his face deepened by a furrow of discontent. The mashed potatoes, a mound of something that seemed to sneer back at us, bore the brunt of his irritation. "Pig slop," he muttered, too loud, earning a glance from the waiter that reeked of disdain. He repeated the phrase later, at home, his voice rising each time, but I knew it wasn’t the food. It was the yogurt, the girl, her easy privilege, the sharp reminder of where we belonged in the silent hierarchy of the dining room. He wanted to explain the indignity, to frame it in something tangible, and so he said, "pig slop." I, too, clung to the detail, though for me it was the yogurt, a symbol of a world I had not yet entered. In that moment, the line between us and them felt etched into the tablecloth, as indelible as the reflection in the mirror.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The air here is brittle, like dried leaves crushed underfoot, and the fluorescent lights buzz with a monotony that drills into the skull. I count the tiles on the ceiling—seventy-four to the vent, then back again—as if mapping their lines might offer a way out. Aunt Sara paces like a metronome, her cattle prod clutched tight, a steel baton of authority. She and Aunt Elizabeth are twin statues of discipline, their faces carved from the same cold stone. Outside, the Angels move, shadows on the edge of vision, their rifles slung low like extensions of their bodies, untouchable, unattainable. We are warned not to look at them too long, but we do. Eyes linger, breath slows, and beneath the fabric that covers us from throat to wrist, the treasonous warmth of skin stirs. We’ve learned to barter in silence, in gestures: a sideways glance, a curve of the lip that could be mistaken for obedience but isn’t. We rehearse it in our minds—the offer, the exchange, the outcome. Would they take it? Would they want it? The thought coils in my chest, shame and thrill mingling. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: We are watched. Always watched, but never truly seen. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrol the corridors with their cattle prods held like scepters, symbols of their petty authority, though it's the Angels outside who hold the real power, with their guns and their untouchable distance. I've memorized the way they stand, these Angels, their backs military-straight against the concrete walls, their eyes hidden beneath the peaks of their caps. Sometimes I imagine their gaze following me, and I let my hips sway ever so slightly – an old habit from before, when such movements held currency. Now they're just muscle memory, like the way my hands still reach for a phone that isn't there, or my fingers itch for a cigarette I can't have. The other women do it too; I see them in the cafeteria, in the exercise yard, their bodies unconsciously remembering freedom. We're like cats in a cage, I think, practicing our hunting crouch though there's nothing left to hunt. At night, in our narrow beds, we whisper about making deals – our bodies for their help, as if we still owned these vessels we inhabit. As if flesh could buy freedom in a place where flesh is all we're reduced to. The routine grinds on: wake, pray, eat, walk, pray, sleep. The cold seeps in through the windows, but it's nothing compared to the chill that's settled in our bones. We are learning to fold ourselves smaller, to take up less space, to become invisible even as we're constantly observed. Yet somewhere, in the midnight hours when even Aunt Sara's footsteps fade, we dream of tomorrow, of a future that feels as distant and unreachable as the stars beyond our barred windows.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt1: The yearning within me is like a phantom limb, a constant ache for something I cannot name.  It is a thirst for touch, for freedom, for the scent of rain on soil. They are the true power in this desolate realm, the enforcers of our isolation.  We crave their attention, their touch, their recognition.  Our bodies, the only currency we possess, become our bargaining chips in silent negotiations.The days bleed into one another, an endless cycle of rituals and routines.  The cold, impersonal walls of this place mirror the chill that has settled deep within our bones.  We are cogs in a machine, our individuality erased, our voices muted.Yet, beneath the surface of our resignation, a spark of rebellion flickers.  We steal glances, share whispered secrets, and dream of a future beyond these walls.  Our bodies may be captive, but our minds remain free.In the dead of night, when the silence is broken only by the rhythmic hum of the surveillance cameras, I close my eyes and envision a world ablaze with color, a world where laughter rings out like music, a world where desires are not forbidden.  It is a world worth fighting for, a world worth dying for.And so we wait, with bated breath, for the moment when the chains will break, and we will emerge from the shadows, like butterflies from their chrysalises, ready to embrace the future, no matter how uncertain it may be.
written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.

But they were women with shorn scalps, black vests and black boots, skulking back and forth across the hallway, brute voices muffled by the door. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.
written_by_MFA004.Reason: Excerpt 2 closely relates with the original because of the tone, imagery, and the dark sensuous lyricism. It blends a kind of brutal realism with poetic reflection, focusing on sensory detail, quiet menace, and a simmering, thwarted eroticism. Excerpt on the other hand reads more like a motivational voice-over with broad strokes and a fewer grounded sensory details.
written_by_MFA004.Original: There was old sex in the room and loneliness, and expectation, of something without a shape or name. I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: The yearning within me is like a phantom limb, a constant ache for something I cannot name.  It is a thirst for touch, for freedom, for the scent of rain on soil.  But these desires are forbidden, locked away in the depths of our sterile existence. Aunt Sara and Elizabeth, the keepers of our gilded cage, watch with hawk-like eyes, their cattle prods a silent threat.  They are the keepers of our morality, the guardians of our chastity.  Their voices echo in the cold, sterile corridors, a constant reminder of our confinement. The Angels, those distant figures in their pristine uniforms, are the only ones permitted to bear arms.  They are the true power in this desolate realm, the enforcers of our isolation.  We crave their attention, their touch, their recognition.  Our bodies, the only currency we possess, become our bargaining chips in silent negotiations.The days bleed into one another, an endless cycle of rituals and routines.  The cold, impersonal walls of this place mirror the chill that has settled deep within our bones.  We are cogs in a machine, our individuality erased, our voices muted.Yet, beneath the surface of our resignation, a spark of rebellion flickers.  We steal glances, share whispered secrets, and dream of a future beyond these walls.  Our bodies may be captive, but our minds remain free.In the dead of night, when the silence is broken only by the rhythmic hum of the surveillance cameras, I close my eyes and envision a world ablaze with color, a world where laughter rings out like music, a world where desires are not forbidden.  It is a world worth fighting for, a world worth dying for.And so we wait, with bated breath, for the moment when the chains will break, and we will emerge from the shadows, like butterflies from their chrysalises, ready to embrace the future, no matter how uncertain it may be.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: It was during that strange winter when I began my obsession with cooking spaghetti. Like a monk devoted to a peculiar religion, I wandered through foreign grocery stores, filling my basket with olive oil bottles that gleamed like ancient artifacts and tomatoes so red they seemed to hold secrets from another world. The specialty shop owner—a thin man with circular glasses who looked like he could speak to cats—sold me a deep blue pot that seemed bottomless and a kitchen timer that ticked with the precision of a heartbeat. Strange how such ordinary objects can suddenly feel magical, as if they've crossed over from a parallel universe where pasta is a sacred thing. In my small apartment, which felt more like a submarine than a living space, I'd stand at the stove watching the water boil, counting the bubbles like stars. The steam would rise and fog my windows, creating a barrier between my spaghetti sanctuary and the outside world. I never invited anyone to these meals—somehow, I knew this was a ritual meant for solitude, like writing poetry at midnight or counting clouds. Every Sunday, I'd prepare the same meal: spaghetti swimming in sauce that I'd cooked for exactly twenty-seven minutes, a green salad that seemed to whisper ancient mysteries, and tea that tasted of distant memories. The garlic and onion fragrance would seep into my clothes, my books, my dreams, until I couldn't tell where the cooking ended and I began.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: Around seven years ago now I would go down to the Italian Market, weekends, to stock up on what I soon deemed the essentials: oregano, bay leaves, fennel seeds, butter, lemon. Among others. Nothing in my life pointed to this beginning. No crises or wayward desires, no history of culinary skills resurfaced, and I cannot say, exactly, what became of me during this time. Why I found myself in the aisles of specialty stores, several miles from home. Why I, each weekend, sought a furtherance: going beyond what I had cooked the week prior, with more tools, sauces, and research on what breed of spaghetti I would cook next. I tracked down a Le Creuset stockpot, a pasta roller, an egg timer. I spent too many hours over my stove at home, simmering garlic in olive oil, and over the cutting board on my countertop, chopping onions, tomatoes, basil. Though innocent at first, soon this meal prep encompassed every evening, Sunday through Sunday, and in this way I practiced what I now call my Spaghetti Days. During this time I never shared a meal with anyone else, coming to believe that spaghetti, along with my evening earl gray and caesar salad, was best enjoyed alone. Soon I realized it wasn’t desire that brought me to the habit, but ritualistic necessity. It was about hands, and what it meant to keep them moving. As soon as this realization came, all the magic of preparing spaghetti washed away.

" whereas in excerpt one they say "The garlic and onion fragrance would seep into my clothes, " There is also the similar types of listing that is present in the original, such as ", my clothes, my books, my records, my tennis racquet," in the original and in excerpt one the author says "my clothes, my books, my dreams,"
written_by_MFA015.Original: I went to a cooking specialty store and bought a kitchen timer and a huge aluminum pot, big enough to bathe a German shepherd in, then went around to all the supermarkets that catered to foreigners, gathering an assortment of odd-sounding spices. I picked up a pasta cookbook at the bookstore, and bought tomatoes by the dozen. I purchased every brand of spaghetti I could lay my hands on, simmered every sauce known to man. Fine particles of garlic, onion, and olive oil swirled in the air, forming a harmonious cloud that penetrated every corner of my tiny apartment, permeating the floor and the ceiling and the walls, my clothes, my books, my records, my tennis racquet, my bundles of old letters. It was a fragrance one might have smelled on ancient Roman aqueducts.This is a story from the Year of Spaghetti, 1971 A.D.As a rule, I cooked spaghetti, and ate it, by myself. I was convinced that spaghetti was a dish best enjoyed alone. I can’t really explain why I felt that way, but there it is.I always drank tea with my spaghetti and ate a simple lettuce-and-cucumber salad. I’d make sure I had plenty of both. I laid everything out neatly on the table and enjoyed a leisurely meal, glancing at the paper as I ate. From Sunday to Saturday, one Spaghetti Day followed another. And each new Sunday started a brand-new Spaghetti Week

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: For an entire year, spaghetti became the core of my existence—a solitary ritual that shaped my days. I’d visit a dimly lit specialty store downtown, where the air carried the faint tang of aged balsamic and oregano, to buy the essentials: a large pot, a precise kitchen timer, and an assortment of imported ingredients. Supermarkets catering to foreigners became my haunts, offering me tomatoes that smelled of distant summers, garlic as pungent as a whispered confession, and every conceivable variety of pasta. Back in my small apartment, I experimented tirelessly with sauces. Rich tomato-based ones simmered for hours, creamy carbonaras that threatened to stick to the pan if I turned my back even for a second. The scent of garlic sizzling in olive oil seeped into my walls, my furniture, even my clothes. Eating spaghetti became a meditative act, the fork twirling endlessly in a repetitive choreography that mirrored my own existence. Tea steeped nearby, a salad of crisp lettuce and vinaigrette sat untouched until the last strand of pasta disappeared. There was no music, no voices, no distraction. Just the warm embrace of routine, filling the cracks left by loneliness. Each Sunday bled into the next, the days indistinguishable but somehow comforting, as if the rhythm of boiling water and clinking plates was a language only I could speak.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: I call them the Spaghetti Days (they lasted an entire week but the singular week standing alone bothers me). On my way home from work, I’d pass the kitchen utility store where, in the shop window, there sat a stack of metal pots. I wanted the bottom one, the one shining against the rain the day I stepped through the shop door. Buying an empty pot felt wrong—too spacious—so I also bought an egg timer. But it rattled hollow around the pot. I kept walking until I reached the foreign supermarket with its crates of imported tomatoes under the awning. I put some tomatoes in that pot along with white onions, garlic, oregano, a green glass bottle of olive oil, and boxes and boxes of dry spaghetti. This, for me, was the start of a deep ritual. Steam from the boiling water fogged my kitchen window as I imagined having guests share my tea and salad. They’d comment on the nuance in smells and praise my subtle changes with the sauce and spices. But an audience would have been too much, too cramped and restricting. Spaghetti was best enjoyed alone. And being alone, there were always leftovers I’d scoop into a plastic container. At the end of the week, when it couldn’t fit any more spaghetti, I emptied all of it into the trash. No matter how hard I scrubbed the container, I couldn’t get the red stains out. I threw out the container too.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: I stared at the television screen, the pixelated image of the Twin Towers collapsing, a grotesque loop of destruction playing over and over.  Reva, my dear Reva, was lost in the chaos, her voice a distant echo on the other end of a dropped phone call."Are you there?" I had asked, the dial tone buzzing in my ear.Hours earlier, the news had crackled to life, the blue glow of the television illuminating the room.  Trevor was away in Barbados, his honeymoon a cruel irony in the face of the unfolding tragedy.  I watched the towers crumble, the smoke billowing, a woman leaping from the inferno, her body a fragile arc against the backdrop of the burning sky. "She looks like Reva," I whispered, a strange sense of admiration washing over me.The woman's beauty, even in the face of death, was mesmerizing. Her courage, her desperation, her final act of defiance against the inevitable.I watched her fall, the image burned into my mind, a haunting reminder of the fragility of life.Reva, my wild, untamed friend, was gone, swallowed by the chaos, her laughter and vibrancy extinguished.  I mourned her loss, the emptiness a gaping hole in my soul.Days turned into weeks, the world a blur of muted colors and hollow sounds.  I watched the footage repeatedly, the woman's fall a morbid fascination, a symbol of our collective mortality.  In her final act, I saw a reflection of my own struggles, my own search for meaning in a world that often felt meaningless.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: I’d spoken with Reva last week, but it was a short conversation filled mostly with platitudes. She’d seemed distracted and said she was at the gym. When the news broke about the towers, I called her a few times, but she didn’t pick up. Without thinking, I went immediately to the store to purchase a TV/VCR machine. Suddenly the most important thing was to record all the news footage that was blaring at me from out of my TV. I thought briefly about calling Trevor, then remembered that he was in Barbados on his honeymoon, probably sipping a drink with some spiky, inedible part of a fruit in it, completely unaware of what had happened. Once the sun went down and I still hadn’t heard from her, I realized that Reva was lost, likely for good. For days I sat watching and rewatching the footage I’d taped of the attacks, unable to move from in front of the TV save to piss or search the bathroom cabinet for more pills. There was a video of a woman leaping from the North Tower, and though it was too grainy for me to ever be able to tell if it was Reva, I liked imagining that it was.She wore a grey pencil skirt with black tights and stilettos – one still gripping her foot while the other had torn free, suspended in the air. She looked so beautiful, jumping like that into the unknown, that I took a kind of strange and holy comfort in her courage.
written_by_MFA011.Reason: I think Excerpt 2 mirrors the original excerpt better. It has clear original structure and seems to focus on a similar narrative progression. It is clear, direct, and closely aligns with the original version. It captures the compulsion to watch and rewatch, the qcceptance of imagining it is Reva and seems closely matched.
written_by_MFA011.Original: Then I called Reva. She answered on the fourth ring, panting and tense."I’m at the gym," she said. "Can we talk later?" We never did.On September 11, I went out and bought a new TV/VCR at Best Buy so I could record the news coverage of the planes crashing into the Twin Towers. Trevor was on a honeymoon in Barbados, I'd later learn, but Reva was lost. Reva was gone. I watched the videotape over and over to soothe myself that day. And I continue to watch it, usually on a lonely afternoon, or any other time I doubt that life is worth living, or when I need courage, or when I am bored. Each time I see the woman leap off the seventy-eighth floor of the North Tower—one high-heeled shoe slipping off and hovering up over her, the other stuck on her foot as though it were too small, her blouse untucked, hair flailing, limbs stiff as she plummets down, one arm raised, like a dive into a summer lake—I am overcome by awe, not because she looks like Reva, and I think it's her, almost exactly her, and not because Reva and I had been friends, or because I'll never see her again, but because she is beautiful. There she is, a human being, diving into the unknown, and she is wide awake.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: The last time I spoke to Reva, she was distant. She looks enough like Reva that if I were feeling sentimental, I could pretend it’s her. The edge of her pencil skirt whipping up could be Reva’s knock-off designer, her shoes flying from her feet and floating up past her head could be Reva’s second hand Manolos, the glints of sunlight that could be Reva’s grandmother’s ring. But it doesn’t have to be. I don’t need her to be Reva. In dreams, when you feel like you’re falling, you jolt awake. I need her to wake me up.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I stood in the dim light of my living room, the boxed TV/VCR perched on the coffee table, its plastic wrapping still intact, a strange relic of the morning. I didn’t know what else to do with myself after the towers fell, after I’d called Reva at the gym and heard her voice on the line—distant, tinny, preoccupied. That voice haunted me, replaying in my head, a loop of “Can we talk later?” as if she had known this was coming and had somewhere better to be. I could have told her to stay on the line, begged her to come over, but I didn’t. Later, I’d sit on the floor, knees pulled to my chest, watching footage of a woman leaping from the North Tower. Her dress caught the wind like a parachute, her body poised, graceful, falling as though she’d chosen to fly instead of burn. The likeness to Reva—her height, her hair—was undeniable, but I didn’t cry. I pressed pause, rewound, played it again, squinting at the screen, wondering if courage could be beautiful or if beauty was just what we saw in things we didn’t understand. Reva was gone. Lost. And yet, in that leap, she was eternal.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I'd stared at my cheap TV/VCR combo for hours that day, recording endless footage while sprawled on my beige couch, still warm from my body's perpetual indent. She looked like Reva – same dark hair, same slight build – but she moved like a dancer, like she'd chosen this terrible performance. I watched her fall hundreds of times, memorizing the way her skirt billowed, how her arms stretched wide as if embracing the sky. She became my obsession, this falling angel in sensible office wear. I understood her choice in a way that frightened me. There was something pure in it, something almost holy – to leap into nothingness rather than wait for it to claim you. I never told anyone how much I admired her courage.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The sun, a molten fist, clenched the city in its fiery grip, the heat so ferocious it could melt the wings of sparrows foolish enough to take flight.  The air, thick with the chanting of prayers from nearby temples and the tinny melodies of Hindi film songs, crackled with the cries of children playing cricket in dusty alleyways.  The aroma of freshly brewed coffee, dark and bitter, snaked through the streets, mingling with the pungent scent of spices from open-air markets.On the fourth floor of a sea-green building, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, stirred in their beds, their bodies attuned to the city's relentless rhythm.  As if bound by an invisible thread, they woke up at precisely the same moment, their eyes fluttering open in unison.  They stepped out onto their respective verandas, their movements slow and deliberate, a stark contrast to the frenetic energy of the streets below. Downstairs, the younger generation buzzed with anticipation, their voices a chorus of excitement as they planned their evening escapades at Elliot's Beach.  But the old men remained unfazed, their world a sanctuary of quietude amidst the chaos.  Senior gazed at the distant sea, its shimmering surface mirroring the turmoil within his own soul.  Junior, his eyes fixed on the horizon, seemed lost in a reverie, the past and present blurring in his mind's eye
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: One morning in a town quite near Chennai, the sun arose with a ferocity and began beating down on the town's residents, and there was no time to blink back dawn, the children were already awake and fussing for food, and Miss Aadhya had started on the first pot of coffee, and from her window she could hear Bollywood music, already blaring, and below her the old man whose name no one knew was praying, and above her, on the fourth floor of the Aquamarine building, Senior struggled against that veil that separates dream from reality, and broke through, and was awake. At the same time, his neighbor, Junior, awoke. The two men's eyes opened at the same time. Kabir was now calling to his friends, everyone making plans for an evening at the Elliot’s beach, the promise of cool water the only thing making it bearable to get through the hot afternoon. All the members of the town were connected to each other, as a marionette has strings attached to each of its joints, each small movement producing an equal and opposite reaction. Senior swung his legs out of bed and Junior finished brushing his teeth. The clamor of the town stirred something in both of them, and, with one elegant pull, they both lifted their heads and decided to go out, onto their own veranda.

written_by_MFA001.Original: The day that Junior fell down began like any other day: the explosion of heat rippling the air, the trumpeting sunlight, the traffic’s tidal surges, the prayer chants in the distance, the cheap film music rising from the floor below, the loud pelvic thrusts of an 'item number' dancing across a neighbor’s TV, a child’s cry, a mother’s rebuke, unexplained laughter, scarlet expectorations, bicycles, the newly plaited hair of schoolgirls, the smell of strong sweet coffee, a green wing flashing in a tree. The poor were puritans by night and day. As for the old, they had rites of their own and did not need to wait for evening. With the sun stabbing at them through their window blinds, the two old men struggled to their feet and lurched out onto their adjacent verandas, emerging at almost the same moment, like characters in an ancient tale, trapped in fateful coincidences, unable to escape the consequences of chance.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: The sun, a molten fist, clenched the city in its fiery grip, the heat so ferocious it could melt the wings of sparrows foolish enough to take flight.  The air, thick with the chanting of prayers from nearby temples and the tinny melodies of Hindi film songs, crackled with the cries of children playing cricket in dusty alleyways.  The aroma of freshly brewed coffee, dark and bitter, snaked through the streets, mingling with the pungent scent of spices from open-air markets.On the fourth floor of a sea-green building, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, stirred in their beds, their bodies attuned to the city's relentless rhythm.  As if bound by an invisible thread, they woke up at precisely the same moment, their eyes fluttering open in unison.  They stepped out onto their respective verandas, their movements slow and deliberate, a stark contrast to the frenetic energy of the streets below. Downstairs, the younger generation buzzed with anticipation, their voices a chorus of excitement as they planned their evening escapades at Elliot's Beach.  But the old men remained unfazed, their world a sanctuary of quietude amidst the chaos.  Senior gazed at the distant sea, its shimmering surface mirroring the turmoil within his own soul.  Junior, his eyes fixed on the horizon, seemed lost in a reverie, the past and present blurring in his mind's eye
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: One morning in a town quite near Chennai, the sun arose with a ferocity and began beating down on the town's residents, and there was no time to blink back dawn, the children were already awake and fussing for food, and Miss Aadhya had started on the first pot of coffee, and from her window she could hear Bollywood music, already blaring, and below her the old man whose name no one knew was praying, and above her, on the fourth floor of the Aquamarine building, Senior struggled against that veil that separates dream from reality, and broke through, and was awake. At the same time, his neighbor, Junior, awoke. The two men's eyes opened at the same time. Kabir was now calling to his friends, everyone making plans for an evening at the Elliot’s beach, the promise of cool water the only thing making it bearable to get through the hot afternoon. All the members of the town were connected to each other, as a marionette has strings attached to each of its joints, each small movement producing an equal and opposite reaction. Senior swung his legs out of bed and Junior finished brushing his teeth. The clamor of the town stirred something in both of them, and, with one elegant pull, they both lifted their heads and decided to go out, onto their own veranda.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Under the heavy weight of the late afternoon sun, the city was bursting with heat, the sound of chanting prayers—Surya Mangalam, said for hope of peaceful evenings—sitar and tabla-heavy soundtracks, and children's cries rising like heat shimmers, with sweetened filter coffee laden in the air, one final push to get through to the fast-approaching dusk. But on the fourth floor of the sea-green building overlooking the blisteringly blue Indian Ocean, two elderly men, Senior and Junior, only just began their day, even as the younger generation gathered in clumps like swarms of ants, singing along to hit Tamil songs and preparing to dance and drink on Elliot's Beach once the sun set. Moving to an instinctual, silent rhythm, Senior and Junior rose as one, like two men bound by strings of fate, their walk to their verandahs as sure as the sun's journey across the sky until they sank into their chairs with the same achy movements, tilting their heads back once comfortable, two mirrors reflecting back at each other. Nothing in the world could halt this routine, their path so worn they seemed guided by more than gravity. Beneath them, a jubilant cheer rose up to greet the old men, and twin smiles stretched slowly across their faces, for they were soothed by their repetition and the companionship that repetition brings.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: In that sea-green building which stood like a tired sentinel near Elliot's Beach (where young lovers would soon gather with their smartphones and their dreams, as predictable as the tide), there lived two old men whose synchronicity of existence would have alarmed them had they ever bothered to notice it—but they never did, for such is the peculiar blindness that affects those who are bound together by the invisible threads of fate. The fourth floor (ah, but was it really the fourth? for in this particular building the ground floor was called the first, in the American way, causing endless confusion among visitors and delivery men alike) housed Senior and Junior, names that contained their own little joke, since Junior was himself no spring chicken, and Senior was so ancient that some believed he had witnessed the departure of the British Raj with his own rheumy eyes. Every morning, as predictable as the muezzin's call to prayer that floated across the neighborhood like a ghost's lament, mixing with the timpani of temple bells and the cheerful vulgarity of Tamil film songs blaring from auto-rickshaws, the two men would emerge onto their respective verandas at precisely the same moment, like mechanical figures in some elaborate timepiece. The morning air arrived thick with stories: the dark, intense aroma of filter coffee from the houses below, where young IT professionals fueled themselves for their days in air-conditioned offices; the shouts of children in pressed uniforms hurrying to school, their watches synchronized to their mothers' anxieties; the eternal complaint of crows who had seen it all before and were distinctly unimpressed. The heat rose from the streets like a malevolent spirit, distorting the reality of things, so that the two old men, standing on their respective verandas with their respective cups of tea, might have been mirror images of each other, or perhaps the same man caught in two different moments of time, or even (though they would have scoffed at such fancy) two aspects of the same soul, divided at birth and now slowly, incrementally, moving toward an inevitable reunion, like two drops of water on a window pane, drawn together by forces beyond their comprehension or control.

Senior and Junior looked out at Elliot’s Beach, this strange sandy coin that had been cast away by fate.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: The grandmother’s face, shadowed by the wide brim of her hat, turned toward The Misfit, her trembling hand reaching as if to steady herself against the weight of her own words. Her voice, cracked and earnest, declared him as one of her own children, the statement hanging between them like a fragile thread in the stifling air. The Misfit’s pale eyes blinked behind thick glasses that reflected the distant sun, making him appear less man, more hollow instrument, tuned to discord. Hiram and Bobby Lee stood like rough-hewn statues, their hands idle but primed, their smirks a mockery of the tension thickening the moment. The grandmother’s outstretched hand shook with an urgency that seemed to belie her fragile clarity—a clarity forged by fear and sudden grace.Then came the shots, three in succession, each one punching the air with finality. Her body folded into the red clay ditch as if she were part of the earth all along, her hand still outstretched but now unyielding. A faint, enigmatic smile lingered on her lips, a puzzling counterpoint to the violence that had stilled her breath. The Misfit lowered his weapon slowly, his face twisted not in rage but something deeper—a silent rage turned inward, an unanswered question echoing in his marrow. He removed his glasses, wiped them carefully, and stared at the starkness of her lifeless form, his pale eyes vulnerable, almost raw.Bobby Lee chuckled, kicking a stone idly. “That was a fun one,” he said, his grin cruel. The Misfit turned his head sharply, his voice low and flinty. “She was closer to something than I’ll ever be,” he muttered, almost to himself. Then louder, with a bitter edge, “No pleasure in this life, none at all.” He spat into the dirt as they dragged her into the shadows.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: The Misfit looked at the old woman who had risen on to her knees in the damp grass and begun to pray. Hearing the familiar words made him lose his sense of urgency for it recalled to his mind the prayers he had memorized and repeated as a boy. The promise of redemption had appealed to him then but as a grown man he knew to trust only those things he could see for himself and verify firsthand. He would have given anything to have proof of his own everlasting soul or anyone else’s, but no sign had ever revealed itself to him and so the promises had turned curdled and turned bitter in his heart. The grandmother watched the Misfit’s face change as she prayed. She saw him illuminated and transformed into a young child, long before he was ever a killer, with a soul as pure and innocent as her son’s had once been. “You’re one of my own children!” she cried and reached out to him. But the sudden flicker of her outstretched white hand made the Misfit recoil and shoot. He shot three times in quick succession until she had crumpled and fallen back into the ditch. He stood over her in the ditch and watched her lips settle into a faint smile. He removed his wire-rimmed glasses and used his handkerchief to wipe the flecks of blood off them. Without the lenses his eyes were pale and defenseless and he let them pass over her lifeless body once before he replaced the frames and turned to Bobby Lee and Hiram. “Bury her with the others,” he said. “Boy, ain’t we havin’ some fun today?” Bobby Lee hooted, but the Misfit cut him off. “There’s no real pleasure in life,” he said sharply and walked back to the car.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: The Misfit stood there with his black hat tilted back on his head and his eyes gleaming like two wet stones in the gathering dusk. His face was all angles and shadows, the kind that spoke of something gone wrong in the blood generations back. The grandmother, sprawled in the red clay ditch like a broken china doll in her navy dress with the violet spray still pinned crooked at her collar, reached out one trembling hand toward him as if she might touch salvation itself. "Why you're one of my babies," she said, her voice crackling with a terrible tenderness that made The Misfit jerk back as if he'd been scalded by boiling water from heaven. The bullet cracked through the air three times, precise as scripture, and the grandmother's face froze in a smile that would have made any passing motorist know she had died in a state of grace. The Misfit removed his glasses and there was nothing behind them but two pale holes, like windows in an empty house where someone had forgotten to draw the shade. "Take her with the others," he said, his voice flat as a snake's belly on hot pavement. Bobby Lee's face split in a yellow grin. "Some fun!" he said, but The Misfit's eyes had gone distant, like he was watching something terrible coming down the road toward them all. "It's no real pleasure in life," he said, and for a moment his face looked like it might crack open and show whatever darkness had been growing inside him since before he could remember. The sky above them was the exact color of a bruise, and somewhere in the distance a whip-poor-will called like it was mourning something that hadn't died yet.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Standing on the yellow road in the bright sun, the grandmother before him and Hiram and Bobby Lee just behind, The Misfit sunk deeper into his bitter thinking. There can be no proof of anything—nothing earthly and nothing above—and certainly nothing like salvation for good deeds, or a father waiting and observing from some heavenly perch—and if there was no way to verify the existence of a real God, why live as if that God was watching? The Misfit wondered. The grandmother had on a hat with a brim that cast her face into aged shadows. Her mouth, a flat line, disturbed The Misfit and put a lump in his throat. But the grandmother’s face changed then, softened and clarified, and a beautiful smile spread from her to him. “You are one of my own children,” she said with great compassion, her voice loud and certain, outstretching feeble arms. The Misfit felt a wave of revulsion rising hot and tumorous in his chest and, recoiling, raised his gun and shot her three times. After, the grandmother’s body limp and lifeless in the ditch, the smile remained on her face. Even slumped, her hat upturned beside her, she had an air of perfect grace. Some question of forgiveness came then to The Misfit, which he carefully discarded and, taking off his glasses, surveyed her briefly with pale, defenseless eyes. “Get rid of her,” he told Hiram and Bobby Lee. “Put her with the others.” Bobby Lee chuckled, slapping Hiram on the shoulder, and said “Fun, real fun.” The Misfit turned cool eyes toward him, setting his jaw. “No, Bobby Lee,” he said, “it is not fun—not fun. There is no real pleasure in life.” He turned away from the body and walked on down the yellow road.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I sat in the corner of the room, watching Kevin's face light up as he talked about exploring the West, and felt the familiar twist of unease in my stomach. The shame wasn't sharp anymore – that's what frightened me most. We had learned to live here, learned to accept the unacceptable with a casualness that made my skin crawl when I let myself think about it. The work wasn't what haunted me; it was the easy way we slipped into this life, like wearing someone else's clothes until they started to feel like your own. Margaret's presence loomed over us, not because she might seduce our master – that would have been too simple, too normal – but because she represented everything we were becoming: adaptable, compliant, surviving. Kevin didn't see it that way. His eyes held that historian's gleam, that detached fascination with a time he saw as a story to be witnessed. "Think of seeing the Old West firsthand," he said, and I had to bite back bitter laughter. I wanted to shake him, make him understand that while black bodies were being broken in these Southern fields, native peoples were being slaughtered in his romantic frontier. There was no safe place to stand and observe, no neutral ground from which to watch history unfold. We were in it, drowning in it, and our very ability to adapt was becoming our curse.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I lay on the hard floor in the slave quarters, worrying about Margaret. I knew she was mean and vindictive, and looking for places to put her anger. She could get me whipped, or kicked out. Not for something as normal as sleeping with one's master - there were already slaves who were forced to do that. No, my transgressions would be more subtle - and so I would have to be on closer guard. I made a note to speak to Kevin about this. In the weeks we had been at the house, I'd notice how we'd both adjusted to our new life. I did the work of a slave with the same attitude I had done my chores as a child. Endless drudgery. Bowed heads when the white folks passed. And then dinner out back and a dreamless sleep on the floor. Meanwhile Kevin spent his days in the library; asking Tom questions about how to get out West. "Maybe we could escape, to California," Kevin had said, a few nights ago. "California's a thousand miles away," I said, shaking my head. "Even if we could forge convincing freedom papers, we'd probably die of dengue fever along the way." I didn't add the other thing I was thinking - that it wouldn't be any better out West, where Native Americans were being slaughtered. I couldn't stand to see Kevin get that mystified look on his face. The longer we remained in the house, the more aware I became of our differences.

written_by_MFA001.Original: That was all. I knew then that if Margaret got me kicked out, it wouldn’t be for doing a thing as normal as sleeping with my master. And somehow, that disturbed me. I felt almost as though I really was doing something shameful, happily playing whore for my supposed owner. I went away feeling uncomfortable, vaguely ashamed.Time passed. Kevin and I became more a part of the household, familiar, accepted, accepting. That disturbed me too when I thought about it. How easily we seemed to acclimatize. Not that I wanted us to have trouble, but it seemed as though we should have had a harder time adjusting to this particular segment of history—adjusting to our places in the household of a slaveholder. For me, the work could be hard, but was usually more boring than physically wearing. And Kevin complained of boredom, and of having to be sociable with a steady stream of ignorant pretentious guests who visited the Weylin house. But for drop-ins from another century, I thought we had had a remarkably easy time. And I was perverse enough to be bothered by the ease.“This could be a great time to live in.”Kevin said once. “I keep thinking what an experience it would be to stay in it—go West and watch the building of the country, see how much of the Old West mythology is true.”“West,” I said bitterly. “That’s where they’re doing it to the Indians instead of the blacks!”

written_by_MFA031.Excerpt1: Kevin sat by the window, staring out at the land he claimed was filled with opportunity. “Imagine it,” he said, his voice tinged with awe, “traveling west, seeing the land untouched and untamed.” His excitement was palpable, like a boy imagining adventures in a storybook, but I couldn’t bring myself to share it. “Untamed for who?” I asked, keeping my tone measured. He looked at me then, his brow furrowed in confusion. “Do you think the people already there see it as empty? Do you think they want explorers or settlers taking their homes, their lives?” He didn’t answer immediately, only turned back to the window. The days had been dragging on, each one blurring into the next. Kevin filled his time with idle musings and trivial social obligations, frustrated by the lack of stimulation. I filled mine with a monotony that, while easier than I feared, left me feeling complicit in something vile. Margaret's constant watchful eyes didn’t help; she wasn’t a threat like the physical punishments or the lashings some endured, but her presence unsettled me nonetheless. It wasn’t anything as simple as jealousy—it was something more insidious, a lingering discomfort I couldn’t name. When I finally spoke again, my words were bitter and sharp. “You’re fascinated by their myths, but they’re built on blood. While you dream of cowboys and frontiers, others are living nightmares of chains and whips.” He didn’t look at me, didn’t respond, and for a moment, I hated the silence between us almost as much as the world we were trapped in. It wasn’t just Margaret, wasn’t just Kevin. It was the slow, gnawing realization that we were adapting. That we were becoming something we swore we’d never be.
written_by_MFA031.Excerpt2: After our fourth week on the plantation, what had begun as horrifying became mundane. The muscle memory of sweeping Kevin’s constant stream of coffee mugs from the computer desk blended with the new habits of setting the table just well enough to avoid Margaret’s scrutiny. What was trivial to her was a mystery — sleeping with the master was fine, but leaving out a dish could mean being “fired”. I never realized how dailiness, even under the most brutal form of slavery ever conceived, could lull you into false security. written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The shame burned in my throat, a sour taste I couldn't swallow. Here I was, in this house, in this time, a part of this… this obscenity. Kevin beside me, and us both belonging to a man who thought us less than human.Margaret, with her sly smiles and knowing glances, she was a threat, I knew it. But not the normal kind, not the kind that would have Kevin bedding down with the master. No, this was something different, something more insidious.The days blurred, one into the next. The work, surprisingly, wasn't the hard part. It was the waiting, the knowing, the constant awareness of our place here. Kevin, bless his heart, seemed to find it all rather romantic. "Imagine," he'd say, his eyes alight, "exploring the West, seeing the cowboys and Indians."I'd just stare at him, the bile rising in my throat. "Cowboys and Indians," I'd scoff, "more like thieves and the stolen. While we're chained here in the South, they're out West taking land that never belonged to them."He'd frown, his romantic notions shattered. "It's not the same," he'd argue, "they're not slaves.""No," I'd retort, "but they're not free either. Not when their land is being taken, their way of life destroyed."He'd sigh, the conversation turning sour, as it always did. We were in this together, but we saw it so differently. He, with his head in the clouds, romanticizing the past. Me, with my feet on the ground, seeing the ugliness for what it was.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: My husband’s plan, while shame-inducing, worked. The master of the house believed I was Kevin’s slave, not his wife. I felt awkward around the house’s slaves. I’d tasted a freedom they would never see. Our only threat was Margaret, who seemed to notice that something was amiss. She could tell that we slept together, but a master taking a slave to bed was normal enough — Margaret was all too familiar with that. But perhaps she could tell that we didn’t belong in her era. We awaited that dangerous revelation for some time, but it never came. My work was bland, as was Kevin’s new social life. He always wanted a break despite never having to work. “I think, maybe,” he said, tossing an apple up and down as I cleaned, “we should get out of here. Explore. Visit the west? We could meet a real cowboy!” “So you suggest being nothing more than tourists? As my ancestors stay enslaved in the south? As the natives in the west are exploited?” I felt my voice shifting, becoming sharper, ready to stab. “We’ve traveled through time. Maybe we ought to change history.” Kevin contemplated my outburst, thoughtful but unemotional. “A tempting idea, but we shouldn’t interfere,” he said casually, bit into his apple, and left the room. I scrubbed away at the floor angrily. In this time, and even in our own, his life was made easier by history proceeding exactly as it had. Of course he didn’t want anything to change.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: “Brokeback Mountain’s the only place I’ve ever felt happy. ” Jack’s voice, a raw rasp of longing and frustration, sliced through the quiet Wyoming air.“Four measly weeks a year, that’s all we get. Four weeks, Ennis, while the rest of the year you keep me on a goddamn short leash. Like I’m some kinda stray dog you picked up along the road. ” “I wish I knew how to quit you.”The words hung heavy, a confession and a curse.   Jack’s eyes, the blue of a high-desert sky, were clouded with torment.   “But I can’t.   I’m no good at quittin’. Never have been. Not you, not anything. ”Ennis, his face a mask of pain, crumpled to his knees.   Jack’s words, sharp as barbed wire, had pierced his defenses, drawing blood from his soul.The silence that followed was deafening, broken only by the wind whistling through the pines.“Ennis? ” Jack’s voice was thick with alarm. “What’s wrong? You sick? ”“Jesus,” Ennis choked out, his breath coming in ragged gasps.Jack watched, helpless, as Ennis wrestled with the emotional storm. He’d seen Ennis break horses, wrestle calves, but he’d never seen him like this.Raw, exposed, a man stripped bare by the force of his own feelings.Ennis slowly regained his composure, the storm within subsiding into a dull ache. He stood up, his legs shaky, his eyes fixed on the distant horizon, a vast expanse of sagebrush and sky. The confrontation had changed nothing. Their pain, unspoken yet palpable, hung between them like clouds of steam rising from damp earth on a cold morning.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: “Thing is,” Jack said, “I’m fucking sick of it. Tired of goin nowhere but up the mountain with you. Givin me just Brokeback Mountain is bout as good as givin me nothin, and you know it. I want more–I want it all–and I don’t reckon you’ll ever give it to me. I’m like your dog, chokin on your short leash. All I want is to…it doesn’t matter, do it? Imma dog frothin at the end of your fuckin leash. Goddammit.” He paused for a moment, his breath coming out in short, steaming pants that warmed the tent. “Goddammit. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Jack’s words acted like a rusted arrow upon Ennis–tired, worn out, but not without their raw edge, dangerously sharp. They pierced through him, brought him down to his knees. He lay there on the ground, clutching himself, pale, his wide-eyed gaze fixed on the mountain. “Jesus–” Jack stooped down as if to help him. Was he sick? Jack wondered. Was he finally able to see? Jack’s hands hovered around the other man’s body, but Ennis looked so far away, as if dreaming, and impossible to touch. Ennis got up without his help, recomposing his face into that flat, familiar expression. He rose up from his knees, a man rewound–the dramatic act reversed, so that again he became just a man with a lockbox of feelings. Just Ennis, slumped against the valley. That same far off expression on his face, his hand, gently trembling, grasping at nothing. And that same pain was there too, a shared pain–hot, palpable, unresolved and unrelenting–like clouds of steam rising between them.

written_by_MFA006.Original: “Try this one,” said Jack, “and I’ll say it just one time. Tell you what, we could a had a good life together, a fuckin real good life. You wouldn’t do it, Ennis, so what we got now is Brokeback Mountain. Everything built on that. It’s all we got, boy, fuckin all, so I hope you know that if you don’t never know the rest. Measure the fuckin short leash you keep me on, then ask me about Mexico and then tell me you’ll kill me for needin it and not hardly never gettin it. You got no fuckin idea how bad it gets. Nothing ended, nothing begun, nothing resolved.

Nothing was mended, no path forward uncovered. written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: “You the storm that stranded me here,” said Jack. “Ain’t no other way to put it. I been thinkin on it, bustin my brain to try and fit the bits together, but it’s bullshit. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.
