written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: Once gleaming and luxurious, the resort now tells stories of upheaval in every ballroom and courtyard. This resort of yesterday fares poorly today, and no one comes. Beige African sidewalks collect debris, chairs in the European style and English books. A discarded packet of Belga cigarettes transports visitors to another time, allowing them to trespass on the resort in its antebellum years. The whole discarded era becomes visible—Europeans on holiday attempting to make a home of another's home. Visitors may traipse through the relics spilling from sidewalk to grass, walking on both. Now it is a place hung between that past and a present that has not shaken what came before. Children from town tell stories about the resort, what it was and what lives there now: ghosts of both the travelers and the locals who worked in the lobbies and kitchens when the building retained its purpose, ghosts in luxury clothing inappropriate for the climate and ghosts in neatly pressed uniforms. The older teens climb inside through gaps in the boarded windows and explore the detritus, daring each other to venture deeper and deeper down unlit hallways smelling of mold and dust. They speak in whispers. This small entertainment is laced with the petty danger that emanates now from the building. It can be called a harmless thing, a relic of before: before the departures of the whites and the Asians, before independence, before the mutinies. Yet the building, an ugly shell of itself, persists. It says: "But here I still am."
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: The resort bore the weight of its past in every crumbling façade and every shattered tile strewn across the once-immaculate promenade. The sidewalks were now a repository for the discarded detritus of another era—splintered furniture, faded paperbacks, and Belga cigarette packets flattened underfoot, their familiar logo a ghostly reminder of European elegance. The air, still humid and heavy, carried a vague scent of salt and mildew, mingled with the decay of abandonment. Here, the whisper of colonial nostalgia lingered, like a shadow over the resort's decline. Once a haven for settlers who sought to conjure a slice of Europe amidst Africa's heat, it now stood as a relic of disillusionment. The verandas where drinks had clinked under the laughter of expatriates were hollow, their railings stripped of paint, exposing a rusted skeleton beneath.The tide of independence had washed away the veneer of its purpose. Military mutinies had marked its walls with bullet scars; the exodus of the white and Asian populations had left its rooms unclaimed, their emptiness profound. The palm trees swayed in the wind, their silhouettes etched against a bruised sky, but even they seemed tired, their leaves curling at the edges like burnt paper. What once exuded vitality now lay inert, a tableau of exile and loss. The resort, like the colonizers who had built it, was unmoored—a monument to ambitions that had eroded under the weight of history, leaving behind only silence and the memory of what had been.

written_by_MFA026.Original: Many of the houses that looked abandoned were occupied, by Africans who had come in from the forest and had used the awkward, angular objects they had found, walls, doors, windows, furniture, to re-create the shelter of the round forest hut. Within drawing-rooms they had built shelters; they had raised roofs on verandah half-walls. Fires burned on pieces of corrugated iron; bricks were the cooking stones. On the sidewalks grass had grown around rubbish from the houses, things that couldn’t be used and had been thrown out: cracked squares of picture glass, fragments of upholstered chairs, mattresses that had been disembowelled for their springs, books and magazines whose pages had stuck together in solid, crinkled pads. Once Bobby saw a flattened cigarette packet, black on faded red: Belga. The sidewalks, once bustling with tourists, were now littered with the remnants of a bygone era: broken furniture, discarded books, and flattened cigarette packets.  Among the debris, a Belga cigarette packet, a relic of European holidays, hinted at the resort's colonial past.  It was a place built by settlers who sought to recreate a familiar European lifestyle in the heart of Africa.The resort's decline mirrored the broader social and political changes that had reshaped the region.  Independence, military mutinies, and the exodus of white and Asian settlers had left the resort without purpose, a ghost of its former self.  The buildings, once grand and imposing, now bore the scars of neglect, their paint peeling and their windows boarded up.  The gardens, once meticulously manicured, were now overgrown and wild, a testament to the absence of the hands that once tended them.The resort's decline was not merely physical; it was also a reflection of the societal shifts that had accompanied decolonization.  The old order, with its rigid hierarchies and its imported European culture, had been swept away, leaving behind a void that was yet to be filled.  The resort, once a symbol of colonial power and privilege, now stood as a monument to the complexities of post-colonial identity.  It was a place where the past and the present collided, where the remnants of a colonial past were juxtaposed with the uncertainties of a post-colonial future.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: The forecourt wore it well—time, and the fickle seasons of democracy in this place. The moldings decorating the façade betrayed nothing either, except perhaps the usual negligence, the fine patina of dust that came over everything in Africa. But in its interior courtyards, in its once-ornate villas and lush gardens, where the Crown’s servants had dealt out their decks of cards atop white tablecloths, nothing stirred. A grim silence overwhelmed the resort. The grass yellowed under termite-ridden bedframes and writing desks; around them, rags of newspaper and littered correspondences. Vague ink-stains remained on these pages; and a sentence that, ten years ago, could martial an army from one corner of the empire to another was now indecipherable. A pack of “Belga” cigarettes had survived free Africa, escaped the line of white and Asian refugees at the docks, the inevitable mutiny and the mutiny after that. It lay sedately on a bench. For years, its odor would not leave the wooden slats; and in its slim shape it carried the vestiges of wet, European summers, trails of water from the pool to the bar, the rattle of ice in a tumbler, liveried black boys sweating in the corner, out of sight and at hand. There had been no native plants, no local liquors, no reminders of Africa at the resort—except its conveniences. The brand of cigarettes, of course, was extinct; the company had settled into ruin when its directors left on the outbound ships. The cigarettes were manufactured, now, in the countryside, by Africans; everybody smoked, and the sky slowly turned gray.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: The dilapidation that had befallen the resort was to be expected; it had been a place for rest for those who had come to sow unrest, and now that the country was in a state of repair, that which had once been repaired was left to rot. But there were still definite traces of life—beetles that scuttled about licking up dots of water from rivets in aged tiles, vines that wrapped up and through the sides of the canopy built to allow proprietors to gaze at a view without being at the mercy of the cruel sun, thickets of brush with twig-like branches that lined the path to the long-sealed front doors now grew unwieldy and sharp, as their nature demanded. But so too, prominent, were the signs of abandon. A pack of Belga cigarettes, the faded packaging promising style and mystical aura, lay on a patio table. If one listened in the silence, one could almost hear the smacking of thin European lips that may have once suckled the tobacco while remarking about the grand African sun or commenting on the foliage. But the sound would soon be drowned out by the noise of a country that had moved on to larger things—where words like "reclaim," "rebuild," "remove" erupted out of automobiles, cafes, town halls, meeting circles, makeshift stages, military bases, parliament buildings, and where, yes, perhaps, there was still space for the word "resort," but only if used in the phrase "last resort." And so the empty building sat, bludgeoned by the naked sun, waiting again for peace, for purpose.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: The resort lay like a discarded memory, its swimming pools filled with brackish water and fallen leaves – not the romantic decay of abandoned European castles, but the hasty, unplanned desertion of a colonial dream. Walking along the cracked sidewalks, where weeds pushed through with primitive determination, I saw the debris of departed lives: a sodden Belga cigarette packet, its blue and white design still visible, speaking of evenings when settlers sat in wicker chairs discussing home leave and servant troubles; a broken tennis racquet, its strings dangling like the exposed nerves of a dead thing, recalling Sunday afternoon games followed by gin and tonics on the clubhouse veranda. Everything here had been arranged to deny Africa, to create an illusion of Surrey or Sussex: the neat flowerbeds, now choked with wild grass, the carefully planned paths that led to viewing points designed to frame the landscape like an English watercolor. But Africa had returned, seeping through the cracks, asserting itself in the persistent growth that threatened to swallow the mock-Tudor buildings, in the small creatures that had made homes in abandoned tea rooms. The place possessed now a particular sadness – not of ruins, which suggest grandeur, but of irrelevance. Like the colonial administrators' files still rotting in some government office, like the old settlers' clubs with their dated photographs and empty bars, it belonged to a world that had ended not with ceremony but with a series of small surrenders, each one unremarkable in itself, until one day the illusion simply ceased to hold.

Once Bobby saw a flattened cigarette packet, black on faded red: Belga. It recalled European holidays: as though Belgium and Europe had once lain across the water, and the lake had only been a version of the English Channel. This resort hadn’t been built for tourists in Africa; it had been created by people who thought they had come to Africa to stay, and looked in a resort for a version of the things of home: a park, a pier, a waterside promenade. Now, after the troubles across the lake, after independence and the property scare, after the army mutiny, after the white exodus South and the Asian deportations, after all these deaths, the resort no longer had a function.

written_by_MFA010.Original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. Perhaps my father’s support ended now, perhaps I had failed him, perhaps this moment would end this chapter of my life and its purpose. All my anxieties melted when we embraced. He surged toward me as we met, pumping his arms to pat me on the back with reverent enthusiasm, then pulling me close to his chest as he had when I was a child, and I felt his pride. He held me out in front of him and smiled. “You will succeed, my son,” he said. “You will win prestigious prizes and teach somewhere.” It is this memory I cling to after his death in 2002—how he remained such a father to me.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I remember the moment I handed over my first novel, "Cevdet Bey and His Sons," to my father as if it were encased in amber, frozen in a delicate yet trembling moment of time. In the quiet of our Istanbul apartment, the weight of the manuscript in my hands mirrored the gravity of the step I was about to take. My mother, though ever loving, had dismissed my ambitions as mere indulgence, a detour from the secure path she imagined for me. My father, however, had always encouraged the flickering flame of my aspirations. He took the manuscript with an easy, almost playful smile, as though we were conspirators in some artistic rebellion. When he returned, his embrace was not rushed or obligatory—it was deliberate, a gesture heavy with the unspoken weight of approval. It was as if he had passed a verdict, not only on the book but on the very path I had chosen for my life. He didn’t speak immediately; instead, he held me, his silence filled with a fatherly pride that words might have diminished. Then, in a voice steadied by conviction, he said I would succeed and even prophesied a prestigious prize in my future. The precision of his faith startled me—how could he be so sure when I wasn’t? This memory, so vivid and immutable, grew to anchor me, particularly after his death in 2002. It is strange how the weight of approval from someone who is no longer there can linger like a ghost in the room, shaping the contours of your own self-belief. My father’s prediction, his prophecy of my future success, stands as a monument to his faith in me, a beacon amidst the ever-shifting uncertainties of life and art.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: On that spring evening in Istanbul, when the Bosphorus was painted in shades of amber and violet, I handed my father the manuscript of "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" with trembling hands that betrayed both hope and terror. The pages, worn from countless revisions and bearing the weight of my artistic ambitions, disappeared into his leather briefcase – the same briefcase I had watched him carry to his office countless times throughout my childhood. In the days that followed, I wandered the streets of Nişantaşı like a guilty man, examining the faces of passersby as if they might offer some preview of my father's judgment. Unlike my mother, who had always viewed my literary aspirations with the kind of worried skepticism reserved for a child's dangerous games, my father had maintained a curious silence about my choice to abandon architecture for the solitary life of a novelist. I remember sitting in the old Pamuk Apartments, listening to the distant ferry horns and watching the dust particles dance in the afternoon light that filtered through the heavy curtains, wondering if I had disappointed him. When he finally returned home that evening, before any words could form between us, he embraced me with an intensity that spoke volumes in our family's language of unspoken emotions. Later, as we sat in his study surrounded by his beloved books – the ones that had first taught me to love literature – he broke our emotional silence with words that would echo through the decades: "You will win great prizes one day." That moment hung between us like a photograph yellowing with age, gaining new meaning after his death in 2002, when I found myself standing alone in that same study, running my fingers along the spines of his books, feeling the weight of his absence and the enduring power of his belief in me.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.

written_by_MFA032.Excerpt1: She was in danger of a mood; if I am to remain still, Clarissa thought, it will overtake me, it will make the world unwelcome with me, turn it dim and desiccated, and poor Lucy will bear the brunt, or Rumpelmayer’s men, who were laying the table. “I’ll do it,” Clarissa said, and she said it again, as if worried that the words had not escaped the confines of her thought, “I’ll get the flowers, Lucy.” She left the house. Yes, at Bourton, the thought of sending Lucy would not have arisen; Clarissa would purchase the flowers and admire them freely. But in London, a strong wind carried the brine of the Thames; it stank; it irritated her lungs, her heart; the odor of the flowers would, too. And there came Peter Walsh, sailing in on an airy, unnamed ship, saying, “What match is a cauliflower for a man?” (Around his voice, Clarissa recognized the faint crunch and tinkling of a decade-old breakfast.) Peter will return from India like that—on which date and at which time his ship would dock in England should have been unimportant to Clarissa, and yet she wondered; she called up his last letters, filed away in a familiar groove, and read them again, and with each word, London decayed, fell away like petals, and in its place, she erected another cathedral. Inside it, relics, some potent to the touch, some no more than shriveled digits, long-empty boxes.
written_by_MFA032.Excerpt2: Clarissa stepped into the brisk morning air, her gaze lifting to the soft haze of London streets, a breath catching in her chest, carrying with it the scent of fresh blooms and the faint rumble of Rumpelmayer’s men unloading their crates. She would buy the flowers herself, sparing Lucy the trouble, and in the act, indulging that faint, persistent thrill of slipping out unencumbered, her steps crisp, her thoughts unfurling. Bourton, as if summoned by the cool touch of the breeze, rose vivid before her. The mornings there had carried a peculiar gravity, the air saturated with the promise of youth, of life, at eighteen—the world trembling on the cusp of discovery. She could feel it still, the dewy grass against her shoes, the sharp burst of laughter carried on the wind, and Peter Walsh, always Peter, his voice teasing yet tethered to something deeper. “I prefer men to cauliflowers,” he had said once, over breakfast, as if the absurdity of the phrase could mask the intensity beneath it. And now, after all these years, Peter was returning. From India, of all places, with letters she could scarcely recall opening properly, their pages crammed with the tangents of a restless mind. She had always thought of him as a man on the edge of some revelation, never quite within reach. His words lingered, some sharp, some softened with time, like the murmur of a distant wave retreating. Yet it was the texture of him she remembered most—the way his presence filled the room, the peculiar weight of his silences. The day unfolded before her, rich and strange, and as the sunlight broke through the fog, she felt herself poised, a solitary figure on the cusp of past and present, out in the world, yet curiously, utterly alone.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Orin’s mornings often began as a kind of existential residue, the aftermath of dreams that seemed to gnaw their way out from the deep recesses of the psyche’s cellar, dreams that were equal parts spiders and sheer verticality, both suffocating and vertiginous. The mornings required ritual, regimented almost to the point of ceremony: coffee brewed to a darkness that could rival the void, showers so scalding they left his skin reddened, runs that turned his lungs into bellows just to remind himself he was alive. Yet the presence of a Subject—the capital "S" both deliberate and derisive, a holdover from what Orin thought of as his internal marketing manual for coping with emotional distance—would complicate the sequence. Subjects had a tendency toward earnest, unbidden gestures: talking as though morning were a shared phenomenon, attempting to wrap him in the tangled warmth of their limbs, even cooking eggs with a kind of oblivious cheer that Orin could only describe as offensive. The worst was the silence, the gap in conversation where their gaze hung too long on him, expectant. Alone, though, wasn’t better. The walls of his apartment took on the sheen of inevitability, the day ahead a Sisyphean incline of meetings and errands and human interactions that he already knew would leave him feeling as drained as the coffee grounds spiraling down his sink. This, he thought, was life’s greatest irony: that waking up alive could feel so much like falling.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: That it's somehow both pathetic and profound how Orin's post-dream consciousness becomes this sort of infinite regression of anxieties, each one feeding into and sort of birthing the next, like those Russian nesting dolls except imagine each smaller doll is progressively more damaged than its container. written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: Orin woke up next to the subject, mentally flaying himself for referring to this person as such, but using the same voice to berate himself that he used to describe this person as a subject, so the whole process became moot. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It seemed to me that it had never rained that hard. I might as well have been out in the next great flood with all that rain, but I didn’t mind. Watching Phoebe in her new blue coat go round and round on that shiny carousel horse made me feel so damn warm, that I hardly even noticed the cold wet of it all. My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. Do you intend to try in school?” My brother, D.B., the screenwriter, likes to visit and ask me mind-numbing questions, too, though he’s not nearly as bad at the psycho- babblers. He’s not so bad because he’s my brother, and I do love him, so I tolerate the million- and-one questions, but I still wish he’d cut back on the interrogations. He brought this glamorous actress, a Brit, to visit with him, and while she’s off powdering her nose or whatever girls do in the bathroom, D.B. asks me: “How are you feeling, champ, about everything that’s happened?” I tell him, slowly, the details of the last few days. It’s strange to say it out loud, rather than just in my head, where I can say whatever I want. But it’s nice, too, a relief, even. Telling D.B. about it makes him lean in close to listen, and I feel close to him, not just physically but emotionally. Like my brother is really with me. Talking about Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice, it feels like they’re with me, too. I don’t even like those guys, but talking about them makes me feel…surrounded. I don’t think I’m a happy person, but talking about when I was happy, with Phoebe, I feel like I could be.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.

written_by_MFA025.Original: Boy, it began to rain like a bastard. In buckets, I swear to God. All the parents and mothers and everybody went over and stood right under the roof of the carrousel, so they wouldn’t get soaked to the skin or anything, but I stuck around on the bench for quite a while. I got pretty soaking wet, especially my neck and my pants. My hunting hat really gave me quite a lot of protection, in a way; but I got soaked anyway. I didn’t care, though. I felt so damn happy all of sudden, the way old Phoebe kept going around and around. I was damn near bawling, I felt so damn happy, if you want to know the truth. I don’t know why. It was just that she looked so damn nice, the way she kept going around and around, in her blue coat and all. God, I wish you could’ve been there.That’s all I’m going to tell about. I could probably tell you what I did after I went home, and how I got sick and all, and what school I’m supposed to go to next fall, after I get out of here, but I don’t feel like it. I really don’t. That stuﬀ doesn’t interest me too much right now.A lot of people, especially this one psychoanalyst guy they have here, keeps asking me if I’m going apply myself when I go back to school next September. It’s such a stupid question, in my opinion. I mean how do you know what you’re going to do till you do it? The answer is, you don’t. I think I am, but how do I know? I swear it’s a stupid question. D.B. isn’t as bad as the rest of them, but he keeps asking me a lot of questions, too. He drove over last Saturday with this English babe that’s in this new picture he’s writing. She was pretty aﬀected, but very good-looking. Anyway, one time when she went to the ladies’ room way the hell down in the other wing D.B. asked me what I thought about all this stuﬀ I just ﬁnished telling you about. I didn’t know what the hell to say. If you want to know the truth, I don’t know what I think about it. I’m sorry I told so many people about it. About all I know is, I sort of miss everybody I told about. Even old Stradlater and Ackley, for instance. I think I even miss that goddam Maurice. It’s funny. Don’t ever tell anybody anything. If you do, you start missing everybody.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: It seemed to me that it had never rained that hard. I might as well have been out in the next great flood with all that rain, but I didn’t mind. Watching Phoebe in her new blue coat go round and round on that shiny carousel horse made me feel so damn warm, that I hardly even noticed the cold wet of it all. My hunting hat shielded me a bit, but that got soaked fast. In no time at all, I was drenched. Totally soaked, but totally happy, too. I could hear Phoebe laughing on the horse, and of course she wasn’t wet under the carousel’s awning. She seemed to me completely free. I guess I could have gotten upset, shivering as I was and my clothes so heavy with water that they were falling off of me. My shoes squished when I moved even a little, but I felt like a million bucks watching Phoebe. The happiness didn’t last, though, not through to right now. I’m stuck in this miserable “rest” home, where I can’t even rest. How am I meant to relax when these idiot psychoanalysts keep pelting me with idiot questions? One of them badgers me with nonsense like, “But how do you expect do have a future if you don’t care to maintain your present? You need to try in school. Do you intend to try in school?” My brother, D.B., the screenwriter, likes to visit and ask me mind-numbing questions, too, though he’s not nearly as bad at the psycho- babblers. He’s not so bad because he’s my brother, and I do love him, so I tolerate the million- and-one questions, but I still wish he’d cut back on the interrogations. He brought this glamorous actress, a Brit, to visit with him, and while she’s off powdering her nose or whatever girls do in the bathroom, D.B. asks me: “How are you feeling, champ, about everything that’s happened?” I tell him, slowly, the details of the last few days. It’s strange to say it out loud, rather than just in my head, where I can say whatever I want. But it’s nice, too, a relief, even. Telling D.B. about it makes him lean in close to listen, and I feel close to him, not just physically but emotionally. Like my brother is really with me. Talking about Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice, it feels like they’re with me, too. I don’t even like those guys, but talking about them makes me feel…surrounded. I don’t think I’m a happy person, but talking about when I was happy, with Phoebe, I feel like I could be.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: It started raining like hell out of nowhere, the way it does when you don’t have a goddam umbrella. I was standing there, freezing my tail off, watching Phoebe ride the carousel. She was wearing this blue coat that flared out every time the horse went up, like it had its own personality or something. I swear, she was the only one who didn’t look phony on the whole goddam planet. I pulled my hunting hat down tight, the one I always wore backward, like some kind of idiot. It didn’t do much, but I didn’t give a damn. Watching her, I got this weird lump in my throat, like I wanted to bawl and laugh at the same time. It was the damnedest thing. I just stood there getting soaked and didn’t even care. The next part’s harder to talk about. It’s all tied up with that place I’m in now—the rest home or whatever the hell they call it. The shrink keeps asking me about my plans, like he’s expecting me to say I want to be a goddam astronaut or something. “Are you going to apply yourself?” he keeps asking, like that’s the magic question that’ll unlock the universe. I told him I didn’t know and asked if he had a cigarette. He didn’t think that was funny. Shrinks never do. D.B. came to visit me once. He brought this actress he’s dating—some glamorous British type who probably says “lovely” instead of “nice.” She went to the bathroom, and D.B. leaned over like he was about to share some deep, brotherly wisdom. He asked me what I thought about everything that happened, the whole damn mess. I didn’t know what to say. I mean, I hate talking about stuff like that. It just makes you miss people. Even the ones you don’t like all that much, like Stradlater and Ackley. Hell, even Maurice, that lousy pimp. It’s like, the more you tell the story, the more it feels like they’re right there with you, and then, poof, they’re gone again. I told D.B. it was fine, just fine, and then the actress came back, smelling like expensive soap or something.Anyway, that’s the thing about telling people stuff. You think it’ll make you feel better, but it just makes you feel worse, like you’re carrying around this big, stupid ache. But maybe that’s the point. Maybe you’re supposed to miss people. Even the ones you don’t want to. It’s goddam beautiful and sad all at the same time, and I don’t know if I’ll ever figure it out. Maybe nobody does. Maybe that’s the whole thing.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: While I was watching Phoebe circle round and round on the carousel, it started to rain real hard. It was the heaviest rain I’d seen in a long, long time. Maybe ever. It was coming down in buckets. Even barrels. My hunting hat helped protect my hair a little, but I was soaked all the way to my bones. I didn’t think I’d ever get dry. But even though I was cold and wet, I couldn’t stop feeling so happy that every raindrop was like a miniature sun. I watched Phoebe laughing and waving in her blue coat. She was smiling real big, and after a little while, I realized I was smiling too. The painted horses on the carousel went up and down, and I didn’t want them to ever stop. Then I ended up here, where nobody smiles like Phoebe and I’m not allowed outside by myself. It doesn’t rain very often around here, but when it does, I sit by the windows and remember what it felt like to stand in that crazy downpour. Then I smile just to myself, like a secret. Everybody here asks me the stupidest questions I’ve ever heard. Especially that one doctor. He asked me the other day about whether I plan on applying myself when I go back to school. “That’s none of your goddamn business,” I said to him. “You’re right,” he said. “It isn’t really my business. But it’s your business, isn’t it? Don’t you think your future deserves some consideration?” I told him he was the biggest phony I’d ever met in my life. It probably wasn’t true, but in the moment, it sure felt like it. This doctor keeps telling me I have lots of potential and that if I don’t get better, I’ll waste it. I think he should worry about wasting his own potential. What kind of doctor wants to be stuck in a place like this talking to people like me? Sometimes my brother D.B. comes to visit. He’s a screenwriter, and not as bad as the other people here, but he still asks lots of questions. Mostly stuff about medicine, which I don’t like talking about, and television, which I’m not even allowed to watch here. The last time he came, he brought along an English actress who wore lots of sparkles. She seemed nervous and kept telling me how brave I was. When she left to go to the bathroom, D.B. asked me what I thought about everything that happened. And I realized that talking about everything made me miss everyone it happened with. Even people I didn’t like—even Stradlater, Ackley, and Maurice. And I don’t want to miss anyone anymore.

written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: Ernie Botts. Ernie. My younger cousin, who was to remain a lifelong bachelor, had once spent each summer with us on the farm, showing up shyly in tow that first season in the shadow of my Aunt Nell. I hadn’t liked having to share a room with my sister, as I did when he came to visit. But he made up for it, with his good-natured affability, and his curious habit of punctilious grooming. I’d had the idea to call him Earnest Bottom-and my use of this nickname behind his back brought my sister and myself no end of amusement. The visits stopped when Aunt Nell passed, Ernie then thirteen. His presence in our house dwindled to a card each Christmas in his spidery handwriting. At eighteen I took the train out to the city, planning to start university at last and my new life. That my cousin lived there too was the last thing on my mind. It was my mother who reminded me. She told me I should look him up, conjuring at once his easy, slightly high-pitched laugh, his perfectly brushed wool sweaters. From then, Ernie and I had dinner every other Sunday, at a place called the Old Chelsea. I wasn’t sure why. I couldn’t tell if he had real fondness for me. His old habits of grooming were accompanied now by a certain formality of speech. It wasn’t a cheap restaurant either, but one of those old-style, stiff tablecloth establishments that used to be in vogue then. We always had three courses and wine. I assumed his loyalty to the Old Chelsea, and to me, meant he could easily afford such luxuries.
written_by_MFA033.Excerpt2: Ernie Botts—whom I privately called "Earnest Bottom" in those days of ruthless teenage cleverness—would arrive at our farm each summer with Aunt Nell, his clothes pressed and his hair neatly combed, as if the three-hour drive on dusty country roads had somehow failed to touch him. He had that particular quality of bachelor sons, a kind of pristine wholesomeness that spoke of carefully maintained routines and unspoken maternal guidance. After Aunt Nell died (a quick death, heart attack while hanging laundry), the summer visits stopped, though Christmas cards arrived without fail, bearing generic winter scenes and his meticulously penned signature. Years later, when I started college in his city, he began taking me to dinner at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday—a restaurant with heavy maroon drapes and waiters who wore black bow ties with an air of weary dignity. I suspected these dinners cost more than he should have spent, but there was something both touching and slightly oppressive about his insistence on maintaining this connection, as if he were fulfilling some deathbed promise to Aunt Nell that I'd never been told about. I assumed he could afford it; after all, he lived in an apartment building with a doorman and wore suits that looked expensive in their subtle way. But sometimes I'd catch him studying the menu with a carefully blank expression, and I'd remember how Aunt Nell used to darken last year's coat with shoe polish to make it look new. There are some kinds of family duty that run deeper than affection, I suppose, though I never quite knew which one brought Ernie to that restaurant every other Sunday, in his good suit, precisely on time.

It probably cost more, strictly speaking, than he could afford, but I did not think of that, having a country girl’s notion that all men who lived in the city, wore a suit every day, and sported such clean fingernails had reached a level of prosperity where indulgences like this were a matter of course.

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: Ernie Botts—Earnest Bottom, as I’d christened him in the foolish privacy of my head—was the clean and well-groomed sort of boy my mother admired.  He was always neat, pressed, and polite, the kind who’d never show up with grass stains or a ripped shirt.  Each summer, he’d arrive at our farm with his mother, Aunt Nell, a high-pitched echo of my mother’s pronouncements on how a young man ought to behave.  After Aunt Nell passed, the summer visits stopped, replaced by the steady arrival of Christmas cards—always signed “Ernie,” never the “Earnest Bottom” of my childhood.    Years later, when I found myself in his city for college, Ernie took it upon himself to take me out to dinner every other Sunday.  The Old Chelsea, the restaurant he chose, was the kind of place with heavy silverware and hushed conversations, the sort of place I figured Ernie frequented—though how a bachelor school teacher could afford it, I didn’t know.  Perhaps I’d underestimated a school teacher’s salary, or perhaps, like the old aunts I’d left back home, he’d scrimped and saved for the sake of appearances.  Ernie wasn’t much of a conversationalist, and I often found myself making idle chatter, filling the silences between his polite inquiries about my studies and his pronouncements on the weather.  I figured it was family duty that brought him, not any real desire for my company.  Still, there was something amusing about being seen in such a place with a man like Ernie—Earnest Bottom, the clean-cut boy turned proper bachelor.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: Aunt Nell used to tote Cousin Ernie Botts to the farm every summer like he was an old handbag or umbrella. He never seemed to mind, smiling banally to show off his fantastic straight, white teeth. He was a clean boy, a good boy, so much so that in the privacy of my own mind, I called him Earnest Bottom. When Aunt Nell passed, there was no one to drag sweet Ernie around, so we stopped seeing him for a while. Mother made sure to send him Christmas cards every year, and I’d doodle him little flowers and rainbows on the back. After I was accepted into college, I wrote him a little note instead, telling him I’d be moving to his city. He wrote back saying we really ought to get dinner once I was settled. We did, and it morphed into an every-other-Sunday affair. Ernie would pick me up at my dorm and drive me to a charming little restaurant called the Old Chelsea. Ernie insisted on us ordering two appetizers each, a main course, dessert, and of course, an after-dinner coffee. The checks, when I managed to glimpse them, always made my eyes bug. But Ernie was a good person, and the elaborate dinners never seemed to me a desire to show off, but rather a way to remain a part of the family. If he could spend so confidently every other week, I presumed he was working one of those legitimate office jobs. He never did talk all that much about himself.

Ernie was prim and manicured and always seemed to be dusting off his pants or scraping mud from the soles of his shoes. At Aunt Nell's funeral, he shook everyone's hands in his freshly pressed suit and thanked them for the flowers. He stopped coming to the farm after that, but we kept in touch through Christmas cards, which he always signed with a kind, personalized note. Our paths ran perpendicular again when I went to graduate school in his city. As soon as he heard I was in town, he locked me into his calendar for dinner every other Sunday. The Old Chelsea had an excellent fillet mignon, he told me, and it was true. The food offset the conversation, which was stale at best. Talk of work and school died out quickly, and I felt guilty talking about my social life—while I was making friends and had started going steady with a classmate, Ernie seemed to be suspended in self-imposed monkhood. Somehow, the bill always ended up in Ernie's hands. “It’s the least I can do,” he’d say, batting away the money I offered, and I couldn’t help but wonder what he thought he owed me.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: During those summers on the farm, Ernie Botts, who we’d mischievously dubbed “Earnest Bottom,” became a predictable part of the season, like the first crop of sweet corn or the relentless hum of cicadas. He was always impeccably groomed—his blond hair neatly combed, his fingernails somehow untouched by dirt, even after a day spent traipsing through the fields. He was good-natured in a way that set him apart from the brashness of other cousins who fought over fishing rods or snickered at Aunt Nell’s awkward manners. Ernie simply smiled and carried on, often humming quietly as he helped with chores or indulged my younger siblings by playing checkers on the front porch. When Aunt Nell passed away, his visits ended, replaced only by his dutiful Christmas cards that seemed to grow shorter with each year. By the time I moved to his city for college, he was a figure shrouded in distant nostalgia, though he reappeared with an almost rehearsed sincerity, treating me to dinners at the Old Chelsea every other Sunday. The crisp white napkins, the polite waitstaff, the gleaming wine glasses—it all seemed to mirror Ernie himself, and I couldn’t shake the feeling that these outings were more about obligation than genuine kinship. But still, I didn’t protest. His generosity, even if tinged with a faint remoteness, filled the silences left by years and miles, a duty performed with meticulous care and quiet resolve.

written_by_MFA029.Original: My mother had a bachelor cousin a good deal younger than her, who used to visit us on the farm every summer. He brought along his mother, Aunt Nell Botts. His own name was Ernie Botts. He was a tall, florid man with a good-natured expression, a big square face, and fair curly hair springing straight up from his forehead. His hands, his fingernails were as clean as soap itself; his hips were a little plump. My name for him—when he was not around—was Earnest Bottom. I had a mean tongue.But I meant no harm. Or hardly any harm.After Aunt Nell Botts died Ernie did not come to visit anymore, but he always sent a Christmas card.When I started college in the city where he lived, he began a custom of taking me out to dinner every other Sunday evening. He did this because I was a relative—it’s unlikely that he even considered whether we were suited to spending time together. He always took me to the same place, a restaurant called the Old Chelsea, which was on the second floor of a building, looking down on Dundas Street. It had velvet curtains, white tablecloths, little rose-shaded lamps on the tables. It probably cost more, strictly speaking, than he could afford, but I did not think of that, having a country girl’s notion that all men who lived in the city, wore a suit every day, and sported such clean fingernails had reached a level of prosperity where indulgences like this were a matter of course.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Like most people, Walter and Patty Berglund had a past life. Unlike most people, this past life took place in St. Paul, Minnesota. In the Berglunds’ current life in Washington D.C., where they had moved two years prior, Walter was falling from grace. It was perhaps less like a fall and more like a plummet. An article in the New York Times had just been published, ruthlessly exposing his corrupt dealings with the coal industry. These misdeeds included but were not limited to bribery, extortion, embezzlement, and profiteering. In describing Walter, the article made generous use of words like “arrogant” and “ethically compromised,” which Walter’s old neighbors in Ramsey Hill found difficult to process. In their memories, he had been an idealistic, environmentally conscious man who commuted across town by bike even in the most vicious of sleet and hail. Many had once considered Walter to be the embodiment of rural, green values—someone who set an aspirational standard for the rest to follow. It seemed he had experienced a change of heart since leaving town. When the Berglunds first moved to Ramsey Hill, they worked doggedly to revitalize the neglected neighborhood. When asked what brought them to Ramsey Hill, the Berglunds gave vague half-answers about the real estate market and wanting to be involved in something from the ground floor. They bought a cheap, shambling Victorian house and renovated it with stoic resolve. Together, they slowly won out over every obstacle they faced, from vandalism to unruly neighbors to general disrepair. Patty, a former athlete, always liked a challenge. She wheeled her infant son’s stroller through the gritty neighborhood, weaving deftly between cracks in the sidewalk, never breaking her strong, assured pace. She marched through a regiment of cooking, cleaning, repairing, and caring for the baby with an endurance forged in years of grueling, all-day swim practices. Even her indulgences—public radio and zinfandel—were stringently measured, slotted into the schedule with militant rigidity. Walter and Patty gave every indication that they were here in Ramsey Hill to stay, and nobody thought otherwise. But as the Berglunds built up their house and the surrounding area, they were really building less of a home and more of a ladder.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The irony of Walter's transformation from eco-warrior to coal industry collaborator wasn't lost on the former neighbors in Ramsey Hill, though they nursed their disappointment with the kind of passive-aggressive Midwestern restraint that had always made Patty want to scream into her wine glass. The Times piece had painted him as a sellout, which wasn't exactly wrong but missed the essentially Walter-ish quality of his failure – the way his very righteousness had somehow curdled into its opposite, like milk left too long in a virtuous organic glass bottle. In the early days, watching him pedal off to work on his secondhand Schwinn, his messenger bag stuffed with environmental impact reports and local-economy manifestos, the neighbors had seen him as a kind of secular saint, the sort of man who made them feel better about their own smaller gestures toward planetary salvation. Patty, meanwhile, had performed her own theatre of domestic virtue, pushing that double-wide stroller past crack houses and shuttered storefronts with the kind of aggressive cheer that suggested she was either oblivious to danger or actively courting it. The Victorian they'd bought for a song had been their shared project, their statement of faith in the possibility of redemption – not just of a house or a neighborhood, but of a whole way of life that was vanishing as surely as the ozone layer they worried about while listening to All Things Considered. Every stripped floorboard and replastered wall had seemed to say: See? This is how you do it. This is how you live righteously in a fallen world. But righteousness, it turned out, was a kind of intoxicant, and Walter had drunk deeper than most. The coal deal was just the logical endpoint of his conviction that he alone could save the world – a conviction that had grown more desperate and less discriminating as the world had shown itself increasingly resistant to being saved. The neighbors, sipping their own carefully sourced wine and tending their own carefully curated gardens, could afford to judge him now, secure in the knowledge that they, at least, had never tried quite so hard to be good.

written_by_MFA029.Original: The news about Walter Berglund wasn’t picked up locally—he and Patty had moved away to Washington two years earlier and meant nothing to St. Paul now—but the urban gentry of Ramsey Hill were not so loyal to their city as not to read the New York Times. According to a long and very unflattering story in the Times, Walter had made quite a mess of his professional life out there in the nation’s capital. His old neighbors had some difficulty reconciling the quotes about him in the Times (“arrogant,” “high-handed,” “ethically compromised”) with the generous, smiling, red-faced 3M employee they remembered pedaling his commuter bicycle up Summit Avenue in February snow; it seemed strange that Walter, who was greener than Greenpeace and whose own roots were rural, should be in trouble now for conniving with the coal industry and mistreating country people. Then again, there had always been something not quite right about the Berglunds.Walter and Patty were the young pioneers of Ramsey Hill—the first college grads to buy a house on Barrier Street since the old heart of St.Paul had fallen on hard times three decades earlier. They paid nothing for their Victorian and then killed themselves for ten years renovating it. Early on, some very determined person torched their garage and twice broke into their car before they got the garage rebuilt. Sunburned bikers descended on the vacant lot across the alley to drink Schlitz and grill knockwurst and rev engines at small hours until Patty went outside in sweatclothes and said, “Hey, you guys, you know what?” Patty frightened nobody, but she’d been a standout athlete in high school and college and possessed a jock sort of fearlessness. From her first day in the neighborhood, she was helplessly conspicuous. Tall, ponytailed, absurdly young, pushing a stroller past stripped cars and broken beer bottles and barfed-upon old snow, she might have been carrying all the hours of her day in the string bags that hung from her stroller. Behind her you could see the baby-encumbered preparations for a morning of baby-encumbered errands; ahead of her, an afternoon of public radio, the Silver Palate Cookbook, cloth diapers, drywall compound, and latex paint; and then Goodnight Moon, then zinfandel.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The people of St. Paul did not know what to make of the article; no, they could not even begin to wrap their heads around it. The New York Times, unforgiving and direct as they were, used such terms as "arrogant," "ethically compromised," and "Machiavellian" to describe Walter. These descriptions did not resonate with the mild folks of St. Paul, and, with Walter and Patty so far away in that vague place called DC, they found themselves remarkably able to preserve the veneer of what they believed Walter, and Patty for that matter, to be. The local women remembered handsome Walter, gold-skinned and smiling, commuting to work by bike, that sheen of sweat making a mustache of diamonds over his handsomely curved upper lip. The men remembered Walter rolling out the evergreen-colored recycling bin on those Wednesday mornings, the way it teetered with the weight of everything he had so meticulously and carefully separated from the regular trash.It just wouldn't do; no, it didn't compute—this image of Walter snuggled up in bed with the coal industry. That couple had poured life into Ramsey Hill, buying that decrepit and dirt-cheap Victorian house with the Napoleonic turrets and the cream wraparound porch. If they squinted, they could all picture Patty outside, painting over the word "Fuck" that a hooligan had sprayed onto the house's flank one night: she with her unflinching athleticism, the kind acquired in college sports, pushing a stroller with that well-weathered batting arm, a bag of apples in the other. If she was not standing on a ladder, scraping out the gutters like a man, she was drinking zinfandel at that gorgeous kitchen island she'd done herself, the public radio on, too loudly for most of the other women's tastes. It was the "house on the hill"—that was what everybody called it—and the Berglund children were disheveled and beautiful. The couple would throw dinner parties and put signs up in their yards about the ocean and sometimes fight so loudly that the people down the hill had to shut their windows to protect them, in their kind Midwestern way, from the shame of having been heard.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Walter and Patty Berglund had become a story, but not in the way anyone back in Ramsey Hill would have predicted. The couple who had once embodied the stubborn optimism of urban pioneers now found themselves marred by scandal—a New York Times exposé of Walter's coal industry dealings had labeled him "ethically compromised" and "arrogant." These descriptions felt alien to the neighbors who remembered the Berglunds as the beating heart of their crumbling Victorian enclave, a pair who had practically willed their corner of St. Paul back to life. Walter, the mild-mannered environmentalist biking to his nonprofit job rain or shine, had seemed incapable of the kind of cynical maneuvering now attributed to him. Patty, with her unapologetic bluntness and visible exhaustion, had once been the maternal force of the block, a woman who weathered stroller wars and zoning battles with an athlete’s unrelenting drive. That they’d traded their struggling but righteous lives in Ramsey Hill for a high-powered existence in Washington, D.C., seemed almost like betrayal, though no one would say it out loud.Back then, the Berglunds had been a testament to the grind. Their Victorian was a disaster when they bought it—broken windows, a rotting porch, graffiti tagging its sides—and their marriage hadn’t seemed much better off for a while, given the tensions that leaked out at block parties and PTA meetings. Still, they’d worked, pouring themselves into the kind of relentless self-improvement Ramsey Hill had demanded. Walter in his gardening gloves, Patty with a paint-splattered bandana tied around her head, both knee-deep in home renovation projects, had been symbols of what the neighborhood aspired to: upward mobility dressed in scrappy altruism. But the cracks had been visible even then—Patty’s wineglass refilled too often during neighborhood dinners, Walter’s simmering annoyance when the compost bin went unturned. Now, from a distance, those years seemed almost quaint. The Berglunds had been good at being admired, even if they’d never quite learned how to admire themselves. The irony of Walter's public disgrace was not lost on anyone, least of all Patty, whose clipped “I told you so” had lost its sting after years of being only half-true.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: In St. Paul — or, at the very least, in the Ramsey Hill neighborhood — Walter and Patty Berglund were remembered as decent folks, despite the fact that they’d moved to Washington, D.C. two years ago. When he lived in Ramsey Hill, Walter would commute to work on his bike because it reduced carbon emissions, never mind the below-zero winters or the bluffs after Summit Avenue. During city council meetings, he gave passionate speeches about sorting plastics from paper. The Walter of Ramsey Hill believed in a better America, a green America, wild in its terrain, a patchwork of sustainable farms. Now the news, or at least the decent people at The New York Times and The Associated Press and The Washington Post, too, accused him of taking bribes from the coal industry. Walter and Petty first moved to Ramsey Hill back when it was still a neglected neighborhood; they thought of themselves as pioneers, do-gooders who could be the first to clean it up. With the little money they had, they’d bought a run-down Victorian house, and through the following years, they poured everything into that house’s restoration, fighting off plumbing failures, electrical outages, a neighbor with a penchant for yelling at his wife on the street, rotted wood, basement floods, and teen vandals — to address the latter, Patty had used a bat and a few stern, almost maternal, words. Patty, a former cheerleader for UMN, never fit into the neighborhood, visually speaking, though it hardly seemed to bother her. In the mornings, she jogged with her stroller, her blonde ponytail swinging behind her as she swerved to avoid the sidewalk feces, her face unflinching as the occasional truck driver whistled at her. In the afternoons, she painted the sidings of the house or installed kitchen tile between diaper changes and nursing sessions. In the evenings, she sat on the couch after preparing dinner, sipping a glass of zinfandel and listening to NPR, a radio station that would, in the unforeseeable future, refer to her as “the wife of disgraced politician, Walter Berglund.”

written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: The truth is much uglier than the sweet story I’ve given them. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis never saw each other again, both having perished during the war. Robbie fell to septicemia at Bray Dunes, his wounds never healing right. Cecilia, my glamorous older sister, died in a bombing at the Balham Underground, dressed in the same rationed rags as any other woman. They died alone, a fault I must now agonizingly take the blame for. It was my callous childishness that ripped Robbie from Cecilia, but it is my better nature that has prompted me to write them a better ending. They find each other again, they live, and they are happy. What good would it do, I beg to know, in telling the foul truth? I’ll tell it, here and now, if only to prove my point. I never saw either of them again that year, how could I, after what I had done to Cecilia? Their love died with them, isolated and unfulfilled, with the sole evidence that they knew each other being those romantic letters preserved only in a war museum. I cannot imagine truth is worth more than the merciful fiction, but I struggle even now to know for certain if my rewrite of history is fair. I’d like to think that this hopeful conclusion, regardless of how factual it may be, holds greater value than an honest, but tragic account.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: In the twilight of her long life, Briony Tallis grappled with the burden of her narrative. Her pages were a desperate reach for atonement, a reckoning with a truth too cruel to bear. Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis had never enjoyed the solace of a country retreat or the satisfaction of a love realized. The world had not been kind enough to allow their survival. Yet in the theater of her imagination, Briony became their savior, conjuring them together, their lives intact, their love unbroken, their letters exchanged with trembling hands. The truth, stark and unrelenting, loomed like the specter of her own guilt: Robbie felled by infection in the mud-soaked trenches, Cecilia extinguished in a cataclysm of rubble and fire. She, the architect of their suffering, could not face the permanence of that ending. What then was the purpose of truth, she wondered, if it could not redeem? In her constructed fiction, she gave them joy, continuity, the soft rebellion of a life shared. But as the ink dried on her final pages, she was left with the echo of a question that gnawed at her sense of justice and her fragile hope for forgiveness: was it better to honor the brutal finality of fact or to bestow upon them, and herself, the balm of a beautiful lie? At the edge of her fading strength, she allowed herself the faintest smile, perhaps at last, a merciful fiction was the highest form of kindness.

written_by_MFA025.Original: There was a crime. But there were also the lovers. Lovers and their happy ends have been on my mind all night long. As into the sunset we sail. An unhappy inversion. It occurs to me that I have not traveled so very far after all, since I wrote my little play. Or rather, I’ve made a huge digression and doubled back to my starting place. It is only in this last version that my lovers end well, standing side by side on a South London pavement as I walk away. All the preceding drafts were pitiless. But now I can no longer think what purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on 1 June 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station. That I never saw them in that year. That my walk across London ended at the church on Clapham Common, and that a cowardly Briony limped back to the hospital, unable to confront her recently bereaved sister. That the letters the lovers wrote are in the archives of the War Museum. How could that constitute an ending? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love?

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.

It is only in this last version that my lovers end well, standing side by side on a South London pavement as I walk away. All the preceding drafts were pitiless. But now I can no longer think what purpose would be served if, say, I tried to persuade my reader, by direct or indirect means, that Robbie Turner died of septicemia at Bray Dunes on 1 June 1940, or that Cecilia was killed in September of the same year by the bomb that destroyed Balham Underground station. That I never saw them in that year. That my walk across London ended at the church on Clapham Common, and that a cowardly Briony limped back to the hospital, unable to confront her recently bereaved sister. That the letters the lovers wrote are in the archives of the War Museum. How could that constitute an ending? What sense or hope or satisfaction could a reader draw from such an account? Who would want to believe that they never met again, never fulfilled their love?

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: I am Briony, and I am sad to report on the tragic fate of two lovers, Robbie Turner and Cecilia Tallis. Because I invented them myself, their tragedy is my own fault, but because their characters are based in reality, I cannot help but feel loyal to the truth. The fact is that Robbie and Cecilia died during World War II. Robbie succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes, and Cecilia perished in a bombing at Balham Underground station. Neither of them knew that I had committed a terrible wrong against them both. In my youth, I was wickedly jealous of Robbie and Cecilia and resented the affection they held for one another. Not because I desired either of them, but because I was angry and lonely and hiding in a bunker of cynicism. I was a postboy, and when Robbie went off to war, I would intercept the letters he sent to Cecelia and slide them into the rain-filled gutters. I did the same to Cecelia’s letters, and their correspondence slowly dwindled. Eventually, they stopped writing to each other altogether. I’ve been approaching this all wrong. Now is the time to let Robbie and Cecelia survive and be together, even if only in these pages. Telling the truth wouldn’t do any good, because it’s an ugly truth. I never saw Robbie and Cecelia again, their love stayed unfulfilled, and their few remaining letters are preserved only in a war museum. Maybe truth is not always better than mercy. Maybe hope survives through lies.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The lingering image of Robbie and Cecilia, their figures receding down the driveway into the white mist, remains etched in my memory. It's a scene I've revisited countless times, a reminder of the love I shattered and the atonement I sought through my writing. In the twilight of my life, I question the nature of truth. Is a merciful fabrication, a crafted illusion of happiness, a greater kindness than the stark reality of a love tragically cut short? Robbie likely succumbed to septicemia at Bray Dunes. Cecilia perished in Balham Underground station during a bombing raid. Their letters lie preserved in a war museum, a testament to a love forever unfulfilled. Yet, in my final act of creation, I dared to defy fate. I granted them a reprieve, a fictional sanctuary where their love survived. It was a rebellion against the relentless march of time and tragedy. As the shadows lengthen, I wonder if I was right to weave this tapestry of hope. Would they have preferred the stark truth, the bitter knowledge of their unfulfilled love? Or is it a greater kindness to let them live on in my fictional world, forever young, forever in love? The question lingers, unresolved, like an echo in my mind. Perhaps there is no right answer to this age-old dilemma. Perhaps the truth, like beauty, lies in the eye of the beholder. A hopeful ending, even if untrue, is a more fitting tribute to their love than the harsh reality of their tragic fate.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Truth sits heavily in my hands like an old manuscript, its pages yellow and brittle with time. I could write it all - the harsh reality of their separate deaths, Robbie's slow fade into septicemic darkness at Bray Dunes, Cecilia's final moments in the underground station at Balham, their love scattered like ash across a war-torn continent. The historian in me demands this accuracy, this unflinching record of what actually transpired after my childish testimony tore them apart. But what serves memory better - the brutal facts preserved in glass cases at the Imperial War Museum, those letters never to be answered, those promises never to be kept, or the mercy of imagination that allows them to transcend the circumstances I thrust upon them? In my fiction, they live. In my fiction, their hands find each other across the library table, their eyes meet without the shadow of my betrayal between them. Perhaps this is my final act of cowardice, unable even now to face the full weight of what I did, unable to write the words that would kill them again on the page. Or perhaps it is the only grace left to me - this power to resurrect them from the ashes of history, to give them the moments that war and my testimony stole. The question haunts me: is truth always kinder than fiction? In the end, I choose to let them live in the amber of my imagination, preserved in a love that reality never permitted them to fully express.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Robbie and Cecilia were happy in my story. They faced hardships, certainly, but I conjured them, by the force of my own brittle pen, into two happy people. The world, the real world, was not as kind to them. I cannot be sure of what happened in the end, but, in all likelihood, it was this: Robbie succumbed to the brutal, unforgiving clutch of septicemia— the horror of black limbs and gasping breaths in his final moments. And dear Cecilia was decimated by a bomb at Balham Underground station. Is it selfishness, then, or a mercy, this ending I’ve given them, this happiness? In my tale, there is no sickness traveling through the veins, no limbs blown off. There is only contentment and love, a warm and certain kind. Why tell the truth, when it is something almost unspeakably miserable? The truth: that I never saw them again, after what happened. That I could not face my sister. That their letters—tender and sorrowful —are preserved only in a war museum, words of desperate longing fossilized behind panes of glass. It’s this business of truth I continue to return to—always this business of truth. Is the truth better than what I have done? Have I committed an act of cowardice, in my story, or an act of love? For I loved them both; still, I do. And I gave them mercy, a happy ending, perhaps more meaningful than the tragic nature of their lives. I gave them each other.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: I had gone there and didn’t know what to do after I’d gone there. At my father’s house, I entered his study where he sat at his desk staring at his hands. Next to his hands, his work––book stacks on biblical theology and anti-Semitism. I stood behind him. I stared at his hands. This was a turning point of sorts of ours, his hands, our staring at them. So many hours of ours went to this, had come to this. I thought: when did we get here? And: what do I do now, now that we’ve gone here? My mother came in and laid her own hand on his shoulder. She said, “Gerry” which was my father’s name, “Gerry, remember, you were working on your essay on biblical theology and anti-Semitism.” She made a sweeping motion with her hands before him. When he finally saw me, he said, “My daughter…” and told me how proud he was of me and all that I’d been doing. Then he said he had nothing else to say to me. He went back to his hands. Later that evening, my mother and I sat in the dining room together, where she showed me an old photograph of my father. “What happened to him?” my mother said, and I couldn’t tell her. I couldn’t even come close to saying.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: My father, a stranger in his own house, sits hunched in his armchair, a shadow of the man I knew.  His eyes, once bright and full of life, are now clouded with confusion.  He struggles to remember what he's working on, a question met with a sigh and a shake of his head.  My mother, her face etched with worry, reminds him gently, "Your writing, dear, on the Bible and anti-Semitism."  A flicker of recognition crosses his face, a brief spark in the fading embers of his mind.He looks at me, a ghost of a smile touching his lips.  "My daughter," he says, his voice a fragile whisper, "so proud of you."  But the light fades quickly, replaced by a vacant stare.  "Nothing to say," he murmurs, lost in the labyrinth of his own thoughts.  The silence that follows is heavy, filled with unspoken words and a growing sense of loss.Later, my mother shows me a photograph from forty years ago.  My father, young and vibrant, stands with his arm around her, both of them radiating joy.  My mother's voice cracks as she speaks, her words laced with a quiet despair.  "It's like he's already gone," she says, her eyes filled with tears.  I look at the photograph again, the image of my father frozen in time, a stark contrast to the frail figure sitting in the other room.  The weight of his absence, even in his presence, settles over me, a heavy cloak of sorrow that I cannot shake off.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt 1 has a closer tone to the original because it is not too flowery, whereas excerpt 2 has added a lot more description and adjectives: 'his fading lips', 'vacant stare' etc. Excerpt 1 keeps some of the matter-of-factness of the original which is part of what makes it so sad.
written_by_MFA015.Original: On my last visit, my father seemed in worse condition than I had seen him before. When I asked him if he was working on anything in particular now, he said no and then turned his head slowly to my mother and looked at her in bewilderment, his mouth hanging open. There was an expression of pain or agony on his face that seemed habitual. She looked back at him, waited a moment, impassive, and then said: “Yes, you are. You’re writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism.” He continued to stare at her. Later that evening, before he went to bed, he said: “This is symptomatic of my condition: You’re my daughter, and I’m proud of you, but I have nothing to say to you.” He left to get ready for bed, and then came back into the room wearing dazzling white pajamas. My mother asked me to admire his pajamas, and he stood quietly while I did. Then he said: “I don’t know what I will be like in the morning.” After he went to bed, my mother showed me a picture of him forty years before sitting at a seminar table surrounded by students. “Just look at him there!” she said in distress, as though it were some sort of punishment that he had become what he was now—an old man with a beaked profile like a nutcracker.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: He sat in the chair by the window, where he always sat, though I wasn’t sure if he recognized the chair.
