She held it up next to his face, as if she could prove something that way. He did not look at the picture. He closed his eyes. My mother sighed. Later, she would tuck the photo back into the album, where it belonged. He would remain in his chair, where he belonged. I would leave, where I belonged. It was not that we did not love each other, only that love had become a kind of stillness, a sitting together, a waiting for words that had already been forgotten.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I went to see my father and found him in a much worse state than I had left him. He was disoriented and dazed, mumbling to himself about taxes and missionaries knocking on the door. He couldn't remember much about what he was working on. My mother gently reminded him that he was writing about the Bible and anti-Semitism. "Oh yes," he said, "that's right," and nodded as if to confirm this to himself. While the three of us ate supper, he turned to me and told me that he was quite proud of me. "You are a good kid," he said. "Always have been." "Is that so?" I asked. He nodded again. "I just have nothing to say to you," he said, and I told him I understood. After my mother and I washed the dishes together, she showed me a photograph from forty years ago. In it, my father had a full head of dark curls. His eyes were alert and his smile untroubled. I was perched in his lap like a small pet, staring up at him as if I had just noticed he was there. All five of my fingers could fit around his thumb. Everything that would follow in the years to come might never happen. "This was such a nice day," said my mother, stroking the photograph. "You probably don't remember, do you?" I had forgotten what her smile looked like, so I told her I remembered it perfectly.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: He sat in the chair by the window, where he always sat, though I wasn’t sure if he recognized the chair. He had been writing about the Bible, about anti-Semitism, about something urgent, something that had mattered. My mother told him this. “Your work,” she said. “You’ve been writing about the Bible.” He nodded, as if this was something he could accept, though not something he quite believed. He looked at me and said he was proud of me, but then added, almost apologetically, that he had nothing to say to me. I nodded back. We sat, the three of us, not saying anything. He looked out the window, or at the window. My mother left the room and came back holding a photograph. “This was him,” she said. “Forty years ago.” I looked at it. She held it up next to his face, as if she could prove something that way. He did not look at the picture. He closed his eyes. My mother sighed. Later, she would tuck the photo back into the album, where it belonged. He would remain in his chair, where he belonged. I would leave, where I belonged. It was not that we did not love each other, only that love had become a kind of stillness, a sitting together, a waiting for words that had already been forgotten.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I went to see my father and found him in a much worse state than I had left him. written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: She’d said, “I want to handle this in my own way, on my own terms.”Her words hung in the air, heavy with finality and a hint of defiance.“I’m tired of waiting,” she continued, her voice a mix of weariness and determination.“I’m tired of this body failing me, of the endless treatments, the uncertainty.”She spoke of wanting to die peacefully, naturally, without any interference.“I don’t want any interventions, any disruptions,” she’d said.“I don’t want anyone trying to prolong this… existence.” She paused, a wry smile flickering across her face.“I don’t want anyone trying to play God,” she added, her tone a blend of humor and solemnity.Her words echoed in my mind as I walked down the street, the weight of our conversation pressing on me.I thought about her situation, her desire for autonomy, her frustration with the slow, unpredictable decay of her body.I thought about her wish for a peaceful, natural death, her refusal to let anyone “play God.”I thought about her insistence on secrecy, her plea for me not to mention her plans to anyone, not even my closest confidantes.I felt a knot of tension tighten in my chest, a conflict between my loyalty to her and my own need to process this heavy situation.I thought about the consequences of her choice, the potential legal ramifications, the emotional toll it would take on those who cared about her. I thought about my own role in this, my promise to support her, my fear of being implicated, my desire to protect her and myself.I felt a surge of guilt, a sense of betrayal, as I remembered the conversation I’d had with my therapist, the one person I’d confided in, breaking my promise to her.I tried to justify my actions, telling myself that I needed someone to talk to, someone to help me navigate this emotional minefield.But the guilt lingered, a constant reminder of my broken promise.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I remember things. I remember how I felt when my friend talked about taking her own life. She wasn’t planning to commit suicide exactly. But she wanted her life to come to an end, she said. Her honesty made me pause and I wondered what I should do in such a situation. Could I make her change her mind? Would I have to look after her things and live with guilt? It would’ve been different if my friend didn’t want to handle “her situation” on her own terms. She, who had always been a planner, had even decided which drug she wanted to use to die, and asked me to keep it a secret, both for her sake and for my “protection,” whatever that meant. What concerned me though was that she wanted to do it soon. She said it slowly and calmly, but her tone was riddled with impatience and readiness. My friend had been ill for a long time and her body had not been responding well to treatments. She had spent so much in hospitals that now she wanted death to feel natural, without any interventions or disruptions. Smooth and clean. She hoped death would arrive like an unexpected guest. “Like the coming of the Lord, you know?” she said, with a laugh. I was in two minds. I wanted to know when she was planning for it all to go down, but it felt unthinkable to probe directly about her timeline. And, I felt equally concerned with more practical issues. If I were to stay with my friend during her final days, my mail would pile up. What would I do then? And what would happen to everything she had? It was all this and more about her, including her choice of pill, that I recounted to another friend of mine later in the day.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: She had it all planned out, she said, though she wouldn't tell me exactly when. Like the coming of the Lord, she joked, no one knows the day or the hour. I won't tell you what they are or where they came from. It's better that way. For your protection, she added, though I wondered if it wasn't more for her peace of mind. The secret felt heavy between us, like a third presence in the room. Looking at her face, lined with pain but still beautiful in its determination, I found it unthinkable to ask the questions that pressed against my throat: When? How soon? Will I be here? Later that night, I called S. and told her everything, breaking my promise of silence before it was even a day old. "I just need someone else to know," I said, and she understood, or said she did. But afterward I lay awake, thinking about loyalty and betrayal, about the boundaries between caring for someone and caring for yourself. About how even in death—especially in death—we are never quite as alone as we might wish to be.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: A good friend of mine told me about her plans for death. More precisely, she told me she was planning to take matters into her own hands. I asked her what she meant by this, and she just gave me a look that said, are you going to make me spell it out for you? No, I wasn’t going to make her spell it out, and she went on, saying that she had gotten quite impatient about the whole thing. She was ready, she said, and she wanted to bow out while there was still time. My friend’s body had never fared well when it was invaded by illness. It also didn’t fare well when it was invaded by medicine. As a teenager, she had lots of problems with headaches. Stomachaches, too, but she didn’t talk about that as much. She was also allergic to many things. Of dying, she said this: I want it to feel natural, without anything getting in the way. She wouldn’t say how this would happen. Just like the coming of the Lord, nobody would know until it was already here. I had two main concerns. One of them was practical—if I came to stay with her and supervise her wellbeing, my mail would pile up. The other was that I found it unthinkable to ask her any direct questions. Questions like, when? Questions like, where? My friend insisted on secrecy and made me promise not to tell anyone about her plan, and especially not about her drug of choice. She said this would bring her peace and give me protection. To be honest, I did want both of those things. But sometimes I can’t help myself. I told someone without even meaning to. I made him promise not to tell.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: It’s strange, how quickly we adapt to the unthinkable. Sitting across from her that day, I tried not to fixate on her trembling hands or the way her voice, once so commanding, now wavered. “I don’t want to know when,” I said, a cowardly dodge that felt both honest and unkind. She gave a short laugh, the kind that cuts, and said, “You think it’ll be like the Rapture—poof, and I’m gone? Sorry to disappoint.” The drugs were hidden somewhere, and I knew better than to ask. Still, I couldn’t stop my mind from wandering to the mechanics of it: where, when, how. She didn’t want witnesses, she said, though she spoke about it with the eerie calm of someone discussing weather forecasts. “No surprises,” she added, “except maybe for you, if you’re still here.” She wanted the mail collected, the apartment left tidy, as if planning for a long vacation. But I could see in her eyes a quiet insistence: this wasn’t for my benefit. It was for hers.I nodded along, complicit in the silence she demanded, though guilt sat heavy in my chest. “It’s your choice,” I managed, the words dry in my mouth. I didn’t tell her about the conversation I’d already had, late one night, with someone who wasn’t her. Someone who had listened as I stumbled over explanations and shared the weight she was handing me. My betrayal, small and selfish, would never reach her ears, but it lived between us nonetheless, a thing unspoken but palpable. And when she turned back to her tea, her gaze distant and inward, I wondered how much she already suspected. In that moment, she seemed to belong not to this world or the next but to the narrow, flickering space between.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.

written_by_MFA001.Original: We could have it for a month, she told me over the phone. Not that I think I’ll need that much time.Would I ever get used to this kind of talk? Even as I wondered what to do about my mail—let it pile up, have the post office forward it or hold it for me—I found it unthinkable to ask how long I should plan to be gone.It’s not like I’ve picked a date, she said. Though, as I say, I am ready to go. You could even say I’m impatient to go, which comes partly from my having already given so much thought to dying but also from having reached the limits of what I think I can bear. But I don’t know what my body will do.Though she’d been feeling much better since she went off chemo, her symptoms could change from day to day, and the meds she was taking to suppress them had some side effects too.In any case, I want things to happen naturally, she said. I feel like I’ll know when it’s time.But you—well, you won’t know, she said. Obviously I won’t be making a big announcement. Like the coming of the Lord, she said jokingly: You will not know the day or hour.She had decided not to tell anyone about our plans. I’ve come this far, I don’t want to risk some stupid intervention, she said, or even a tiny disruption. I want peace.No one was to know where we were.And, for your own protection, she told me, you need to play dumb: I never told you what I was going to do, you weren’t even aware that I had the drug.I had, in fact, already told one other person everything, but I did not say this.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: It’s strange, how quickly we adapt to the unthinkable. Sitting across from her that day, I tried not to fixate on her trembling hands or the way her voice, once so commanding, now wavered. “I don’t want to know when,” I said, a cowardly dodge that felt both honest and unkind. She gave a short laugh, the kind that cuts, and said, “You think it’ll be like the Rapture—poof, and I’m gone? Sorry to disappoint.” The drugs were hidden somewhere, and I knew better than to ask. Still, I couldn’t stop my mind from wandering to the mechanics of it: where, when, how. She didn’t want witnesses, she said, though she spoke about it with the eerie calm of someone discussing weather forecasts. “No surprises,” she added, “except maybe for you, if you’re still here.” She wanted the mail collected, the apartment left tidy, as if planning for a long vacation. But I could see in her eyes a quiet insistence: this wasn’t for my benefit. It was for hers.I nodded along, complicit in the silence she demanded, though guilt sat heavy in my chest. “It’s your choice,” I managed, the words dry in my mouth. I didn’t tell her about the conversation I’d already had, late one night, with someone who wasn’t her. Someone who had listened as I stumbled over explanations and shared the weight she was handing me. My betrayal, small and selfish, would never reach her ears, but it lived between us nonetheless, a thing unspoken but palpable. And when she turned back to her tea, her gaze distant and inward, I wondered how much she already suspected. In that moment, she seemed to belong not to this world or the next but to the narrow, flickering space between.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: Kant writes the email and spends a long time editing it, making minor changes to the wording only to change them back to exactly what he’d written before. He thinks about his upbringing and all the years that this information has weighed on him: the kids in middle school who tackled him in the locker room and forced him to eat dog shit, the fact that he couldn’t even admit to himself that he wanted to watch gay porn until he was twenty-five. Paralyzed, still editing, he imagines his mother’s disgust upon reading the email, imagining her 31-year-old son doing exactly what he’d done for the better part of the last two decades: that is, fanatasizing about some buff, hairy dude he saw online. He imagines himself dying alone, ostracized from anyone who might love him, the nerves in his dick beginning to desensitize from too much dry-hand masturbation. When he sends the email, though, the responses are surprisingly anticlimactic. He gets a few heart emojis from friends; some coworkers reply with “nice,” and “good for you!” Even his parents are mostly supportive, though his mom expresses some mild annoyance that he hadn’t called first to warn them. Kant feels a mixture of intense relief, combined with an unpleasant sense of disappointment that he finds difficult to face. Where was the fallout, the dramatic messages and cut-off relationships from family members? Why didn’t anyone care? He had once imagined his post-coming out life as a time of transformation, a new life like a beautiful patterned carpet rolling out before him, but instead he finds himself stuck in the exact same state of stasis that emboldened him to write the email in the first place. He begins to call this period his “Year of Damp Feet,” as his feet are constantly sweaty despite the fact that he rarely moves them from beneath his computer desk.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Kant spent hours drafting the email, toggling between subject lines (“A Word to Everyone,” “FYI,” and, finally, “Coming Out”) like they were tarot cards predicting his fate. In his head, each recipient’s reaction unspooled in unrelenting technicolor: his mother, weeping silently in the kitchen as she diced onions for the biryani she thought would fix his mood; his old college roommate forwarding the email to their group chat with the caption, “Knew it”; his boss, furrowing his brow at the computer, typing, “Not sure why this concerns me professionally.” These imagined catastrophes paraded through his thoughts as he clicked send, his trembling hand a cheap metaphor for the fear wedged in his sternum. Then: nothing. The world didn’t combust. Instead, his notifications flooded with low-stakes affirmations—heart emojis from friends, a “proud of you, dude” text from a cousin, even a begrudging “love you” from his father, which Kant suspected had been typed under duress from his mother. He should’ve felt relief, triumph even, but instead, there was this sneaking, hollow ache. He’d braced himself for rejection, a narrative arc with stakes, but life handed him a shrug and a pat on the back. What was the point of all that dread if no one made it cinematic? The next few weeks stretched out like an overcooked spaghetti noodle—soft, limp, no bite. Without the anticipated martyrdom, Kant drifted into what he called his “Year of Damp Feet,” shuffling around his apartment in unwashed socks, ignoring texts inviting him to “finally celebrate.” He scrolled through his inbox, rereading replies, hoping to stumble on something more… dramatic. Wasn’t this supposed to be the pivot point of his life? Instead, he remained unchanged, realizing that even monumental self-revelations couldn’t save him from the everyday inertia of being Kant. A hero’s journey, sure—but with no villain, no fight, just the lukewarm end credits rolling over silence.

written_by_MFA011.Original: It takes Kant a year to write the one-excerpt mass email, another three weeks to compile the Coming Out mailing list of friends, family, and colleagues, and three bourbons to actually send it. For his entire life he has so grotesquely imagined the consequences of public exposure that he’s only recently, at thirty-one, stopped hedging to himself that he is bi or “flexible.” He pictures his mother saying she never wants to speak to him again; he imagines dying alone in an unheated tenement, though he knows this is unlikely to happen to a video-game asset designer with two degrees. Part of him had believed that as long as his proclivities resided only in his head, and sometimes on his computer, they didn’t “count.” Now everyone will know; his sexuality will exist as an open fact. After sending the email, he turns off his phone and spends the night vomiting from stress.But the response is unanimously supportive. His friends reply with the visible spectrum of heart emojis. His coworkers politely underreact (“Oh neat! Psyched for you”). Kant’s parents are not thrilled exactly—they wish he’d called them first, though he couldn’t fathom doing this twice—yet they are neither disapproving nor surprised. The recent legalization of gay marriage probably helped; mainly his parents want to know whether he still plans on having kids, and he says yes, just to give them something.Perversely he sort of wishes the response had been more dramatic and adverse, to give him something to overcome, forcing growth in the process, though he knows he doesn’t really want that. But having tailored his life to compensate for its lack of relationships, there’s nothing compelling him to act on his new freedom, and instead he’s masturbating more than ever. He will recall this post-coming-out phase of his life as the Year of Damp Feet, spent forever popping into the shower to rinse off his dick and stomach.

Part of him had believed that as long as his proclivities resided only in his head, and sometimes on his computer, they didn’t “count.” Now everyone will know; his sexuality will exist as an open fact. After sending the email, he turns off his phone and spends the night vomiting from stress.But the response is unanimously supportive. His friends reply with the visible spectrum of heart emojis. His coworkers politely underreact (“Oh neat! Psyched for you”). Kant’s parents are not thrilled exactly—they wish he’d called them first, though he couldn’t fathom doing this twice—yet they are neither disapproving nor surprised. The recent legalization of gay marriage probably helped; mainly his parents want to know whether he still plans on having kids, and he says yes, just to give them something.Perversely he sort of wishes the response had been more dramatic and adverse, to give him something to overcome, forcing growth in the process, though he knows he doesn’t really want that. But having tailored his life to compensate for its lack of relationships, there’s nothing compelling him to act on his new freedom, and instead he’s masturbating more than ever. He will recall this post-coming-out phase of his life as the Year of Damp Feet, spent forever popping into the shower to rinse off his dick and stomach.

written_by_MFA024.Excerpt1: Kant's coming out email sat in his drafts folder like a grenade with the pin half-pulled, while he spent weeks A/B testing subject lines, as if the right combination of words could defuse three decades of queerness into something digestible for his mother's WeChat circles. He'd crafted seventeen versions, each more baroque than the last, padding them with disclaimers and preemptive responses to imagined objections, until the final draft read like a corporate merger announcement crossed with a hostage negotiation. The responses, when they finally came, were an anticlimactic parade of heart emojis and "love you no matter what"s—the kind of tepid acceptance that made him wonder if perhaps he wasn't gay enough to warrant proper drama. His coworkers replied with the practiced neutrality of people who'd attended exactly one diversity training, while his mother's response ("Ok. Did you eat dinner?") felt like being handed a participation trophy for surviving thirty-one years of internal torment. He'd prepared for scorched earth but got lukewarm validation, and now here he was, somehow lonelier in his freedom, spending his newly authentic life watching YouTube compilations of gay wedding flash mobs and ordering rainbow-colored socks he'd never wear. The Year of Damp Feet, he called it in his journal, though he knew the phrase would sound better in someone else's memoir. His therapist called this "adjustment period" progress, but it felt more like trading one closet for another—this one just happened to have better lighting and an Amazon Prime subscription. The truth was, he'd gotten good at being afraid, had built his personality around it like a pearl around grit, and now that the fear was gone, he couldn't shake the suspicion that he'd peaked at being closeted, that he'd somehow gentrified his own identity into something too palatable to matter, too sanitized for the revolution he'd imagined himself starring in.
written_by_MFA024.Excerpt2: Kant wrote thirty versions of his coming-out email over the course of ten months. Though he knew better, he couldn’t keep from anticipating and meticulously addressing, in the email itself, the various surprised, dismissive, or condemnatory responses of his friends and family, to the point where the email was less an act of claiming his own reality than a bullish bracing of himself against an incoming bilgewater tide of others’ realities. He clicked send. Feeling noble, self-satisfied, and above all ready, he camped at his laptop with an energy drink and spammed refresh. A couple hours later, an email from his father sent a spike of fear into his chest: he was about to be disowned. But while not exactly celebratory, the message indicated uncomplicated respect and acceptance. An email from an old college friend came in next, composed only of emojis. Where was their disgust? Their bitterness and disdain? The underwhelm was itself an overwhelm: he felt ridiculous, mocked by precisely an absence of mockery. Coming out should feel like something, shouldn’t it? He considered, by way of analogy, his own naïve expectation every birthday that he might experience an inner shift adequate to the day’s significance, a radiance, a spiritual lift, some kind of internal popping sound at least—I’m twenty-nine!—and instead met again and again just another day. Wasn’t this exactly how all life’s big events felt? A non-feeling? Supportive replies rolled in, and each refused to move the plot of his life forward. He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself. What he’d imagined calling The Year of Freedom had become The Year of Damp Feet.

The story reeks of desperate chemicals and the acrid stench of burning rubber on asphalt, all wrapped up in the frenzied quest for the Great American Convertible. My attorney, that chrome-domed harbinger of chaos, is barking into payphones at terrified salesmen while I hover near the bar of some godforsaken Polynesian tomb, mainlining Singapore Slings and wondering if we'll ever make it out of LA alive. The whole scene has the surgical precision of a hurricane - first the maniac phone calls, then the ugly business with the recording equipment, and somewhere in between, the grotesque spectacle of that poor bastard getting mowed down by a Stingray on Sunset. Jesus, what a place. What a time. The salesmen are wielding tire irons now, passing our gear through a crack in the door like they're feeding raw meat to a cage full of rabid wolverines. Can't blame them, really - not with what's happening out there in the streets. The whole country's gone belly-up with fear and loathing, and here we are, two professional journalists, supposedly documenting this circus of depravity. But the real story isn't in the facts - it's in the white-knuckled grip on the wheel at 110 mph, in the savage heart of the American Dream gone wrong. At the same time, I sent my attorney out to look for a decent convertible with a high-quality stereo so that we could listen to music as loud as we wanted while driving through the desert. There were a lot of false starts; for several hours my attorney spoke aggressively on the phone with several car rental agencies while we sat at a Polynesian bar, with me sneaking off occasionally to do hits of acid in the bathroom. He kept needing to demand respect from these salesmen guys who were jerking him around, which I felt completely reflected the energy of Los Angeles at the time… everyone talking over one another and wanting desperately to wring the other’s neck, and yet nobody capable of listening to a single word the other is saying…eventually he got it straightened out, after hanging up angrily a few times and cursing while this ugly group of veins nearly popped out of his neck, and while we drive back to my place we saw a Stingray car hit a woman crossing Sunset Boulevard—she lay there, spread-eagled, and I remember thinking that this was what America had come to now, reduced to lying lifeless among the bird shit on the street. When we finally made it to the store with the audio equipment, things became even more unbearable, everything rushing down on me like a wave made from needles. Through a half-cracked open door, my attorney argued with the salespeople, who clearly wanted us out of there as quickly as possible. They held their tire irons like baseball bats, and I felt scared, but intrigued, although maybe it was the acid making me feel scared…I wanted to know what would happen, and I wanted, more than anything, for the rushing feeling to stop. Back and forth and back and forth and back and forth they went, until eventually, it was over and we started our drive through the desert.

written_by_MFA011.Original: Every now and then when your life gets complicated and the weasels start closing in, the only real cure is to load up on heinous chemicals and then drive like a bastard from Hollywood to Las Vegas. To relax, as it were, in the womb of the desert sun. Just roll the roof back and screw it on, grease the face with white tanning butter and move out with the music at top volume, and at least a pint of ether.Getting hold of the drugs had been no problem, but the car and the tape recorder were not easy things to round up at 6:30 on a Friday afternoon in Hollywood. I already had one car, but it was far too small and slow for desert work. We went to a Polynesian bar, where my attorney made seventeen calls before locating a convertible with adequate horsepower and proper coloring. "Hang onto it," I heard him say into the phone. "We’ll be over to make the trade in thirty minutes." Then after a pause, he began shouting: "What? Of course the gentleman has a major credit card! Do you realize who the fuck you’re talking to?" "Don’t take any guff from these swine," I said as he slammed the phone down. "Now we need a sound store with the finest equipment. Nothing dinky. We want one of those new Belgian Heliowatts with a voice—activated shotgun mike, for picking up conversations in oncoming cars." We made several more calls and finally located our equip—ment in a store about five miles away. It was closed, but the salesman said he would wait, if we hurried. But we were de—layed en route when a Stingray in front of us killed a pedestrian on Sunset Boulevard. The store was closed by the time we got there. There were people inside, but they refused to come to the double—glass door until we gave it a few belts and made ourselves clear.“Finally two salesmen brandishing tire irons came to the door and we managed to negotiate the sale through a tiny slit. Then they opened the door just wide enough to shove the equipment out, before slamming and locking it again. "Now take that stuff and get the hell away from here," one of them shouted through the slit

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: The attorney was on the phone, his voice a guttural rasp against the faux-Polynesian backdrop of the bar. "Red," he barked, "not pink. And make it snappy, the goddamn plane leaves in three hours."  I swiveled on the barstool, the vinyl squeaking in protest, and surveyed the wreckage of our preparations. Empty Mai Tai glasses stood like fallen soldiers, casualties in the war against sobriety. A crumpled napkin bore the cryptic message,"Convertible. Red. Not a goddamn boat."Outside, the Hollywood sun beat down with the malevolence of a loan shark. A pack of tourists shuffled past, their eyes glazed over with the vacant stare of the terminally sunburned. A low-slung Stingray roared by, leaving behind the faint scent of burnt rubber and the echo of a scream.  "Jesus," I muttered, "this town is a goddamn meat grinder."The attorney slammed the phone down, his face a mask of grim determination. "Got it," he snarled, "a red convertible. Picking it up in an hour."  He fixed me with a bloodshot stare. "Now, about that recording equipment..."We found the electronics store tucked away in a seedy strip mall, sandwiched between a bail bondsman and an adult bookstore. The salesmen eyed us with the suspicion of a pit bull eyeing a poodle. "We're closed," one growled, brandishing a tire iron."Bullshit," the attorney snarled back, "we just need some high-quality recording equipment. And we're in a hurry."  The door cracked open a few inches, revealing a glimpse of darkened aisles and the glint of chrome. A hand emerged, clutching a hefty price list. "Cash only," a voice rasped.An hour later, we emerged from the store, blinking against the harsh sunlight. The attorney clutched a bag crammed with microphones, recorders, and enough batteries to power a small city. I hefted a suitcase filled with enough "heinous chemicals" to fuel a weekend-long bender.We piled into the waiting convertible, the red paint gleaming like a fresh coat of blood. The attorney gunned the engine, and we roared off into the desert, leaving behind the madness of Hollywood and heading towards the even greater madness of Las Vegas.  The wind whipped through our hair, carrying with it the scent of freedom and the promise of adventure. This was the Gonzo life, and we were riding it full throttle, straight into the heart of the American Dream.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: I was invited to lunch by a billionaire who wanted to start a literary magazine. The London club was opulent, the atmosphere carefully crafted through gilded light fixtures and dark accents. I was late, carrying my heavy suitcase and sweating, but the billionaire wore casual clothes and seemed unbothered by my lateness, launching into an explanation of his software project for predicting employee betrayal. The literary journal had not come up when the waitress brought bread to us, nor when she brought a range of appetizers. I realized the billionaire had ordered for us both. He insisted then on paying for a taxi to the airport, a generosity I would not decline given the rush of my morning. As we ate, he unfurled his life story. ‘It’s all what you’d expect,’ he said. ‘Rags-to-riches, you know—to be rich and unbothered, that’s the real achievement. To feel calm,’ he told me. ‘That’s what it allows.’ I wondered if he thought of the literary magazine as an entry point into writing. written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: Home, that perennial thing. The place we’ve heard a million aphorisms about—telling us how much it matters, that it’s always there for us, and trying to answer the biggest question: where to find it. Thomas Wolfe’s novel, You Can’t Go Home Again, seems to offer a concerning counter to this, but this is actually a trick of the light, for one can never truly leave home to begin with. Home is in the sinew, in the flesh, home, in all of its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons, is a place deep in the bosom, straight in the center, right up the spine and down through the feet. And what is truly at the core of home is not the wood beams, the forest hills, the patio furniture, metal gates and paved roads—it’s the youthful perception, those rose-tinted glasses, a time of understanding before the world laid its full hands on us. It is childhood, not just the memory or the idea of it, but the physical self that was once to a child, learning the way of the world, ignorant to the ways of man, the race, the place, the pace. It is a version of the self that navigates only through imagination, through interaction with those mysterious figures of the land, the adults, the mailman, the clerk, the aunt, the neighbor, the siblings. And it is this version of the self, the child, that we try to run to when we get older when the bills pile, when you can’t find a place to park, when the kids won’t listen, when we crave that time again, that little pocket in our chest we can tuck into to know that there was life before these little bothers. When we nestle in there, we find the key to ultimate return, to a place of comfort, to belonging to your own world— to coming home.
written_by_MFA030.Excerpt2: When Thomas Wolfe declared you can't go home again, he hadn't reckoned with the stubborn geography of the heart, that relentless compass that forever points to our beginning place. Home isn't merely the creaking floorboards beneath our feet or the worn doorknobs our palms remember—it's the shadow-dance of memory that lives in our bones, as natural as breathing and just as necessary. I've watched children, those clear-eyed prophets of truth, who know nothing of north or south, east or west, but understand perfectly the latitude of belonging. In their world, grown folks move like planets in a universe they haven't yet learned to question, their orbits unbroken by doubt. Mama's laugh rings true as church bells, and daddy's footsteps mark time like drums in the evening, while neighbors drift through the streets like familiar ghosts, their stories settling into the soil of young minds like seeds waiting to bloom. Lord, how we fool ourselves thinking we've grown up just because we've learned to navigate parking meters and mortgage payments! The truth is, most of us are still those wide-eyed children wearing adult clothes, playing at being grown, while deep inside we're running home through twilight streets that exist now only in memory. We carry our dragons and dreams tucked away in secret pockets, and when the world proves too sharp, too cold, we retreat to that internal sanctuary where everything makes sense according to the logic of childhood. Home isn't a place you leave behind—it's the story that writes itself in your blood, the mirror that shows you your truest face, the song that keeps singing long after the music has stopped. It's the place where our first tears fell and our earliest laughter echoed, where we learned the shape of love and fear, and where we return, again and again, in the quiet moments when our hearts need healing.

written_by_MFA030.Original: Thomas Wolfe warned in the title of America’s great novel that “You Can’t Go Home Again.” I enjoyed the book but I never agreed with the title. I believe that one can never leave home. I believe that one carries the shadows, the dreams, the fears and dragons of home under one’s skin, at the extreme corners of ones eyes and possibly in the gristle of the ear lobe.Home is that youthful region where a child is the only real living inhabitant. Parents, siblings, and neighbors, are mysterious apparitions, who come, go, and do strange unfathomable things in and around the child, the region’s only enfranchised citizen.Geography, as such, has little meaning to the child observer. If one grows up in the Southwest, the desert and open skies are natural. New York, with the elevators and subway rumble and millions of people, and Southeast Florida with its palm trees and sun and beaches are to the children of those regions the way the outer world is, has been, and will always be. Since the child cannot control that environment, she has to find her own place, a region where only she lives and no one else can enter.I am convinced that most people do not grow up. We find parking spaces and honor our credit cards. We marry and dare to have children and call that growing up. I think what we do is mostly grow old. We carry accumulation of years in our bodies and on our faces, but generally our real selves, the children inside, are still innocent and shy as magnolias.We may act sophisticated and worldly but I believe we feel safest when we go inside ourselves and find home, a place where we belong and maybe the only place we really do.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: Home, I have found, is not simply a place but a feeling that nestles deep in the folds of one’s soul. It is the shadowed hallway of memory, the faint scent of grandmother’s soap, the creak of a floorboard that seemed alive under hurried feet. Thomas Wolfe’s declaration that one “can’t go home again” lingers in the air like a challenge, for he must not have known that home is not a place you return to; it is a space you carry, ever-present, with its jagged edges and tender sanctuaries. It is where your fears grow fangs and your dreams sprout wings, where dragons curl in the corners of your mind, guarding treasures of old laughter and quiet heartbreak.In the eyes of a child, home stretches as far as the world itself—an empire shaped by the curve of a dirt road or the towering majesty of a neighbor’s oak tree. Adults are gods of that kingdom, figures who wield their power with mystery, speaking in codes that seem unknowable. Yet, even as we grow, we seldom outgrow the pull of home. We may wear the masks of adulthood—secure parking spots, pay bills on time, and rehearse the lines of responsibility—but inside, we are still children. We navigate the world like sailors tracing their fingers over a map, searching for familiar shores that no longer exist except in the sanctity of our own minds.Home is a refuge, a sanctuary of belonging, but not because of its walls or windows. It is the gathering of whispers, the embrace of something so profoundly personal it could never be truly shared. And so, as I carry its essence within me, I know that the journey is not about leaving or returning—it is about understanding that home was never outside of me to begin with.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: I imagined him taller than he should have been, his head near the ceiling of an unfamiliar apartment he couldn’t love as he wrote his novel You Can’t Go Home Again looming over his refrigerator. Home, to Thomas Wolfe, was a quiet town in a temperate valley of the Blue Ridge Mountains. From such vantage points, the world becomes diminutive, entirely comprehensible. Only when you venture into those views do you see the world’s vastness beyond its landscapes, how you can’t see home through eyes that have left, that have taken in new views, new worlds, a new you. But can home be truly gone without you? Is home not a dark chamber you carry within, with its shadows, dreams, fears, and dragons? I remembered my childhood home for the woods that circled the property, where things belonged because they resided there. A childhood home is the childhood. It is the wilderness unknowing children frolic through. It is the security of a warm blanket before they learn it can be ripped away. The adults in their lives seem impossibly, staggeringly old, years beyond the years children know. Like enigmatic peaks of mountain ranges, parents, older siblings, and neighbors loom from a distance. They cast only shadows on the sunny region of play that is the childhood home. But the sun falls and the shadows grow long. With time, the children grow taller than they should, than they feel they should. They leave the wilderness. Through the vague groping around in the night to their parkings spaces and their dinner tables strewn with bills, they long for childhood, for return. But as sure as that longing pulls from within them, there is that dark chamber waiting for light. It has always been there. You have never left home.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: I disagree with Thomas Wolfe. Home, it seems, is something you can never leave. It is a shadow, a dream, a fear, a dragon that follows you, forever tucked away in the deepest corner of your heart. It is the space you were first allowed to be yourself, the place where you learned to see the world through your own eyes, a child's eyes, where everything seemed as it should be.The adults in this region of your world, your parents, neighbors, siblings, were mysterious figures, moving in and out of your awareness like fleeting shadows. Their voices echoed in the hallways of your mind, their laughter and tears shaping the contours of your memories. You never questioned their presence, their belonging. They were as much a part of your world as the sun and the moon, the trees and the stars.And then, one day, you grew up. Or so they said. But did you really? Did you ever truly shed the skin of your childhood, the innocence of your youth? Or did you simply grow old, fulfilling the roles and responsibilities that society thrust upon you, finding parking spaces, paying bills, all the while carrying that child within, seeking the safety and comfort of home?Home is not a place, not really. It is a feeling, a sense of belonging, of being truly known and accepted. It is the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much, the place where you can always return, no matter how far you may have strayed. It is the echo of your childhood, the whisper of your dreams, the shadow of your fears, the dragon of your heart. It is the place where you are always welcome, the place where you are always loved.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Though I understand the meaning behind ‘You Can’t Go Home’, the title of that great novel by Thomas Wolfe, I myself cannot agree with his sentiment. I have found myself returning home many times over the years. There may no longer be a geographical place that bears more than a passing resemblance to the home of my girlhood, yet “home” itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life. I have returned again and again to that place, an imaginative landscape mapped and defined not by geography nor by cultural differences but by our youthful perceptions, during a time when the adults in our lives—parents, neighbors, siblings—are but shadowy figures whose actions are an enigma to us even as they shape our very selves. Many of us will grow old without truly growing up. We may fulfill the roles demanded of us as we age, whether by paying a bill, finding a parking space, or any of those actions that comprise an adult life. We may wander to other continents and may never return to the physical houses of our pasts, if these houses even remain standing for us to visit. But we are always one moment away from retreating to this inner world. It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence. I have returned home in spirit countless times, to this inner world that is a refuge and sanctuary, a place of ultimate belonging. It is this home which keeps me whole, a place I will never fully leave.

I believe that one can never leave home. I believe that one carries the shadows, the dreams, the fears and dragons of home under one’s skin, at the extreme corners of ones eyes and possibly in the gristle of the ear lobe.Home is that youthful region where a child is the only real living inhabitant. Parents, siblings, and neighbors, are mysterious apparitions, who come, go, and do strange unfathomable things in and around the child, the region’s only enfranchised citizen.Geography, as such, has little meaning to the child observer. Since the child cannot control that environment, she has to find her own place, a region where only she lives and no one else can enter.I am convinced that most people do not grow up. We find parking spaces and honor our credit cards. We marry and dare to have children and call that growing up. I think what we do is mostly grow old. written_by_MFA005.Excerpt1: I disagree with Thomas Wolfe. Home, it seems, is something you can never leave. Their voices echoed in the hallways of your mind, their laughter and tears shaping the contours of your memories. You never questioned their presence, their belonging. They were as much a part of your world as the sun and the moon, the trees and the stars.And then, one day, you grew up. Or so they said. But did you really? Did you ever truly shed the skin of your childhood, the innocence of your youth? It is a feeling, a sense of belonging, of being truly known and accepted. It is the refuge you seek when the world becomes too much, the place where you can always return, no matter how far you may have strayed. It is the echo of your childhood, the whisper of your dreams, the shadow of your fears, the dragon of your heart. It is the place where you are always welcome, the place where you are always loved.
written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Though I understand the meaning behind ‘You Can’t Go Home’, the title of that great novel by Thomas Wolfe, I myself cannot agree with his sentiment. I have found myself returning home many times over the years. There may no longer be a geographical place that bears more than a passing resemblance to the home of my girlhood, yet “home” itself is something inescapable and internal, a place of shadows, dreams, fears and dragons that is formed in childhood and carried deep inside for the rest of one’s life. I have returned again and again to that place, an imaginative landscape mapped and defined not by geography nor by cultural differences but by our youthful perceptions, during a time when the adults in our lives—parents, neighbors, siblings—are but shadowy figures whose actions are an enigma to us even as they shape our very selves. Many of us will grow old without truly growing up. We may fulfill the roles demanded of us as we age, whether by paying a bill, finding a parking space, or any of those actions that comprise an adult life. We may wander to other continents and may never return to the physical houses of our pasts, if these houses even remain standing for us to visit. But we are always one moment away from retreating to this inner world. It is here where we immerse ourselves in the comforts that defined our sense of home as children, whether those comforts were real or half imagined and exaggerated by our childlike innocence. I have returned home in spirit countless times, to this inner world that is a refuge and sanctuary, a place of ultimate belonging. It is this home which keeps me whole, a place I will never fully leave.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: The chiffon curtain like a pleated hourglass hung cinched by the dark of the sash. It stood unstirred in the limpid bedroom air. No, the empty air was preoccupied with the counting of its ceaseless age. My grandfather’s watch–which still belonged to my father even after his death as dogs belong to their buried owners, circling their grave and howling the premonitions my grandfather had uttered in his own bed: life being one big fever dream, all its hills and troughs in one fell swoop wrenched from under you, a dream from which you will be wrenched, and you wake in the unending dark where you take no triumphs with you, and the ceaseless hounds of timestamp flat your burial mound and the sky’s days pass beyond–ticked incessantly somewhere in the dark. My father talked about the dark in a similar night’s stifled room. How Saint Francis welcomed Little Sister Death as the dark all around Jesus when he walked along the long and lonely light-rays. Beyond that dark is nothing but dark, that we only know dark from the little light we got. We only know time because we count it, but countless time goes unticked in the unending dark, so much time there is no before, no after, the unnumbered breezes with no curtain to shape them. No, my time is never truly had. I felt the air too thick to breathe.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: The shadow of the sash falls down the curtain, a pallid crescent in the gloom of the room.  I can hear the ticking of the watch, a steady pulse in the quiet.  It was Grandfather’s watch, and now it is Father’s, and someday it will be mine.  The watch ticks on, a metronome marking the inexorable passage of time.  Father said, “You cannot conquer time.  You can only try to forget it.”  But how can one forget time when it is always there, ticking away, a constant reminder of our mortality?  The watch hands move, a slow, relentless dance towards the end.  “Time is a relentless and hungry force,” Father said.  “It devours all things – youth, beauty, even memory.”  The watch ticks on, a tiny machine marking the moments of our lives.  Each tick brings us closer to the end, to the final silence.  “Victories in life are fleeting,” Father said.  “They are but illusions in the face of time’s infinite and hungry maw.”  The watch ticks on, a constant reminder of our mortality.  It is a sound that haunts me, a sound that echoes the futility of our existence.  “Jesus walking on Galilee,” Father said, “and Saint Francis, speaking to his Little Sister Death.  Both of them knew that time could not be conquered, that it could only be endured.”  The watch ticks on, a steady beat in the silence of the room.  It is a sound that I cannot escape, a sound that reminds me of my own mortality.

written_by_MFA003.Original: When the shadow of the sash appeared on the curtains it was between seven and eight oclock and then I was in time again, hearing the watch. It was Grandfather’s and when Father gave it to me he said, Quentin, I give you the mausoleum of all hope and desire; it’s rather excrutiatingly apt that you will use it to gain the reducto absurdum of all human experience which can fit your individual needs no better than it fitted his or his father’s. I give it to you not that you may remember time, but that you might forget it now and then for a moment and not spend all your breath trying to conquer it. Because no battle is ever won he said. They are not even fought. The field only reveals to man his own folly and despair, and victory is an illusion of philosophers and fools. It was propped against the collar box and I lay listening to it. Hearing it, that is. I dont suppose anybody ever deliberately listens to a watch or a clock. You dont have to. You can be oblivious to the sound for a long while, then in a second of ticking it can create in the mind unbroken the long diminishing parade of time you didn’t hear. Like Father said down the long and lonely light-rays you might see Jesus walking, like. And the good Saint Francis that said Little Sister Death, that never had a sister.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: A moment came when I stirred from my private twilight and noticed two things. First, the stain of shadow upon the curtains. Then, the ticking of the watch. It was a fine instrument that had been passed down from my grandfather to my father to me. Both of these men were long dead, and it seemed that in my inheriting the watch, I had inherited their fate: the impending loss of a war with time. It was a fate my father had tried in vain to prepare me for.“Time,” he once said to me, “is inexorable. It can be fought, but never conquered. Our victories are as futile as our struggles.” Time was and is and had and always would win. All I could do was lay in bed and listen to the steady, measured thump of its advance, like the footsteps of an army unafraid of being spotted by its enemy. The ticking seemed to stop coming from the watch. Now, it was coming from everywhere. Time bled from the walls and windows and floors, and with the flood came memory. I thought of my father describing Jesus walking along long and lonely light rays. I thought of his stories about St. Francis’s “Little Sister Death” who left no flower un-plucked. written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: The shadow of the sash curved across the dim curtains, and the watch on the nightstand ticked steadily, a quiet insistence that time itself bore witness to all that was and all that ever would be. I could feel it in my chest, that weight, a pressing reminder of my grandfather's words—words handed down through my father like a relic, tarnished by the grime of despair, polished by futility. Time does not pause, does not forgive. Its victories are hollow, its passing immutable, carving grooves into the soul like water wears down stone, relentless and unyielding.The ticking grew louder, or perhaps it was my thoughts that gave it resonance, filling the room, saturating the air. And in that sound, that metronome of inevitability, I found the tether of memory and the dread of its permanence. Was it my father’s voice I heard or my own thoughts as they spiraled? His words wrapped around my consciousness like the fraying tendrils of a dream that refuses to die. Jesus walked once, on light-rays long and lonely, and Francis whispered to Death as though she were kin, a sister who waited not cruelly but certainly.I lay there, the watch’s rhythm tethering me to the present even as my spirit floated, weightless, into the past and future. Time, unbroken and unseen, bore its teeth, gnawing at the fragile membrane between what is and what is not, what could be and what will never be. I closed my eyes, and still, the ticking remained.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: And before long lying in bed in this room my senses narrowed in totality. There was no escaping the shadow on the sash of the curtains flooding out in further shadows darkening the windowsill and washing the floorboards in lengthening patches of darker darknesses though still I attempted to move away from them even as they drifted over my legs in bed. They almost had me then. But I would not let them. No I would never let them. Not once. Because once is always. And the ticking hiccups of my grandfather’s watch that my father gave me in my pocket I could not either escape. Its rhythm beating hiccups against my leg made me think only of my father and every word he ever gave me to hold on to. The inescapability of clocks never outweighed by the conquered, momentary kingdoms of victories, he said, never outdone by wordly doings done in the face of all that we are faced with. These are but illusions and facades in the battlegrounds of time, he once said. But consider Jesus walking forty days forty nights and the long and lonely light-rays and consider even still Saint Francis’s Little Sister Death, consider the weight of Jesus and light and death, he said. Consider them. Thinking of my father in this way and his words in bed amid the shadows and the ticking he gave me so long ago only deepened my fear of the inevitable. The ineffable. The possible, terrible pointlessness of it all.

Time does not pause, does not forgive. Its victories are hollow, its passing immutable, carving grooves into the soul like water wears down stone, relentless and unyielding.The ticking grew louder, or perhaps it was my thoughts that gave it resonance, filling the room, saturating the air. And in that sound, that metronome of inevitability, I found the tether of memory and the dread of its permanence. Was it my father’s voice I heard or my own thoughts as they spiraled? His words wrapped around my consciousness like the fraying tendrils of a dream that refuses to die. Jesus walked once, on light-rays long and lonely, and Francis whispered to Death as though she were kin, a sister who waited not cruelly but certainly.I lay there, the watch’s rhythm tethering me to the present even as my spirit floated, weightless, into the past and future. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: The Swede. It was a name that echoed through the streets of Weequahic like a myth in the making. Seymour Irving Levov, the golden-haired boy with eyes as blue as the summer sky, a figure so different from the rest of us, the dark-haired, sallow-skinned sons of Abraham. He was an anomaly, a beautiful paradox in our world of traditions and books, where the mind was king and the body a mere vessel. Yet, there he was, our very own Apollo, a god in cleats and a varsity jacket, conquering not with intellect but with the raw power of his physique.He was a football hero, a basketball star, a baseball legend, all rolled into one. He wasn't just playing these games; he was dominating them, bending them to his will with the same effortless grace that seemed to permeate his every move. And we, the spectators, the witnesses to his greatness, we were lifted out of our ordinary lives, our worries and anxieties momentarily forgotten in the roar of the crowd, the thrill of the game.In those war-torn years, when the world seemed to be crumbling around us, when the news from Europe was filled with darkness and despair, the Swede was our beacon of hope, our symbol of triumph. He was the embodiment of invincibility, the proof that even in the face of overwhelming odds, victory was still possible. We clung to his success like a life raft, finding solace in his achievements, a temporary escape from the harsh realities of the world. He was more than just a high school athlete; he was a symbol, a myth, a legend that we created and nurtured, a projection of our deepest desires and aspirations. He was the embodiment of the American dream, the proof that even a Jewish boy from Newark could rise to the top, could achieve greatness, could become a god among men. And in those dark days, when the future seemed so uncertain, we needed that dream, we needed that myth, we needed the Swede.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: In Newark, the war was a permanent fixture—at the dinner table, in the classroom, everywhere. But I was just a pimply and unsettled boy, and my understanding of the war was somewhat opaque. What I remember most about that time is not the constant barrage of terrible news or the hushed conversations about the Germans, but rather a boy, well, a young man, named Seymour Irving Levov, though we all called him “The Swede,” because he looked about as Nordic as they come with his white-blond hair and his blue eyes, all the Jewishness rinsed out of him at birth. He was beloved, and it was strange the way he was beloved, because the favorites in the community were usually the smart ones. And The Swede was smart, sure, but it was his athletic prowess that made him godlike, his speed, his strength, the effortless way he wound his arm back to crack a baseball through the air. You could feel it when he weaved around the basketball court, the way the crowd tensed and relaxed and oozed as one entity when he climbed through the air toward the hoop, the wing of his shoulder blade bringing him higher, higher to victory. I was preoccupied with other things; I was not afraid of the war but I knew they were. I could see it on their faces and in the way they held their purses tighter, the way their lips began to turn down when they performed mundane tasks, my mother folding laundry with a look of terror on her face, my father driving to the grocery store, his hands so tight around the steering wheel that his knuckles went white. The Swede became a symbol of innocence and invincibility to them. He was our Apollo, a religious totem you could hold tightly and press to your lips in those dark hours of the night.Watch us in the stadium, in the football field stands, as he dove nose-first into the end zone. You would have seen a group of people utterly unafraid.

written_by_MFA008.Original: The Swede. During the war years, when I was still a grade school boy, this was a magical name in our Newark neighborhood, even to adults just a generation removed from the city's old Prince Street ghetto and not yet so flawlessly Americanized as to be bowled over by the prowess of a high school athlete. The name was magical; so was the anomalous face. Of the few fair-complexioned Jewish students in our preponderantly Jewish public high school, none possessed anything remotely like the steep-jawed, insentient Viking mask of this blue-eyed blond born into our tribe as Seymour Irving Levov.The Swede starred as end in football, center in basketball, and first baseman in baseball. Only the basketball team was ever any good—twice winning the city championship while he was its leading scorer—but as long as the Swede excelled, the fate of our sports teams didn't matter much to a student body whose elders, largely undereducated and overburdened, venerated academic achievement above all else. Physical aggression, even camouflaged by athletic uniforms and official rules and intended to do no harm to Jews, was not a traditional source of pleasure in our community—advanced degrees were. Nonetheless, through the Swede, the neighborhood entered into a fantasy about itself and about the world, the fantasy of sports fans everywhere: almost like Gentiles (as they imagined Gentiles), our families could forget the way things actually work and make an athletic performance the repository of all their hopes. Primarily, they could forget the war.The elevation of Swede Levov into the household Apollo of the Weequahic Jews can best be explained, I think, by the war against the Germans and the Japanese and the fears that it fostered. With the Swede indomitable on the playing field, the meaningless surface of life provided a bizarre, delusionary kind of sustenance, the happy release into a Swedian innocence, for those who lived in dread of never seeing their sons or their brothers or their husbands again.

He was the embodiment of invincibility, the proof that even in the face of overwhelming odds, victory was still possible. We clung to his success like a life raft, finding solace in his achievements, a temporary escape from the harsh realities of the world. He was the embodiment of the American dream, the proof that even a Jewish boy from Newark could rise to the top, could achieve greatness, could become a god among men. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: In Newark, the war was a permanent fixture—at the dinner table, in the classroom, everywhere. But I was just a pimply and unsettled boy, and my understanding of the war was somewhat opaque. He was beloved, and it was strange the way he was beloved, because the favorites in the community were usually the smart ones. And The Swede was smart, sure, but it was his athletic prowess that made him godlike, his speed, his strength, the effortless way he wound his arm back to crack a baseball through the air. You could feel it when he weaved around the basketball court, the way the crowd tensed and relaxed and oozed as one entity when he climbed through the air toward the hoop, the wing of his shoulder blade bringing him higher, higher to victory. I was preoccupied with other things; I was not afraid of the war but I knew they were. I could see it on their faces and in the way they held their purses tighter, the way their lips began to turn down when they performed mundane tasks, my mother folding laundry with a look of terror on her face, my father driving to the grocery store, his hands so tight around the steering wheel that his knuckles went white. The Swede became a symbol of innocence and invincibility to them. He was our Apollo, a religious totem you could hold tightly and press to your lips in those dark hours of the night.Watch us in the stadium, in the football field stands, as he dove nose-first into the end zone. You would have seen a group of people utterly unafraid.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: In the heart of Newark, during those tense years of World War II, there existed among us a boy whose mere existence seemed to defy the contours of our collective identity. Seymour Irving Levov—"The Swede"—his name floated through the whispers of our community like a hymn. Fair-haired and blue-eyed, with the sinews of an Olympian god, he stood in stark contrast to the rest of us, who were more likely to be celebrated for our Talmudic acumen than for any prowess on the athletic field. But there he was, a towering figure of grace and strength, conquering the realms of football, basketball, and baseball with a seeming effortlessness that none of us could emulate. To see him play was to witness something almost sacred, as though the mundane boundaries of our neighborhood had been temporarily lifted to reveal a glimpse of something larger, purer, and profoundly American.We loved him not because he was one of us, but because he was so distinctly other, embodying a kind of transcendence we barely dared to dream of. The Swede was everything we were not allowed to imagine ourselves to be—resilient, fearless, and uncomplicated by the anxieties that knitted themselves into the very fabric of our Jewish existence. To watch him soar above the basketball rim or charge down the football field was to forget, if only for a moment, the war, the ration books, the headlines filled with death. In those fleeting moments, he turned our collective dread into something weightless and buoyant. We made of him an Apollo, a golden boy whose victories on the field were our victories, whose perfection was our imperfect salvation.Even now, I can see him in my mind’s eye, the sunlight catching the blonde halo of his hair as he pitched another strike or sank another jump shot. He was our myth, our impossible hope, the embodiment of a Newark dream in a time when dreaming seemed almost criminal.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: No matter what I thought of myself in childhood, both in times of complimentary self-reference and in self-effacement, I was comparing myself to The Swede, and I never came out on top. I wasn’t trying to out-duel him, that would have been impossible; it was an effort to get closer to his prestige, even if I could never match it. In Newark nobody did what he did. He was striking for many reasons—the blue eyes and fair hair that gave Seymour Irving Levov his nickname wasn’t common in our synagogue. He also carved out a niche in our world we found both bizarre and entrancing. While most of us studied and read till bedtime The Swede must have spent the time lifting weights and punching swinging bags of cotton. In school he excelled in football, basketball, and baseball while we watched with fearful hope. His curled muscles and firm abdomen seemed to defy the laws of our upbringings, of our parents’ schemes, but also to create a new sort of hope, because World War II was underway and surely The Swede could deliver a personal victory against the Germans not only militarily for the United States but for Jews in Newark too. His youth gave him a wide-eyed stupid confidence and his figure gave him an invincibility. He was our Apollo. With every snap of the bat against the ball, we cheered for him and for our brothers and fathers in the war who might just come home safely if they could channel The Swede’s fiendish affinity for dominant physical triumph, a kind of triumph none of us were used to seeing embodied. He spun through defenders on the basketball court and we imagined Newark’s finest darting through enemy lines toward us. He dove into the opponent’s running back and we imagined our male relatives tackling a Nazi and pounding, pounding, pounding down, breaking them into specific wet bits we could never have seen in such luscious detail otherwise.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: In the tremulous years of the Second World War, when fear wrapped itself around our Newark neighborhood like a fog rolling off the Passaic, we had our very own demigod, our walking antidote to Jewish anxiety – Seymour "The Swede" Levov. Here was a Jewish boy who could smash through defensive lines on the football field with the force of a Gentile, who could arc a basketball through the hoop with gymnastic grace, who could swing a baseball bat as if it were his birthright rather than something we'd borrowed from the other America. And how we needed him then, needed to believe in this anomaly, this statistical impossibility of nature who happened to daven at our synagogue! While our mothers whispered anxiously about cousins in Europe and our fathers scanned casualty lists in the Newark News with trembling hands, The Swede was our ticket to invincibility, our pass into that other realm where Jewish boys didn't have to be smart because they were beautiful, didn't have to be crafty because they were strong. We projected onto him all our desperate hopes of acceptance, of transcendence – this boy who looked like he'd stepped out of a Nazi propaganda poster but wore a chai around his neck and could recite his Haftorah portion without a single mistake. The Swede was our temporary escape from who we were, from what we feared, from the relentless drumbeat of war news that threatened to drown out even the sound of our prayers.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: It is December 31, 2004, and I find myself at the intersection of memory and absence, crossing Lexington Avenue on a day John never knew. The light changes, the traffic hums, but the world feels displaced, as though operating on a parallel timeline I can no longer inhabit. I ask myself where we were this day a year ago, but the question folds into itself, unanswered. There was no "we" then. There is no "we" now. It is just me, standing on the edge of a moment I never thought would arrive, tethered to someone who no longer exists in the present tense.Time has turned traitorous, reshaping vivid recollections into something blurred, soft-edged, mudgy. I want the sharpness back—the sound of his voice calling my name, the exact tilt of his head when he laughed—but instead I am left with echoes that refuse to hold their shape. For months I kept time through him: what we ate, where we sat, how the hours unfolded a year ago. That tether, too, is breaking, and I know it must. To live is to keep the dead where they belong, not erased but sequestered, a layer beneath the surface of everything we do and feel. I loved him, love him still, but loving him has become the act of holding his absence, acknowledging the permanence of it, walking forward through the days he will never know. This is the life left, the one that does not wait.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Since John’s death, my memories (of him, but also of most things), once acute, have become soft and mudgy. For a while, I was able to maintain a handle on reality by way of an elaborate method of timekeeping. It was calming to look back at what John and I were doing one year ago, and keep track of the days that way. One year ago today, I would remind myself, we were in Mexico, preparing a dinner of heavily spiced chicken in our rented kitchen. One year ago today, we were at the Met, looking at the new rooftop exhibit, which John loved but I disliked for its uninspired crudeness. These memories were vivid, acute, and I was able to almost watch them, like one would a television show. And then, December 31, 2003 arrived. In that moment, one year ago no longer included him. John had morphed, officially, into a part of the past and not the present. I came to this burning realization while I was crossing Lexington Avenue. I had a bag of groceries in my hand. It was snowing, quite faintly. I realized I had spent the year trying to keep him alive, because I have always believed, been told, that it is our duty to keep the dead alive. But what about the living? I realized it, then, that the key to all of this was to keep them dead. There was no other way, in my view, to continue living myself.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: When I think of John now, whether in grief or joy, time makes a mirage of our parting. Memories are distant, those vibrant, vivid images inevitably softened by the passing days and nights into muddy and distorted reflections. My practice of keeping time in relation to what John and I were doing last year is a game of questions. When he was alive, who did we see today? Where did we go together? Above all: What did he say to me then? Crossing Lexington Avenue in the wintry haze enveloping New York, a cold, damp curtain hung above the city, I come across the date—December 31, 2003—and realize John never saw this day last year. My exercise for keeping time has expired, and my husband lives in the distant past. I might transplant him here, invite him as memory into this moment to maintain our profound connection, the sort unsevered by death so long as he is kept within the perfect safety of memory. Yet it occurs to me—in this exercise of resurrection, I am only ensuring that I, too, never see December 31, 2003. That I, like John, live only in my recollections. Thus: we must keep them dead. To continue living, to draw oneself up from the smudged and mildewy twilight of the place where memory is real to us, there can be no resurrection; for the living to carry on, the dead must remain dead.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: The air in the apartment is heavy, thick with the scent of lilies and the ghost of his presence. Each day is a faded echo of the one before, a year removed.  I find myself trapped in a loop, rewinding the reel of memory, asking, "Where were we a year ago? What were we doing?"  It's a futile attempt to hold onto him, to keep him alive in the only way I know how.Yesterday, I crossed Lexington Avenue, the same way I've done a thousand times before. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The wind whipped around me, tearing at my clothes and sending the scattered debris dancing across the desolate expanse of the field.  It was a place of stark beauty, where the horizon stretched out like an endless ribbon, and the sky, a vast canvas of swirling greys and blues, mirrored the turmoil within my own heart.For a moment, I allowed myself to be swept away by a fantasy, to imagine that all the things I'd lost in life had somehow washed up here, deposited by the relentless tide of time.
