After a while, I turned and walked back to my car, leaving behind the windswept field and the echoes of my fantasy.  The road ahead stretched out before me, a path that I would travel alone, but with a newfound sense of peace.  The world was still there, waiting for me, and life, in all its complexity and beauty, would go on.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The wind was picking up the litter in the field. Trash bags and ripped receipts flew up and over the empty plain. I pictured my own refuse catching alongside it, everything I’d discarded coming up and toward me in the breeze. For a moment I imagined this was the place where everything I'd ever lost had washed up. A figure approached from beyond the horizon, pulled along by the gusts. It was Tommy. I turned away and stopped my imagination, even as I felt the tears falling down my face -- I forced the images to disappear -- and drop back into the grass as I listened to that rush of natural force sweeping over the plain. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: The wind whipped around me, tearing at my clothes and sending the scattered debris dancing across the desolate expanse of the field. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The wind was picking up the litter in the field. Trash bags and ripped receipts flew up and over the empty plain. written_by_MFA013.Excerpt1: The field stretched barren before me, littered with scraps of rubbish that danced and swirled in the wind’s restless grip. Torn plastic bags snagged on brittle weeds, while papers tumbled past, their jagged edges fluttering like messages lost to time. I stood there, unmoving, as the chill seeped into my skin, anchoring me to the emptiness. It was then, amidst this desolation, that I let myself imagine. I pictured this field as a shore where all I’d lost had been washed ashore: friendships eroded by time, promises broken, dreams that had long slipped beyond my reach. And then, through the haze of this thought, I saw him. Tommy. He was walking toward me from the far horizon, his arm lifted in that familiar wave—assured, kind, so unmistakably him. For one brief, aching moment, it felt real, so vivid that I almost called out. But I caught myself, the breath halting in my throat as I reined the vision in, folding it away like something fragile. Tears welled, then fell, unbidden, but I held my composure. After a moment, I turned back to the car, its cold metal unyielding beneath my touch. Life waited, indifferent, as it always had.
written_by_MFA013.Excerpt2: I stood in solitude in the grass field near the beach. Ten feet away, the grass gave way to sand, which then gave way to the ocean. The wind blew, scattering rubbish and abandoned belongings. An umbrella tumbled along the shoreline, and a plastic bag drifted past me. A wide variety of objects – presumably lost at sea or lost by patrons of the beach – washed up on the shore. I imagined that anything I’d lost throughout my life could be returned to me by those waves. Then I pictured Tommy approaching from the horizon, the hair on his legs wet and flat against his skin. I saw him wave at me, and was overcome by the pain of his absence. Tears welled in my eyes. I knew that he was not really there, Tommy had long since passed. Nevertheless, I found myself longing for him to come join me in the grass. I shut my eyes and stood still for a long moment. I dried my tears and became composed. I returned to my car, without looking back. Tommy was gone, I reminded myself. Life must go on.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: At breakfast, my father handed me an envelope thick with cash, a gesture both startling and unsettling. "For Christmas," he said with forced cheer, his eyes flicking toward Chitra, who was sipping her tea, avoiding my gaze. He added, almost apologetically, “And Disney World, with us. The girls are excited.” Rupa and Piu, dressed in matching holiday sweaters, looked at me expectantly, their bright faces blurring into one as I fumbled for words. “I can’t,” I said, the excuse tumbling out. “There’s a project—due after break.” The lie felt hollow, but I let it stand. Chitra placed a dish of fruit on the table, her movements brisk, her expression neutral, as if my refusal required no comment. My father leaned back, resigned, a faint relief softening the tension in his jaw. I sensed how the trip would be easier without me—how my presence reminded them of another family, one they had worked hard to unwrite. Later, when I passed the girls in the hallway, they whispered in hurried tones, their laughter abruptly silenced when I appeared. I thought of my mother, the spaces she had filled now occupied by others, and felt caught between loyalties, between memory and their momentum forward. Outside, the winter sun broke through, exposing everything.
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I held the cash, folded in my hand, and my father asked the question again. Would I like to use the gift to join them for a trip to Disney World? I looked around the room, at the expectant faces of Piu and Rupa, and Chitra’s reserved smile. My mother had always sat in the velvet chair Chitra now inhabited and my mother had even donned a similar posture to hers, pert and classic. I tried to mimic Chitra’s smile. Maybe, I said, of course I’d love to, but exams will be especially wicked this year. I don’t expect to have enough time to get away for a vacation. Piu and Rupa knitted their brows, faces falling for a spell, sensing rejection—hadn’t we been getting close? Chitra’s composed smile remained as if painted on her face. I looked back to my father, hoping to convey my gratitude. A piece of me did want to go. I hadn’t been able to say much to him since the new woman became his world, two half-daughters making him young again. The American family getaway might have been an olive branch to me. Certainly Chitra would not have chosen it. I was surprised to see no resignation in his face, no disappointment, but relief instead.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: There is too much detailed and unnecessary description in excerpt 1 and it tries to elaborate too much with out giving more to the reader. Excerpt 2 is more simplified in the sequencing and descriptions. It is economical and precise with the words. Sentences are short, few commas. Excerpt 2 has the same simplicity as the original.
written_by_MFA016.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.

written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: She sat across from Jean-Marc on the white-washed deck of the seaside restaurant, surrounded by an almost aggressive whiteness that seemed to mock the complexity of her emotions. The white tables, the white lampposts, even the moon hanging above the sea appeared to her as fragments of some cosmic unity she could never quite grasp. What puzzled her was not the nostalgia itself—that familiar heaviness in the chest that accompanies all human existence—but rather its peculiar timing. How could one feel nostalgia for someone sitting right there, living and breathing before them? Jean-Marc, with that subtle wisdom that occasionally visits lovers, understood that nostalgia is less about the past than about the terrifying possibility of future absence. It is memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in the clothes of remembrance. Then, like an uninvited guest at a funeral, came a thought of her dead child, followed by something even more unsettling: a sudden, inexplicable happiness. She felt ashamed of this happiness, as if she had committed an act of betrayal against grief itself. But who can dictate the proper sequence of emotions? We humans, who pride ourselves on our capacity for reason, who construct elaborate systems of moral judgment, who write constitutions and establish courts of law—we remain helpless before the anarchic democracy of our feelings. They come and go as they please, these emotions, paying no attention to the carefully arranged furniture of our convictions.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: The whiteness of the drapes and tablecloth invoked in her the uneasy feeling of one blank canvas. Perhaps, there was an absence she wanted to forget. Her former husband had taken her to such seaside restaurants. But it wasn’t the absence of captured life that stirred in her some unrest but the anticipation of life, of color becoming, the canvas waiting. Even in colorful pockets of her vision–out the deck window to the yellow lampposts and dark ocean–it all bathed in the moon’s white glow. Opaque, the blurred background of a photograph. Yes, a photo, something calling back something that had been. And what of her life now? Why did now pass her as every prior moment had, leaving a feeling, for feelings to be the dropped breadcrumbs of life in its constant evasion? She was struck by an intense nostalgia for Jean-Marc.But how can one feel nostalgia for something — or someone — who sits merely an arm's length away?“Perhaps it’s the grief,” Jean-Marc said. “Your mind is preparing you for loss. Is it not easier to wrap these memories in a protective cloak of nostalgia?”If it was all for impending loss, then her mind was well acquainted. But it wasn’t grief she felt when she thought of her son. She imagined him swinging around the pole of a lamppost. Like breadcrumbs, she happened upon joy in the world’s dark vast woods. Feelings were given, never made. Her child was dead. Her husband was gone. Jean-Marc would one day be gone. And yet.

written_by_MFA003.Original: Much later, after she had left her husband and lived several years with Jean-Marc, she was at the seashore one day: they were dining outdoors, on a wooden deck over the water; she retains an intense memory of whiteness: the deck, the tables, the chairs, the tablecloths, everything was white, the lampposts were painted white and the bulbs beamed a white light against the summer sky, not yet dark, where the moon, itself white too, was whitening everything around them. And in this bath of white she was struck by a feeling of unbearable nostalgia for Jean-Marc. Nostalgia? How could she feel nostalgia when he was right in front of her? How can you suffer from the absence of a person who is present? (Jean-Marc knew how to answer that: you can suffer nostalgia in the presence of the beloved if you glimpse a future where the beloved is no more; if the beloved’s death is, invisibly, already present.) During that moment of strange nostalgia at the seaside, she suddenly thought of her dead child, and a wave of happiness flooded over her. Soon she would be frightened by this feeling. But no one can do a thing about feelings, they exist and there’s no way to censor them. We can reproach ourselves for some action, for a remark, but not for a feeling, quite simply because we have no control at all over it.

How could one feel nostalgia for someone sitting right there, living and breathing before them? It is memory projected forward, the anticipation of loss dressed in the clothes of remembrance. written_by_MFA018.Excerpt1: She sat across from Jean-Marc at the seaside restaurant, her fingers tracing invisible patterns on the white linen tablecloth, as if trying to anchor herself amidst the overwhelming brightness surrounding them. The deck stretched out, pale and gleaming, the lampposts shimmered like ghostly sentinels, and the moon hung low, casting an iridescent glow that seemed to swallow every color except white. The air was still, suffused with the faint, rhythmic whispers of the tide. Jean-Marc watched her, his expression serene yet attentive, as if he could read the kaleidoscope of emotions dancing behind her eyes. She felt a paradoxical pang of nostalgia—sharp and bittersweet—as though mourning something lost, though everything she cherished sat mere inches away. It puzzled her, this longing, this melancholy wrapped in an inexplicable happiness. Was it the memory of her deceased child, flitting unbidden into her mind like a shadow across the moonlight? Or was it the fear of losing Jean-Marc, his presence so vital it seemed like a delicate thread connecting her to the world? She smiled suddenly, a fleeting expression of joy so pure it frightened her. Jean-Marc reached for her hand, silently acknowledging the fragile beauty of her emotion. In that luminous moment, it struck her: we are masters of our actions, perhaps even of our words, but not of our feelings, those wild, untamed creatures that move within us, defying reason and will.
written_by_MFA018.Excerpt2: When she imagined this moment months ago, lying beside her husband, she had pictured herself happy. So why wasn't she? She had left him because she wanted to; to be with the man she loved. The man sitting across from her now, handsome in a white button-down shirt. It suddenly struck her that everything in the seaside restaurant was white: the deck, the table, the lampposts. Even the moon, stark and full, shone unbearably white tonight. Jean-Marc asked: "What is the matter with you, my dear? You are so quiet tonight." "Nothing really," she said, knowing it was a lie. Something was wrong, but she could not put that something into words. It was a strange yet acute longing for what was already hers, sitting right there in front of her. Jean-Marc, feeling the melancholy in the air, said: "Nostalgia comes from the fear of losing someone and imagining life without them." She thought of her child, the only person she had truly lost. The memory struck her with unexpected happiness, followed immediately by fear. What did it mean to feel sadness at dinner with her lover but happiness thinking of her dead child? Was there something wrong with her? Was she a bad mother, a bad person? Not according to Scottish philosopher David Hume. Hume had argued emotions were natural and involuntary. While we could control our actions, we could never control our feelings.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt1: First it was the spotted sickness that unfurled from the south. I was not there, but I remember. Then forced migration westward, to Dakota land, and the Anishinabe signed a treaty. These were made to be broken and to break us. After came more displacements, the government making exiles of us again. So many documents and so much displacement. I lie on my back and these papers press hard on my chest when I think of them. In 1914 it was consumption, creeping slowly through the reservation like woodsmoke. Taking us one by one, and unraveling us, and my family could not escape it either. The Pillagers were unraveled by this new sickness and so was our community, huddled so close together as we were. Unable to escape each other, shoulder, pressed to shoulder, and unable to escape the sickness. I was the only one of us who lived. Nanapush, the sole survivor. For this suffering I am already an elder, but I am only fifty years old. And for this terrible privilege I have been witness to the end of the traditions. I have led the last buffalo hunt, saw the last bear killed. Trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last old birch. Sometimes we understood we were doing these things for the final time. Other times, we didn't realize until after. The loss hurts in my teeth. It lives in my early wrinkles and sore body. But I have saved the Pillager family. When the government comes with more papers, more opportunities to strip us of our land and our identity, I have resisted. I did not sign. I will not sign—we will not be exiles again. Too much has already been taken. The Anishinabe persist, and I will continue to resist for the Pillagers who are lost, and for those of us who carry on.
written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: In the damp quiet of that reservation, I stood as the last thread holding together the vast, frayed tapestry of our people, the Anishinabe. Sickness had come, spotted and relentless, rising from the south to crawl across our bodies, marking us for the grave. We fled westward, believing Dakota land might swallow us whole and offer peace, only to be met with treaties that tangled words into chains we could never untether. The land we walked became paper; paper became exile. Yet it was not over. In 1914, another ghost, slow and smothering, stalked us—consumption, it was called. It seeped through the fragile walls of our homes, latching onto breath, pulling entire families under its cold, merciless blanket. I saw the Pillagers go, one by one, slipping into the quiet where I alone remained. Fifty years old, they called me an elder, though my face bore fewer lines than my spirit. Time had sped in its cruelty. I had seen the last buffalo fall beneath our arrows, the last bear stagger through our woods, the final beaver with a pelt worth holding. The birches I once leaned against as a child, their bark aglow with the sun, were nothing but broken stumps. Each loss carved another hollowness, and still, I stood. I saved what was left—the last of the Pillager family, the name that carried its own strength. When they brought papers, government seals pressed flat against the lives they meant to strip away, I took the pen in my hand but never let it touch the page. They could take everything—our animals, our trees, even the air that filled our lungs. But they would not take the land, not from me, not from what I carried. I stared back at them, unflinching, as if daring them to try harder, without fear, without shame.

written_by_MFA026.Original: We started dying before the snow, and, like the snow, we continued to fall. We were surprised that so many of us were left to die. written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south like a shadow that darkens the earth before a storm. We didn't know then that it was just the beginning, just the first thread being pulled from the fabric of our world. I was young when we were pushed westward to Dakota land, our feet leaving tracks in soil that wasn't ours, our hands reaching out to sign papers we couldn't read. The government men smiled with teeth like tombstones while our people's names were written down, recorded, filed away in drawers that would never open again. Then came 1914, and with it the consumption—slow, patient, hungry as winter. It ate through our families like fire through dry grass, starting with the Pillagers who lived close as bark to wood. I watched them fall, one after another, until the silence in their cabin was louder than any drum. My own family went the same way, leaving me to carry their names like stones in my pocket, weighing me down, making me an elder at fifty though my hair had barely grayed. I led the last buffalo hunt, my heart heavy as I watched the dust rise from their hooves. I was there when the last bear fell, when the last beaver with a mature pelt swam into my trap, when the last ancient birch dropped its leaves for the final time. The old ways slipped through our fingers like water, impossible to hold. But I refused to let it all go. When I saved the last of the Pillagers, I held on tight, my fingers cramping around what remained. Those government papers came again and again, whispering promises of money, of progress, of change. But I knew better. I'd seen enough of their promises turn to dust in our mouths. This time, I kept my pen still, my name unwritten, my piece of earth ungiven.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.

The consumption, it was called by young Father Damien, who came in that year to replace the priest who had succumbed to the same devastation as his flock. This disease was different from the pox and fever, for it came on slowly. The outcome, however, was just as certain. Whole families of Anishinabe lay ill and helpless in its breath. On the reservation, where we were forced close together, the clans dwindled. Our tribe unraveled like a coarse rope, frayed at either end as the old and new among us were taken. My own family was wiped out one by one. I was the only Nanapush who lived. And after, although I had seen no more than fifty winters, I was considered an old man.I guided the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a pelt of more than two years' growth. I spoke aloud the words of the government treaty and refused to sign the settlement papers that would take away our woods and lake. I axed the last birch that was older than I, and I saved the last of the Pillager family.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south like a shadow that darkens the earth before a storm. We didn't know then that it was just the beginning, just the first thread being pulled from the fabric of our world. I was young when we were pushed westward to Dakota land, our feet leaving tracks in soil that wasn't ours, our hands reaching out to sign papers we couldn't read. The government men smiled with teeth like tombstones while our people's names were written down, recorded, filed away in drawers that would never open again. Then came 1914, and with it the consumption—slow, patient, hungry as winter. It ate through our families like fire through dry grass, starting with the Pillagers who lived close as bark to wood. I watched them fall, one after another, until the silence in their cabin was louder than any drum. My own family went the same way, leaving me to carry their names like stones in my pocket, weighing me down, making me an elder at fifty though my hair had barely grayed. I led the last buffalo hunt, my heart heavy as I watched the dust rise from their hooves. I was there when the last bear fell, when the last beaver with a mature pelt swam into my trap, when the last ancient birch dropped its leaves for the final time. The old ways slipped through our fingers like water, impossible to hold. But I refused to let it all go. When I saved the last of the Pillagers, I held on tight, my fingers cramping around what remained. Those government papers came again and again, whispering promises of money, of progress, of change. But I knew better. I'd seen enough of their promises turn to dust in our mouths. This time, I kept my pen still, my name unwritten, my piece of earth ungiven.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I am Nanapush, and my people, the Anishinabe, have borne floods of suffering that rose like tidal waves over the generations. We’ve learned to endure the violent waters. First, there was the terrible spotted sickness that came from the south, killing us by the dozens and scarring the faces of the living. There was the long migration west, where we were marched to the Dakotas with an army at our backs, and the treaty we signed at gunpoint. Then came another exile—a slow dismemberment of the land that remained, bled dry by a series of laws and documents. My people were left alone for some time after that. But in 1914, consumption began to prowl the perimeter of the reservation. Its footfall was silent, though its presence was anything but invisible. When consumption snapped its jaws, it unraveled the community death by death, trapping families like the Pillagers inside, left to huddle in their close quarters and wait out the disease. I see now that the disease was waiting them out instead. The Pillagers succumbed to the sickness one by one—all of them but me. Although I am only fifty, I have risen through the ranks by default. I am considered an elder now. In truth, I am merely a survivor. It is under my watch that our traditional way of life has finally been extinguished. It was I who led the final buffalo hunt, trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt, and felled the last of the old birch trees. Loss is my constant companion. It visits me as it visited my ancestors, but I have found a small mercy within its grasp. I have preserved the last of the Pillager family, refusing the men from the government who come with more papers to sign, seeking more ways to strip the Anishinabe of their land and identity. As long as my name is Nanapush, I will not forfeit that final power.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south. It stole through the village like a hungry ghost, leaving empty spaces where laughter and life once thrived. Then came the long walk westward, the elders leaning heavily on their canes, the children clinging to their mothers’ skirts. We signed a treaty in Dakota land, our fingers tracing unfamiliar symbols on the white man's paper. But treaties are as fragile as spiderwebs in the wind, easily torn and forgotten. The government men came again, their words like sharp stones cutting through our hearts. Exile. Loss. Land stolen, not by force, but by the stroke of a pen on official documents.In 1914, a new sickness arrived, a slow, insidious cough that consumed the lungs and the spirit. Consumption, they called it. It spread through the reservation like wildfire, leaving behind a trail of sorrow and empty beds. The Pillagers, huddled close in their crowded homes, succumbed one by one. My family, my friends, my neighbors, all taken by the relentless disease. I watched them go, helpless to stop the tide of grief that threatened to drown me.And then, there was only me. Nanapush, the last of his line, an elder at fifty, my hair prematurely streaked with the white of winter. I led the last buffalo hunt, the thundering hooves echoing through the vast emptiness of the plains. I saw the last bear fall. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last old birch tree, its leaves whispering secrets to the wind.But even in the face of such overwhelming loss, I found the strength to resist. I saved the last of the Pillager family, their faces etched with the same sorrow that mirrored my own. I refused to sign the government papers, those insidious documents that would erase us, make us invisible in our own land.

For those who survived the spotted sickness from the south and our long fight west to Dakota land, where we signed the treaty, and then a wind from the east, bringing exile in a storm of government papers, what descended from the north in 1914 seemed terrible, and unjust.By then we thought disaster must surely have spent its force, that disease must have claimed all of the Anishinabe that the earth could hold and bury.But along with the first bitter punishments of early winter a new sickness swept down. The consumption, it was called by young Father Damien, who came in that year to replace the priest who had succumbed to the same devastation as his flock. This disease was different from the pox and fever, for it came on slowly. The outcome, however, was just as certain. Whole families of Anishinabe lay ill and helpless in its breath. On the reservation, where we were forced close together, the clans dwindled. Our tribe unraveled like a coarse rope, frayed at either end as the old and new among us were taken. My own family was wiped out one by one. I was the only Nanapush who lived. And after, although I had seen no more than fifty winters, I was considered an old man.I guided the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a pelt of more than two years' growth. I spoke aloud the words of the government treaty and refused to sign the settlement papers that would take away our woods and lake. I axed the last birch that was older than I, and I saved the last of the Pillager family.

written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: First, in the south, we were stormed by the spotted sickness, little red bumps that went from the blanket to the body; then, by the gun, we moved westward to Dakota land, thousands of us dragging our feet across endless miles. Those of us who didn't drop dead from the spots signed a treaty. Before long, we moved once more, condemned to exile, our land taken away by right of the government's stamped document. 1914: Another sickness called 'consumption' rolled in as a terrible storm does, its invisible winds running into our mouths and choking us. After all that, we coughed to our deaths. It came slowly: not like a massacre but like a lost war. We were living six to a room back then, and the cough jumped from one Anishinabe brother to another. The whole Pillager family became ill within a fortnight, the eight of them wasting away in a single room. My whole family went, too. Our tribe, once a tightly woven quilt, unraveled; the knots came loose, the patterns disintegrated into bright threads. Merely fifty years have passed since my birth, yet I am now called an elder, the last of the Nanapush. I remember the end of our lives, the final rites of our traditions. I led the last buffalo hunt. I saw the last bear shot. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last birch tree older than a sapling. I remember how, as the sickness razed our people, I went into the room with the eight members of the Pillager family. I fed them water, buffalo meat, and bread. I brought them wet cloths and herbs to ease their fever and coughing. I saved the last of them, the daughter. And I remember receiving the government papers that would rid us of our land and rights. I refused to sign.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The spotted sickness came first, creeping up from the south. It stole through the village like a hungry ghost, leaving empty spaces where laughter and life once thrived. Then came the long walk westward, the elders leaning heavily on their canes, the children clinging to their mothers’ skirts. We signed a treaty in Dakota land, our fingers tracing unfamiliar symbols on the white man's paper. But treaties are as fragile as spiderwebs in the wind, easily torn and forgotten. The government men came again, their words like sharp stones cutting through our hearts. Exile. Loss. Land stolen, not by force, but by the stroke of a pen on official documents.In 1914, a new sickness arrived, a slow, insidious cough that consumed the lungs and the spirit. Consumption, they called it. It spread through the reservation like wildfire, leaving behind a trail of sorrow and empty beds. The Pillagers, huddled close in their crowded homes, succumbed one by one. My family, my friends, my neighbors, all taken by the relentless disease. I watched them go, helpless to stop the tide of grief that threatened to drown me.And then, there was only me. Nanapush, the last of his line, an elder at fifty, my hair prematurely streaked with the white of winter. I led the last buffalo hunt, the thundering hooves echoing through the vast emptiness of the plains. I saw the last bear fall. I trapped the last beaver with a mature pelt. I felled the last old birch tree, its leaves whispering secrets to the wind.But even in the face of such overwhelming loss, I found the strength to resist. I saved the last of the Pillager family, their faces etched with the same sorrow that mirrored my own. I refused to sign the government papers, those insidious documents that would erase us, make us invisible in our own land.

Bad-ass salcedense, short hair, ass is the stuff of rumors. Throw a brick at a homeboy for looking at her funny. And this salcedense had to throw a couple bricks in her day. But she found out, and it’s bad. Fifty women bad, and for six years. Plus you knew. Of course you fucking knew. She told you, you chancla-headed fuck, you slip once and she’s out. She walks by herself and you watch her. Well, you try not to. You walk up and say baby, baby, grab her ass, make a kiss like you mean it. But she’s cooked. She’s fried. She wants nothing to do with your black ass. What I’m sayin is negro, you’ve fucked up bad. On the way to the hotel, you see this couple, right? H-O-N-E-Y-M-O-O-N. Eyes like the ocean, can’t keep off each other. Like he’d throw his ass into Mordor before he hurt his bae. Like this is what it’s supposed to be. I don’t gotta tell you how that makes you feel. When you get back, she starts crying. Making fists, the whole thing. She says you’re not no fucking man. Her daddy warned her about you. But he’s fuckin dead.
written_by_MFA028.Excerpt2: You should have known better. You should have remembered her face that night in Salcedo, when she told you—plain as day, no flourish, no smile—that if you ever cheated, she’d be gone. Pero no, you had to be that dude. Fifty women, six years. A whole-ass archive of receipts, every click, every email, every I-miss-you-ma written out like a confession just waiting for her to find. And she did. You came home that night and there she was, sitting on the couch, laptop on her knees, the kind of quiet that makes your bones go soft. You tried to talk, to explain—mi amor, please—but she cut you off with a look. Not screaming, not throwing things, not even crying, just staring at you, eyes dark as road tar, full of something you couldn't name yet but would come to know real well: the slow, suffocating unravel. And for some stupid reason, she stayed. Maybe because you had history, because you were there when her father died, because you let her practice cross-examining you for the bar. Because habit is its own kind of handcuff. So y’all tried. A few months, a few trips, trying to patch up something that was already dust. The D.R., Mexico, New Zealand—her dream trip, the one she’d been talking about since The Piano. You watched her walk down that beach alone, black sand, gray sky, the Pacific pulling at her feet like it wanted her too. When you reached for her hand, she flinched, like touching you might burn. The drive back was long. Silent. Until you passed some couple, arms locked, glowing like they’d never known heartbreak. You knew she saw them too. That night in the hotel, when she curled away from you, when she finally let the tears come, you lay beside her, knowing you’d already lost, knowing it was over, knowing it had been over since the moment she clicked that first email.

written_by_MFA028.Original: Your girl catches you cheating. (Well, actually she’s your fiancée, but hey, in a bit it so won’t matter.) She could have caught you with one sucia, she could have caught you with two, but because you’re a totally batshit cuero who never empties his e-mail trash can, she caught you with fifty! Sure, over a six-year period, but still. Fifty fucking girls? God damn! Maybe if you’d been engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita you could have survived it—but you’re not engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita. Your girl is a bad-ass salcedense who doesn’t believe in open anything; in fact, the one thing she warned you about, that she swore she would never forgive, was cheating. I’ll put a machete in you, she promised. And, of course, you swore you wouldn’t do it. You swore you wouldn’t. You swore you wouldn’t.And you did.She’ll stick around for a few months because you been together a long, long time. Because you’ve gone through so much together—her father’s death, your tenure madness, her bar exam (passed on the third attempt). And because love, real love, is not so easily shed. Over a tortured six-month period you fly together to the D.R., to Mexico (for the funeral of a friend), to New Zealand. You walk the beach where they filmed “The Piano,” something she’s always wanted to do, and now, in penitent desperation, you give it to her. She is immensely sad on that beach and she walks up and down the shining sand alone, her bare feet in the freezing water, and when you try to hug her she says, Don’t. She stares at the rocks jutting out of the water, the wind carrying her hair straight back. On the ride out to the hotel, up through those wild steeps, you pick up a pair of hitchhikers, a couple so giddy with love that you almost throw them out of the car. She says nothing. Later, in the hotel, she cries.

But she found out, and it’s bad. Fifty women bad, and for six years. Plus you knew. Of course you fucking knew. She told you, you chancla-headed fuck, you slip once and she’s out. Well, cue the platano peel, because homie, you slipped. Fifty fucking girls. Once a year that’s half a siglo. She’s pissed, but it’s weird. Actually, you find out it’s chill. At least for a few months. Steady as it goes. Knew her too long, it turns out, through the job search, the bar, her father’s entierro. Can’t let go of a good thing. Even when she knows it’s bad. You kick off like that’ll help and hit the DR, CDM, fucking New Zealand. In NZ, fifty miles from Baggins Way, she says she dreamed this beach. Says it was in The Piano. She walks by herself and you watch her. Well, you try not to. You walk up and say baby, baby, grab her ass, make a kiss like you mean it. But she’s cooked. She’s fried. She wants nothing to do with your black ass. What I’m sayin is negro, you’ve fucked up bad. On the way to the hotel, you see this couple, right? H-O-N-E-Y-M-O-O-N. Eyes like the ocean, can’t keep off each other. Like he’d throw his ass into Mordor before he hurt his bae. Like this is what it’s supposed to be. I don’t gotta tell you how that makes you feel. When you get back, she starts crying. Making fists, the whole thing. She says you’re not no fucking man. Her daddy warned her about you. But he’s fuckin dead.
written_by_MFA028.Excerpt2: You should have known better. You should have remembered her face that night in Salcedo, when she told you—plain as day, no flourish, no smile—that if you ever cheated, she’d be gone. Pero no, you had to be that dude. Fifty women, six years. A whole-ass archive of receipts, every click, every email, every I-miss-you-ma written out like a confession just waiting for her to find. And she did. You came home that night and there she was, sitting on the couch, laptop on her knees, the kind of quiet that makes your bones go soft. You tried to talk, to explain—mi amor, please—but she cut you off with a look. Not screaming, not throwing things, not even crying, just staring at you, eyes dark as road tar, full of something you couldn't name yet but would come to know real well: the slow, suffocating unravel. And for some stupid reason, she stayed. Maybe because you had history, because you were there when her father died, because you let her practice cross-examining you for the bar. Because habit is its own kind of handcuff. So y’all tried. A few months, a few trips, trying to patch up something that was already dust. The D.R., Mexico, New Zealand—her dream trip, the one she’d been talking about since The Piano. You watched her walk down that beach alone, black sand, gray sky, the Pacific pulling at her feet like it wanted her too. When you reached for her hand, she flinched, like touching you might burn. The drive back was long. Silent. Until you passed some couple, arms locked, glowing like they’d never known heartbreak. You knew she saw them too. That night in the hotel, when she curled away from you, when she finally let the tears come, you lay beside her, knowing you’d already lost, knowing it was over, knowing it had been over since the moment she clicked that first email.

written_by_MFA028.Original: Your girl catches you cheating. (Well, actually she’s your fiancée, but hey, in a bit it so won’t matter.) She could have caught you with one sucia, she could have caught you with two, but because you’re a totally batshit cuero who never empties his e-mail trash can, she caught you with fifty! Sure, over a six-year period, but still. Fifty fucking girls? God damn! Maybe if you’d been engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita you could have survived it—but you’re not engaged to a super-open-minded blanquita. Your girl is a bad-ass salcedense who doesn’t believe in open anything; in fact, the one thing she warned you about, that she swore she would never forgive, was cheating. I’ll put a machete in you, she promised. And, of course, you swore you wouldn’t do it. You swore you wouldn’t. You swore you wouldn’t.And you did.She’ll stick around for a few months because you been together a long, long time. Because you’ve gone through so much together—her father’s death, your tenure madness, her bar exam (passed on the third attempt). And because love, real love, is not so easily shed. Over a tortured six-month period you fly together to the D.R., to Mexico (for the funeral of a friend), to New Zealand. You walk the beach where they filmed “The Piano,” something she’s always wanted to do, and now, in penitent desperation, you give it to her. She is immensely sad on that beach and she walks up and down the shining sand alone, her bare feet in the freezing water, and when you try to hug her she says, Don’t. She stares at the rocks jutting out of the water, the wind carrying her hair straight back. On the ride out to the hotel, up through those wild steeps, you pick up a pair of hitchhikers, a couple so giddy with love that you almost throw them out of the car. She says nothing. Later, in the hotel, she cries.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: How this went was, you go about your post-cheating days with your bad-ass  from Salcedo, unworried about what you’d done, how you’d done it, who you’d done it with, and for a good long while the two of you are what you might call happy. You were happy. Then out of nowhere you one day walk in on her reading your emails. The emails. Upwards of fifty women over six years she discovered, and for some reason you thought you had messaged more. No significó nada, you said, it was foolish, you said, and what she’d said and told you over and over again over the years, she said again: that cheating was unforgivable. Prohibida. Grounds to shout, Pack your shit and go. Just go. But she stayed. Maybe it was her father’s death or your failures, all those failures, that she stayed with you through, maybe it was her success in passing the bar, but in the end what bound the two of you, why she stayed as long as she did––who the hell knows. After the emails you made an attempt to make good. Travelled with her everywhere from the Dominican Republic, Mexico, to New Zealand. New Zealand. There on the beach she had long dreamed of visiting, that one from The Piano, and that you thought bringing her to would fix everything, she walked on ahead, and you walked in her smaller footsteps in the sand. Mi amor, you said. Walk by my side. You are so far away. Please, she said. Just leave me alone. On the ride home, the two of you shared a cab with a laughing couple tumbling over one another, besar, holding each other’s faces in their hands, and you wanted to die. Back in the hotel room she broke down for good. You never saw such tears, never felt that shame you felt then for having caused them. No more, she said to you. No mas.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: You fucked up, straight up. No way to pretty it up with words your fancy-ass MFA taught you—fifty mujeres over six years, all those emails stacked up like bodies, like evidence in one of them CSI episodes your girl used to love watching with you on the couch, back when she thought you were something else, something better, something more than just another Dominican tigre con su vaina. Your bad-ass salcedense who survived the Bar exam like a warrior, who held your hand through all your broke-ass teaching days eating mangú for dinner three times a week, who cried against your shoulder when her pops passed—she warned your ass about cheating, told you straight up how her old man did her mom dirty, how that shit was unforgivable, how it lived in her bones like a curse. But you did it anyway, thinking you were too smooth to get caught, thinking them delete buttons would save your ass forever, thinking you had some special blessing from Ochún herself. Then comes the fucking emails, each one like a bullet, like them killing blows they teach you about in them martial arts movies. Your girl, she give you them three extra months though—three months of plane rides and hotel rooms, three months of you watching her turn into somebody else, somebody with eyes that looked right through you like you was a ghost. In New Zealand, watching her walking that beach she dreamed about since forever, since that movie with the piano, you knew it was done. She wouldn't let you touch her, wouldn't let you near. Y'all drove past some happy-ass couple all wrapped up in each other and the silence in that rental car could've drowned a thousand islands. Later in the hotel room, when she finally broke down, tears coming like they'd never stop, you knew: some things you break, they don't never get fixed. Some betrayals cut too deep for even the ocean to wash away.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt 2 seemed closer to the original.  I felt that excerpt 1 had the man seem almost dismissive of what he had done.  Excerpt 2, he recognized the errors he had made, and like the original, he saw how this has hurt the girl.  He also listed all the things that they had both been through together, although this was also briefly mentioned in excerpt 1, it seemed more insignificant in that excerpt.  Overall, I felt excerpt 2 was much closer.

written_by_MFA006.Excerpt1: She was the one who said it, mi amor. "If you cheat on me, it's over."  And there it was, laid bare in her inbox: six years, fifty women, a betrayal that stretched back to the very beginning. Maybe it was the years woven together, the memories of her father's funeral, the echo of your own failures, the triumph of her passing the bar.  You clung to those shared moments like a life raft in a sea of your own making.You tried to mend the shattered pieces with trips – the Dominican Republic, Mexico, even the beach in New Zealand she'd dreamed of since "The Piano."  But on that windswept shore, her sadness was a tangible thing, a wall you couldn't breach.  She walked alone, the sand stretching out like a metaphor for the distance between you.In the rental car, a giddy couple, their love a bright, painful contrast, drove past, and you saw the reflection of your guilt in her eyes.  Later, in the hotel room, the tears came, a torrent that mirrored the storm inside you.  You knew then that some things, once broken, can never be truly fixed.The weight of your betrayal pressed down on you, a suffocating blanket of remorse. You remembered her fierce independence, her unwavering loyalty, the way she could light up a room with her smile.  And you had dimmed that light, extinguished it with your own selfishness.You had broken the trust that had been the foundation of your relationship, and the cracks were irreparable.  The guilt gnawed at you, a constant reminder of the pain you had caused.  You had betrayed the woman you loved, and the consequences were devastating.
written_by_MFA006.Excerpt2: You’ve been cheating on your fiance, a bad-ass salcedense from the DR who by all accounts doesn’t deserve it. Why? Because you’re some sort of idiot hijo de cuero, but you knew that about yourself long before she found the emails. Fifty women jammed into six years–it’s almost impressive, when you think about it. Or maybe it’s impressive when you don’t think about it too much. Your chiquita certainly doesn’t think it is–One rule, she spits at you through the expletives, one fucking rule. If you cheated on her, she was outta there. Except she wasn’t outta there–she lingers for a few months, like you are a cough she can’t quite shake. You’ve been through so much together–the death of her father, all your job problems, her rivalry and eventual defeat of the bar exam. You have history, and history doesn’t just go away. Someone has to erase it out of the books, and you sure as hell aren’t going to be the one to do it. And so you jet around the world to prove your love–the Dominican Republic, Mexico, all the way to fucking New Zealand where, on the beach from the movie The Piano, a place she’s always dreamed of going, she walks alone and barefoot on the sand in front of you, her sandals dangling from her fingers. You try to touch those fingers, her waist, her shoulder, but each time she pushes you away with a hiss, the wind lashing her long dark hair against her face, turning her into someone you don’t recognize. To make matters worse, you come across a couple while out for a ride together later that day, so all over each other and stupidly in love that it makes you question why you are here, why she is here, why you were both even born. She watches their love with a thin-lipped, dead-eyed expression. It is only later, in the privacy of your hotel room, that she cries.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I suppose there's nothing quite like discovering your husband is having an affair when you're seven months pregnant. The timing is exquisite, really – your body has morphed into something between a beach ball and a whale, your ankles have disappeared into puffy clouds, and you're crying at paper towel commercials. And then there's Thelma Rice, with her perfect figure and that irritating habit of inscribing children's books with suggestive little notes, as if marking her territory like some literary-minded cat. I tried making jokes about it, naturally. That's what I do – turn tragedy into comedy, preferably before dessert. But somehow, quipping about being undatable while sporting a seven-month baby bump didn't land quite the way I'd hoped. The laughter that followed had that distinct pitch of pity, the kind that makes you wish you could crawl into a hole, except you can't because, well, pregnant. So here I am in my father's apartment in New York, surrounded by furniture that looks like it was rejected from a 1950s detective novel, crying into tissues and wondering how my life turned into this particularly unfunny sitcom. Sam, my toddler, doesn't understand why Mommy keeps staring out windows like she's auditioning for a Tennessee Williams play. The truth is, betrayal is a peculiar thing – it doesn't just break your heart, it retrospectively ruins perfectly good memories. Like how that book of children's songs, the one with Thelma's nauseating inscription, has now tainted every lullaby I've ever sung to Sam. The whole thing would be almost comedic if it weren't so tragically predictable – the younger woman, the secret notes, the pregnant wife. It's like someone took every cliché about infidelity and decided to stage it in my living room, with me as the unwitting star of this domestic drama. At least I can say this: nothing makes you reevaluate your life choices quite like finding your husband's mistress's handwriting in your child's bedtime stories.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: When I started living at my father's place in New York I couldn't stop crying. The weeping would be long and drawn out, dramatic affairs, and through my vision blurred with tears I would see my father's awful furniture, everything wooden and overly embellished, and the ugliness of the space I was in would only make me cry more. Often as I cried, I would think about how he told me about Thelma Rice. What made it all the more horrible was how utterly mundane it was. I was looking through Sam's little bookshelf for something to sing him to sleep. I was on autopilot, already thinking about what I would do after Sam fell asleep. I was not scrounging through my husband's letters, or stalking Thelma on the streets. I just pulled a book at random and flipped it open to the first page and there, in the most flowery, idiotic handwriting, a note: for the man with a mouth do a lot more than singing, love, Thelma. Disgusting, especially because it was a children's book, one that was on my son's bookshelf. Just thinking about her handwriting could make me cry for twenty minutes. To make myself feel better I would think about how ugly she was. Not very women's lib, I know, but she was my husband's mistress. And she was ugly, it was a fact. She had these bulging eyes and a veiny neck and nothing about her face was symmetrical. I would think about that and stop crying and then think about that note and the whole cycle would start all over again. In public, I put on a brave face. One night I went to dinner and at one point I said, no one wants to take out a lady who's seven months pregnant, she'll eat twice as much! It's not very funny when I write it down. When I said it, though, people laughed. Although, now I wonder if they were laughing because it was funny, or because they pitied me. I was certainly quite pitiable.

written_by_MFA001.Original: The first day I did not think it was funny. I didn’t think it was funny the third day either, but I managed to make a little joke about it. “The most unfair thing about this whole business,” I said, “is that I can’t even date.” Well, you had to be there, as they say, because when I put it down on paper it doesn’t sound funny. But what made it funny (trust me) is the word “date,” which when you say it out loud at the end of a sentence has a wonderful teenage quality, and since I am not a teenager (okay, I’m thirty-eight), and since the reason I was hardly in a position to date on first learning that my second husband had taken a lover was that I was seven months pregnant, I got a laugh on it, though for all I know my group was only laughing because they were trying to cheer me up. I needed cheering up. I was in New York, staying in my father’s apartment, I was crying most of the time, and every time I stopped crying I had to look at my father’s incredibly depressing walnut furniture and slate-gray lamps, which made me start crying again.I had gotten on the shuttle to New York a few hours after discovering the affair, which I learned about from a really disgusting inscription to my husband in a book of children’s songs she had given him. Children’s songs. “Now you can sing these songs to Sam” was part of the disgusting inscription, and I can’t begin to tell you how it sent me up the wall, the idea of my two-year-old child, my baby, involved in some dopey inscriptive way in this affair between my husband, a fairly short person, and Thelma Rice, a fairly tall person with a neck as long as an arm and a nose as long as a thumb and you should see her legs, never mind her feet, which are sort of splayed.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: When I started living at my father's place in New York I couldn't stop crying. The weeping would be long and drawn out, dramatic affairs, and through my vision blurred with tears I would see my father's awful furniture, everything wooden and overly embellished, and the ugliness of the space I was in would only make me cry more. Often as I cried, I would think about how he told me about Thelma Rice. What made it all the more horrible was how utterly mundane it was. I was looking through Sam's little bookshelf for something to sing him to sleep. I was on autopilot, already thinking about what I would do after Sam fell asleep. I was not scrounging through my husband's letters, or stalking Thelma on the streets. I just pulled a book at random and flipped it open to the first page and there, in the most flowery, idiotic handwriting, a note: for the man with a mouth do a lot more than singing, love, Thelma. Disgusting, especially because it was a children's book, one that was on my son's bookshelf. Just thinking about her handwriting could make me cry for twenty minutes. To make myself feel better I would think about how ugly she was. Not very women's lib, I know, but she was my husband's mistress. And she was ugly, it was a fact. She had these bulging eyes and a veiny neck and nothing about her face was symmetrical. I would think about that and stop crying and then think about that note and the whole cycle would start all over again. In public, I put on a brave face. written_by_MFA025.Excerpt1: I'm seven months pregnant, and Thelma Rice is sleeping with my husband, so I'm sleeping with no one. Thelma Rice does not understand the struggle of dating inherent to being a 38-year-old pregnant woman, though maybe one day she will! It's a thought I comfort myself with, and it makes me laugh. I miss laughing. I don't think the joke would make anyone so much as giggle, not when said out loud and especially not when I look at it written on paper. It's just pathetic, I can hear the awkward chuckles now, the kind clusters of people make when trying to be sympathetic, or to prevent tears. I'm crying now, but I'm pregnant so it's to be expected. My life has turned quite ugly, filled with droll tragedy and my father's hideous furniture. It's good of him to let me stay in his New York apartment, but the place is so grey and miserable that it makes me grey and miserable. The lights in all the lamps flicker, and the few windows face a brick wall, so the apartment resembles a cave more than a home. It's fitting, I suppose. A nice cave, buried deep in the building, where I can retreat to lick my wounds. If my father's apartment had looked like a real home, I would have been reminded of what I lost. Ever since I found that crude inscription, in a book of children's songs of all places, I've had no home. Thelma Rice, with her endless entitlements, dragged Sam into this too, scrawling out her wantonness on the pages of a book suited for a small child, not a grown man. I can just see her now, her short and stubby fingers clutching at the pen as she tried to rhyme words together into her approximation of a clever lyric. I imagine her chewing her pen with her crooked teeth and smudging her lurid lipstick down her chin. It makes me feel...better, to think of her this way. Like I can see her truest self.
written_by_MFA025.Excerpt2: I was seven months pregnant and couldn’t button my coat, which was how I ended up waddling into the room where my soon-to-be ex-husband Mark was laughing with his friends about something—or more likely, nothing—completely inconsequential. That’s when I said it. I said, “It’s funny, you know, Mark’s not available for affairs right now because he’s pregnant with me.” And they laughed. Oh, they laughed all right, but it wasn’t the right kind of laugh. It was that awkward, pitying chuckle that makes you realize your joke is less of a joke and more of a moment everyone wishes they weren’t part of. I felt like a stand-up comic bombing on open-mic night, only instead of hecklers, I had my own humiliation.That night, after crying for the hundredth time that week, I tried to find some solace in my father’s apartment, which was a masterpiece of misery. His brown corduroy couch sagged like it had given up on life, and every corner of the room was decorated in a way that screamed, “I haven’t been redecorated since Nixon resigned.” It was the kind of place that made sadness feel inevitable. And there I was, crying over Mark, who I now knew had been sneaking around with a woman named Thelma Rice—a name so cloyingly sweet it felt like it belonged on a box of cookies, not the antagonist of my life.The worst part? The discovery. A children’s songbook. A little gift from Thelma to Mark, inscribed with some nauseating drivel like, “For all the songs you’ll sing.” Songs he’d apparently been singing for her while our toddler, Sam, sang solo in his crib. I couldn’t believe the audacity, the gall, the absolute polyester pantsuit-ness of it all. And Thelma herself! I mean, have you seen Thelma? She looked like she spent her weekends alphabetizing her collection of decorative soaps. Yet there I was, a hormonal, bloated mess, crying into a pillow that smelled like mothballs. It was unbearable. And yet, somehow, it was also just another Tuesday.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Picture this: me, seven months pregnant, sprawled on the couch in my father's dreary New York apartment, tears streaming down my face. The backdrop? A symphony of beige, a decor so monotonous it could make a nun scream. The cause of this melodramatic scene? My second husband, Mark had just pulled a classic man move. He'd fallen in love with another woman. Now, I'd always been the type to handle heartbreak with a dash of humor. So, when I told my friends, "I'm not going to be able to date for a while because I'm seven months pregnant," I expected a chuckle. But the joke fell flat, and the silence was deafening. Maybe it was the delivery, the sheer absurdity of the situation. Whatever the reason, the only response I got was a smattering of pitying laughter. Back in my father's apartment, surrounded by furniture that seemed to mock my misery, I couldn't help but feel like a character in a bad sitcom. The beige walls, the lumpy couch, the faded floral wallpaper – it was all a recipe for despair. And then there was the discovery. The inscription in the book of children's songs, a gift from Thelma Rice to my husband. "To Mark, with love, from the other woman." It was like a punch to the gut, my husband's betrayal. Thelma Rice. The name echoed in my mind, a caricature of a woman with a voice like nails on a chalkboard and legs that went on for days. I pictured her, all blonde hair and fake smiles, and my anger burned even brighter. But amidst the tears and the anger, there was a flicker of determination. I wouldn't let this break me. I would pick myself up, dust myself off, and start over. I would find a way to be happy, even if it meant navigating the world of dating with a baby on my hip. After all, I was a woman, and women are resilient. We bend, we don't break. We fall, we get back up. We cry, we laugh. We love, we lose, we love again. And through it all, we find a way to keep going.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Hill House waited, its brooding silence pressing against the walls like a living thing, holding darkness within its brick and timber bones as it had for eighty years. Through its malevolent windows, it watched Dr. John Montague approach, his academic credentials clutched like a shield before him, as though his doctor of philosophy might protect him from whatever dwelled in the house's shadowed corners. He came with his leather briefcase and carefully organized notes, believing that science could explain away the whispers in empty rooms, the footsteps that followed no feet, the cold spots that lingered like breath on glass. The locals spoke of Hill House only in whispers, their eyes sliding away when they mentioned its name, but Dr. Montague saw only the promise of scholarly recognition, of footnotes and bibliographies and peer reviews. He paid his considerable rent to the Sanderson family without hesitation, never noticing how quickly they pocketed the money, as though it might carry some taint of the house itself. In his hotel room, preparing for his first night in Hill House, he arranged his instruments with precise care - thermometers, cameras, tape recorders - tools of rationality to measure the irrational. He did not yet understand that Hill House had been waiting for him, had perhaps called to him through all his years of searching, and that his arrival was merely the beginning of what the house had planned, as it stood against its hills, patient and hungry, its doors sensibly shut against the approaching night.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: At the end of the road, Hill House stood alone with jaws full of silence. Its windows stared unblinkingly. Its long shadow loomed like the hood of a cobra. The tight and winding corridors were not unlike veins, but rather than blood and life, all that ran through them was darkness. Hill House was not sane. Rather, it was a place where reality wobbled and warped into something unrecognizable. And now Dr. John Montague had come to cross the threshold. A Doctor of Philosophy in anthropology, Montague had dedicated his career to the study of supernatural phenomena. He was a reasonable sort of man who insisted on his own soundness of mind. He was stubborn and dogged in his pursuits, but always shuffled shyly around the fringes of academia, insecure about the reputation he had built for himself. He clung to his title of “doctor” with ferocious pride and brandished it like a badge at the slightest hint of skepticism from his colleagues. His ultimate goal had always been to find a genuine haunted house: a place that would offer up evidence so absolute that there could be no room for argument. It was a tumultuous and often disappointing journey that had, at last, led him to Hill House. After several fruitless grant applications for his proposed experiment on psychic disturbances, Montague decided to make a personal investment in the project and rent Hill House using his own savings. The cost was significant, but so was Montague’s belief that it was well worth the price.

written_by_MFA025.Original: No live organism can continue for long to exist sanely under conditions of absolute reality; even larks and katydids are supposed, by some, to dream. Hill House, not sane, stood by itself against its hills, holding darkness within; it had stood so for eighty years and might stand for eighty more. Within, walls continued upright, bricks met neatly, floors were firm, and doors were sensibly shut; silence lay steadily against the wood and stone of Hill House, and whatever walked there, walked alone. Dr John Montague was a doctor of philosophy; he had taken his degree in anthropology, feeling obscurely that in this field he might come closest to his true vocation, the analysis of supernatural manifestations. He was scrupulous about the use of his title because, his investigations being so utterly unscientific, he hoped to borrow an air of respectability, even scholarly authority, from his education. It had cost him a good deal, in money and pride, since he was not a begging man, to rent Hill House for three months, but he expected absolutely to be compensated for his pains by the sensation following upon the publication of his definitive work on the causes and effects of psychic disturbances in a house commonly known as ‘haunted.’ He had been looking for an honestly haunted house all his life. When he heard of Hill House he had been at first doubtful, then hopeful, then indefatigable; he was not the man to let go of Hill House once he had found it.
